text:
Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador were in limbo Wednesday as a deadline neared for the Trump administration to decide if they should end, as they have for hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries.

The Temporary Protected Status designation expired Wednesday but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens. If the Department of Homeland Security takes no action, protections are automatically extended for six months. This rare reprieve happened in May, when the protections were automatically extended to about 11,000 Lebanese, allowing them to stay and work in the U.S. for another 180 days.

READ MORE: We may finally know what makes a country 'unsafe' for TPS deportations: a bromance with Trump

DHS said in a statement Wednesday that it will announce a decision on El Salvador "at the appropriate time" and that protections would remain in place until then.

About 200,000 people from El Salvador have lived in the U.S. since 2001 under TPS, which allows people already in the country to remain with work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months, if the secretary of homeland security determines conditions are unsafe for return. They are eligible for work permits.

In Florida, an estimated 45,000 Salvadorans are at risk of losing the legal protections and work authorization they have relied on for years, Florida Immigrant Coalition Executive Director Tessa Petit said in a statement.

"These are Florida workers, parents, homeowners, business owners, students, neighbors, and community members who have spent decades putting down roots in the only country many of them have known as home," she said. "The Trump administration must immediately extend TPS for El Salvador and stop treating longtime members of our communities as disposable."

Petit also wants Congress to approve legislation that would create a permanent pathway to legal status for all TPS holders and others who have spent decades living, working, and contributing to the U.S.

“We have seen what happens when this administration strips communities of their protections: families are thrown into uncertainty, workers lose their livelihoods, and people who have spent decades building lives in America suddenly find themselves targeted for deportation," she said. "Salvadorans deserve permanent stability, dignity, and a pathway to citizenship.”

Trump administration has ended protections for more than a dozen countries

During President Donald Trump's second term, Homeland Security has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. In addition to El Salvador, only people from three other countries remain protected with termination dates in October for Ukraine and Sudan, and November for Lebanon.

The Trump administration obtained a major victory in June when the Supreme Court ruled that Homeland Security acted within its authority by ending TPS for about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The impact of the decision extends far beyond Haitians and Syrians, potentially affecting nearly 1.3 million people from 17 countries on TPS.

Tom Homan, Trump's "border czar" who has advocated for ending TPS, said Tuesday that the decision rests with the Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"If it expires, it's up to the secretary," Homan said when asked about TPS. "Temporary protected status means temporary. Let's face it, El Salvador is a much safer country than it's ever been now with a new president up there."

Congress created temporary protections in 1990

TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It was granted to El Salvador following two devastating 2001 earthquakes that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden extended TPS for El Salvador for 18 months to Sept. 9, 2026.

El Salvador has been a Trump ally

Once one of the most violent places in the world, El Salvador has become one of the safest countries in the Americas since Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele ordered mass arrests in 2022. In April 2025, the State Department upgraded El Salvador's travel advisory to its highest level, citing a drop in violent crimes and murders.

Bukele has been an ally of Trump's policy of mass deportations and El Salvador was one of the first countries to receive deportees and held them at a mega prison also known as CECOT.

Human rights groups and advocates have denounced mass and arbitrary arrests, torture, and disappearances in the Central American nation's prison system.

Trump received Bukele at the White House in April 2025 and invited him to participate in a military coalition to fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. In July 2026, Trump and Bukele met again in Washington, the Salvadoran president has not publicly stated whether he requested an extension of TPS from the Trump administration.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Bukele asked Trump to extend TPS. It remained because there were lawsuits.

Salvadorans in the U.S. sent $9.9 billion in remittances to El Salvador last year, representing 24% of the country's gross domestic product, according to El Salvador's central bank.

This story has been corrected to show that TPS has ended for people from 13 countries during Trump's second term, not 14.

description:

Three do not list people who are in ICE custody.

text:
The number of federal immigration detainees in Kentucky jails is growing dramatically, but the public knows less and less about them, including whether or not they have criminal records, according to new reports on federal efforts to deport more people.

Some information on U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainees in Kentucky jails is hard to find, a new report from the League of Women Voters of Kentucky says.

The League’s analysis found a few online rosters at Kentucky jails that house federal immigration detainees are unclear on the local crimes charged or status of the detainee. Three do not list people who are in ICE custody.

“Kentucky jails belong to us, the people of Kentucky, so we should know how immigrants are being treated,” wrote League President Jennifer Jackson in a letter about the report. “The people held there are human beings, so Kentuckians should insist on their human rights.”

The League, a group that has been tracking ICE data statewide for a few months, also said in the latest analysis a dozen jails across Kentucky are being paid to house ICE detainees and most do not have a criminal conviction; more than 60 jails in the state have voluntarily placed ICE holds on people arrested locally; most jails that provide ICE custody are overcrowded because of federal roles; and two jails and more than 50 law enforcement agencies have partnerships with ICE.

In November, about 12 local police agencies and three jails in Kentucky had partnerships with ICE under 287(g) agreements. Two bills were filed in the 2026 legislative session to direct Kentucky State Police or local law enforcement agencies to enter such ICE agreements, but they did not get floor votes.

According to data from Relevant Research, Kentucky jails are housing about 1,200 people for ICE as of July.

Last week, progressive think tank Kentucky Center for Economic Policy said in an analysis that arrests through the 287(g) agreements have grown in recent months. In November 2025, there was one arrest in Kentucky through the agreement program. In July 2026, there were 70.

After its report, the League of Women Voters sent letters to leaders in counties with the greatest participation in ICE detention: Boone, Bourbon, Campbell, Christian, Daviess, Fayette, Grayson, Hopkins, Jefferson, Kenton, Laurel, Oldham and Woodford. Among the group’s requests were providing more fully transparent inmate lists and evidence about the treatment of detainees.

The full analysis said jails in Bourbon, Boone, Grayson, Hopkins, Laurel and Oldham counties include ICE detainees in their roster listings. Those people can be identified by an immigration charge listed or that the arresting officer or agency is listed as ICE, Immigration or the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The League said Campbell, Christian and Kenton counties do not list people there in ICE custody. Daviess County “appears to include people in ICE custody in its public roster, but not in a way that makes that status clear, as it may include people arrested by other federal agents, like U.S. Marshals. Fayette and Woodford counties’ “approaches are unclear to the League.”

Matt Mudd, a spokesperson for Louisville Mayor Craig Greenberg, said Louisville Metro Department of Corrections “does not house individuals who are in ICE custody,” but it does honor detainer requests from ICE to hold people 48 hours beyond their scheduled release for local offenses. The American Civil Liberties Union of Kentucky criticized the practice in August, saying it reviewed data that showed a nearly 300% increase in the average number of monthly detainer requests since the city’s policy change last year. Mudd said the cost for the holds “is negligible, and LMDC has not increased its budget to accommodate these holds.”

“To protect individual information, names of those subject to an ICE detainer are not released. Furthermore, information related to immigration detainers is subject to confidentiality requirements of federal law. The individual’s attorney may request additional information in person with proper identification while in person at LMDC,” Mudd added. “However, all local charges for individuals in custody at LMDC are available on a searchable public website that shows all allowable information.”

Mudd also referred to the state law governing conditions for jails, such as the requirement to provide inmates three nutritious meals a day to inmates and health and mental health evaluations and treatment.

ICE detention in Kentucky has made headlines in recent months. U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey, a Democrat who represents Kentucky’s 3rd Congressional District, joined two of his House colleagues to visit the Campbell County jail in July to review conditions for ICE detainees there.

“Trump and Republicans in Congress gave ICE billions in taxpayer money to target and terrorize immigrants in our communities,” McGarvey said in a Wednesday statement to the Kentucky Lantern. “At a bare minimum, we as taxpayers deserve transparency about where our neighbors are being taken and how they’re being treated.”

McGarvey joined family members of a Louisville woman, Sarafinah Bukirwa, who was detained by ICE in calling for better medical care for her while she was in the Grayson County Detention Center in July. Bukirwa, who has sickle cell anemia, was not getting all of her medications, her brother said, but the jailer denied the claim. Bukirwa was later released in August by a federal judge and after her family paid her bond.

title: New Lawsuit Challenges Trump-Vance Administration Plan to Send Armed ICE Officers Into ...
description:

Congress first enacted the prohibition against armed federal personnel at polling places in the final months of the Civil War to protect free and fair elections from federal interference.
Under federal law, armed federal personnel may not be ordered, brought, kept, or maintained at a place where an election is being held except when necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.
“The outcomes of elections define the future for all of us, and in America, voters should be able to cast their ballots without fear of intimidation by armed ICE officers at polling places.
“Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes.
text:
Washington, D.C. — The largest and oldest Latino civil rights membership organization in the United States, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), joined by Common Cause, a voting rights organization with nearly one million members, UnidosUS, the nation’s largest Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization with more than 300 affiliates nationwide, and the city and county of Denver, Colorado, filed a lawsuit today challenging the Trump-Vance administration’s policy of authorizing armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers to enter polling places to conduct immigration enforcement operations during the 2026 midterm elections.

The lawsuit challenges a policy confirmed and clarified by U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin on September 1, when he said that ICE officers could enter polling places to serve warrants or conduct other immigration and customs enforcement activity. The suit explains that the policy violates, among other laws, a federal law that has prohibited anyone from sending armed federal personnel to polling places for more than 150 years, and that the presence of armed officers is intimidating and threatening.

The lawsuit comes as early voting is set to begin in several states later this month and just weeks before Americans across the country cast their ballots in the November 3 midterm elections.

Congress first enacted the prohibition against armed federal personnel at polling places in the final months of the Civil War to protect free and fair elections from federal interference. Under federal law, armed federal personnel may not be ordered, brought, kept, or maintained at a place where an election is being held except when necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.

The complaint alleges that the administration’s new policy directly defies that prohibition by authorizing armed ICE officers to enter polling locations for ordinary immigration enforcement, including serving warrants and detaining people suspected of being unlawfully present in the United States. It also explains that the new policy violates the federal prohibition on arbitrary and capricious government action.

“The right to vote is foundational to our democracy and yet this administration continues in its endless attempts to weaken the very institutions it is entrusted to protect,” said Juan Proaño, CEO of LULAC. “The outcomes of elections define the future for all of us, and in America, voters should be able to cast their ballots without fear of intimidation by armed ICE officers at polling places. We are proud to join this litigation and fight to protect fundamental American freedom.”

“Putting armed officers in polling places is a tactic used by dictators, but we won’t be scared out of exercising our rights,” said Common Cause President & CEO Virginia Kase Solomón. “No American should ever have to walk past armed federal law enforcement just to cast a ballot, yet this administration has adopted a policy that allows exactly that. Everyday Americans refuse to be silenced by the administration’s continuous efforts to meddle with our elections. From taking legal action to stop this policy to leading the nation’s largest nonpartisan Election Protection program, Common Cause is fighting alongside voters to keep our elections free, fair, and accessible.”

“Sending armed ICE officers to polling places is not immigration enforcement — it is voter suppression, plain and simple,” said UnidosUS President & CEO Janet Murguía. “All Americans — including Latino voters — have a constitutional right to cast their ballot without fear of interrogation, detention, or family separation. This case is about protecting voters, preserving confidence in our elections, and ensuring that every eligible voter can participate free from intimidation.”

“The right to vote, and to do so without fear of intimidation, is fundamental to our democracy and to being an American,” said Denver Mayor Mike Johnston. “Stationing ICE agents near polling places is only meant to scare people and suppress votes. We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it.”

“Our right to vote is powerful and enshrined in the U.S. Constitution and U.S. Code,” said Denver Clerk and Recorder Paul López. “Denver is the vanguard of democracy, and with cast-iron certainty we will protect our free and fair elections from any and all attempts at federal intimidation and intrusion.”

The administration’s announcement follows months of actions that the lawsuit alleges constitute a policy of authorizing ICE agents to enter polling places, and which demonstrate an escalating effort to bring federal immigration enforcement into the electoral process. Earlier this year, senior administration officials publicly questioned why ICE officers should not be sent to polling stations, the U.S. Department of Justice removed longstanding guidance explaining restrictions on federal law enforcement activity at polling places, and ICE agents conducted enforcement actions at active polling sites in Texas and New York.

The lawsuit asks the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to declare the Polling Place Policy unlawful and block the administration from implementing it, including by prohibiting federal officers from going to polling places for purposes other than to repel armed enemies of the United States.

The case is League of United Latin American Citizens v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, et al., and the plaintiffs are represented by Democracy Forward and Public Rights Project.

text:
BURLINGTON — U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Congresswoman Lori Trahan conducted an unannounced visit to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Burlington Tuesday, their first surprise visit since ICE was compelled in court to allow such visits earlier this year.

In a joint statement released Wednesday, Trahan and Warren said they exercised their “constitutional responsibilities to conduct oversight” when they made the visit.

“Immigration attorneys and community advocates have shared deeply worrisome testimonies with our offices of individuals being detained by ICE for multiple days without access to adequate food, medical care, or sleeping conditions,” said the two members of Congress. “During the hour-long inspection of the Burlington facility, we walked through every part of the area in which people are detained. We witnessed over two dozen individuals held for processing, questioned ICE regarding our constituents’ concerns, and pressed for more humane treatment of those in custody.”

They said they would “continue showing up and fighting for transparency, decency, and accountability.”

The two join the ranks of other members of the Massachusetts congressional delegation to conduct a surprise visit to the facility since a court ruled earlier this year that ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, cannot prevent lawmakers from inspecting their facilities even without the visit being prearranged.

U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton made a similar visit last month, though he claimed to have been prevented from going beyond the facility’s lobby for about 30 minutes while his staff observed multiple vans leaving the property. Moulton had conducted an unannounced visit last year as well, before DHS began barring lawmakers from making surprise inspections. U.S. Sen. Ed Markey and U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern have made similar visits to the building this year.

The string of inspections and prearranged tours by lawmakers at the Burlington ICE building stems from reports of poor conditions for immigrant detainees inside the building, which has been a home to ICE operations since 2007. After President Donald Trump returned to office last year, the building became a focal point in the discourse over his immigration crackdown due to it being where most detained immigrants are brought first when they are arrested by ICE in Massachusetts.

It has also turned into the focus of local protests against ICE, with multiple groups holding weekly demonstrations going back to spring 2025 when the initial reports about the conditions inside began to emerge.

Those groups include Bearing Witness, which began protesting every Wednesday at the facility that April, and Justice 4 All Thursdays at ICE, which began its weekly demonstrations last September.

Both groups gathered at their usual spot on a grassy area across from the building’s entrance Wednesday for what they called “Hold ICE in Contempt Day,” which organizers said was aimed at urging judges in Massachusetts to “to hold ICE accountable for violations of court orders.”

Jared Berezin, one of the organizers of the Bearing Witness protests, and Todd Palmer, who started Justice 4 All Thursdays, stood together at the demonstration Wednesday and listed a number of incidents in American history where court orders were used against activists.

“When a judge orders ICE officials not to transfer an individual out of Massachusetts, but ICE defies that order and flies them out of [Hanscom Air Force Base] no one is held in contempt,” said Berezin. “When a judge orders ICE to produce a detainee’s arrest warrant and ICE refuses, no one is held in contempt. When a judge orders ICE to release someone but ICE officials keep them locked up anyway, no one is held in contempt. If any of us were to defy an order from a judge we would be fined and jailed, yet judges in Massachusetts and across the country treat ICE officials as if they are exempt from judicial authority.”

Palmer said he and Berezin are “calling for accountability in the courts.”

“We need our federal judges in Massachusetts and across this country to use their powers of contempt. We are not calling for judicial activism, we are calling for judicial action,” said Palmer.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed to no longer count immigrants without green cards in the 2030 census or ask about race and ethnicity, part of an overhaul that would redefine who counts as a U.S. resident in the eyes of the federal government.

The sweeping measures would upend a process that helps determine the allotment of congressional seats, billions of dollars in federal funding and policies to address systemic disparities.

The proposed regulation, published online on Wednesday, would not count noncitizens without green cards in the 2030 census, a significant departure from the process stipulated by the Constitution to occur every 10 years. Historically, the census has asked Americans about their race and ethnicity and counted all U.S. residents regardless of their immigration status.

The overhaul also would bar the U.S. census from asking Americans about their sexual orientation.

While the proposal is likely to face legal challenges, the changes would not only remove immigrants who lack legal status from the official population count used to determine congressional seats, but also immigrants who are in the United States legally and have yet to secure green cards or citizenship. As a result, areas with more immigrants, which tend to vote Democratic, could lose representation and federal funding.

The proposed overhaul, as well as removing questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation from the census, could have major implications for collecting the federal data used to inform antidiscrimination policies and civil rights protections.

“If we don’t have the data in order to see that there’s problems, then we’re sticking our heads in the sand,” said Kimball W. Brace, the president of Election Data Services, an organization working with Democratic and Republican local governments on census and election issues. “We won’t see it. We won’t get a feel for what’s happened.”

An overhaul of the census count would face significant hurdles. The 14th Amendment calls for “counting the whole number of persons in each state,” rather than just citizens. And the rule would take effect only after the 2028 presidential election, meaning a new administration could come in and reverse the changes. Under the U.S. Constitution, Congress is tasked with carrying out the census; however, it has delegated decisions on the census to the Commerce Department.

But some researchers said Trump’s decision to try to resurrect his first-term effort to reshape the census could create a chilling effect and reduce participation.

As part of the proposal released Wednesday, the administration said it was considering including a question in the census about the immigration status of participants, something civil rights groups have warned would deter immigrants with and without legal status from filling out the form out of fear of government retaliation.

“The Trump administration is trying to omit pieces of the population that they don’t feel are real Americans,” said William H. Frey, a demographer at the Brookings Institution. “And in many ways, pulling back some of the trends and important policies that came into effect since the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s.”

text:
The Trump administration no longer plans to convert massive warehouses in Georgia and Utah into immigration detention centers, recent court filings show – the latest reversals in an ambitious effort to reshape the nation’s detention system.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said it plans to turn over the warehouses it purchased to the General Services Administration, which could transfer them to another federal agency or sell them. A similar decision came this summer in Romulus, Michigan, where ICE also abandoned a project for a detention center and moved to dispose of the warehouse.

The price of the three properties combined exceeded $300 million.

In Social Circle, Georgia, the government paid $128 million for a million-square-foot warehouse it planned to turn into one of the largest detention centers in the United States, court records show. It would hold up to 10,000 immigrants and feature medical wings, recreation yards and a staff gun range. The Salt Lake City, Utah, warehouse cost $145.4 million – a premium for the area – and was also expected to hold as many as 10,000 people.

Earlier this year, ICE dropped proposals to convert two rural Pennsylvania warehouses and a three-building warehouse complex in Socorro, Texas, into detention centers.

But other projects remain in limbo. In Arizona, New Jersey and Maryland, local opposition led to lawsuits accusing the Department of Homeland Security of skipping required environmental reviews. The challenges have stalled all three detention center plans while the government studies their potential effects.

In a statement sent to USA TODAY, DHS said it remained “singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so.”

“DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners,” a DHS spokesperson wrote.

The reversals come as the Trump administration continues pursuing mass deportations and detaining immigrants in record numbers. ICE's detained population stood at 65,765 as of July 11, up 66% since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, according to USA TODAY’s tracker. The agency arrested nearly 51,000 people in August – its highest monthly total, according to DHS.

The warehouses were part of an attempt to build enough space for that expanding enforcement – and fundamentally change who owned the country’s immigration detention infrastructure.

For years, ICE has relied largely on a patchwork of county jails and facilities owned or operated by private prison companies. But under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, the agency began buying properties outright, seeking to place more of the detention system in the federal government’s hands.

In the first three months of 2026, ICE purchased nearly a dozen commercial warehouses for about $1 billion. Many of the buildings were cavernous fulfillment centers built during the pandemic-era online-shopping boom that were sitting empty near highways, airports and other transportation hubs.

An internal ICE planning document envisioned converting them into eight detention centers capable of holding between 7,000 and 10,000 people apiece, along with 16 smaller processing sites. The agency estimated the overhaul could cost $38.3 billion and raise its detention capacity to 92,600 beds.

After succeeding Noem, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin paused additional warehouse acquisitions while reviewing several of her initiatives. DHS’s inspector general is investigating whether the warehouse purchases were cost-effective and supported by operational needs.

The warehouse purchases, often completed before local officials or residents learned what ICE intended to do with the properties, also generated backlash across the country. Residents, including in Republican strongholds in Mississippi and Georgia, staged protests at the proposed sites and packed city council meetings to express outrage. Private developers in at least 11 communities withdrew from prospective deals with DHS.

The resistance often crossed party lines.

Most of Social Circle, a city of roughly 5,000 people, sits in Walton County, where nearly 73% of voters backed Trump in 2024. Residents and local officials fiercely opposed plans for a detention center that could have held about twice the city's population.

The city sued DHS and ICE in May, arguing the agencies were moving forward without properly evaluating the project’s effect on the environment or the city’s water, sewer and public safety systems.

When the government confirmed it was abandoning the project, Social Circle thanked the multitude of elected officials, community leaders and residents – as well as both Republican and Democratic lawmakers – who had opposed the plans.

“The engagement, input, and advocacy of so many individuals helped ensure that this community’s voice was heard,” the city wrote.

In its recent filing, the government asked a judge to put the case on hold for 90 days while it begins disposing of the property. The city had opposed the request, noting the federal government had not completed the process and could theoretically change course again.

But while some communities celebrated the canceled plans, others were left wondering whether the warehouses purchased in their neighborhoods would become detention sites.

In June, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said DHS had confirmed it would abandon its plans to use a 470,000-square-foot warehouse in the township of Roxbury as a detention site. A month later, ICE sent a letter to Roxbury's mayor saying the project is “still under review,” and that it would contact federal, state and local officials “once a determination is made.”

Mullin said DHS "will NEVER back down," and will keep the Roxbury site for a detention center.

In Surprise, Arizona, an environmental review is stalling the government's plans to hold up to 1,500 people in a warehouse across the street from Rinchem, a hazardous-chemical storage facility. In a lawsuit seeking to block the project, Arizona warned the chemical facility’s federally required safety plan never contemplated a nearby detention center, potentially putting detainees in harm’s way.

Brent Peak, co-chair of the local activist group Northwest Valley Indivisible, said Surprise should join the list of abandoned sites.

“Attorney General Kris Mayes has warned that the location of this detention facility risks a mass casualty event,” Peak said. “Yet ICE still plans to fill that warehouse with people who won’t be able to evacuate on their own in an emergency.”

text:
MIAMI -- Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador were in limbo Wednesday as a deadline neared for the Trump administration to decide if they should end, as it has done for hundreds of thousands from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries.

The Temporary Protected Status designation was set to expire Wednesday, but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens. If the Department of Homeland Security takes no action, protections are automatically extended for six months. This rare reprieve happened in May, when the protections were automatically extended to about 11,000 Lebanese, allowing them to stay and work in the U.S. for another 180 days.

DHS said in a statement Wednesday that it would announce a decision on El Salvador "at the appropriate time" and that protections would remain in place until then.

About 200,000 people from El Salvador have lived in the U.S. since 2001 under TPS, which allows people already in the country to remain with work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months, if the secretary of homeland security determines conditions are unsafe for return. They are eligible for work permits.

During President Donald Trump's second term, Homeland Security has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. In addition to El Salvador, only people from three other countries remain protected, with termination dates in October for Ukraine and Sudan, and November for Lebanon.

The Trump administration obtained a major victory when the Supreme Court ruled in June that Homeland Security acted within its authority by ending TPS for about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The impact of the decision extends far beyond Haitians and Syrians, potentially affecting nearly 1.3 million people from 17 countries on TPS.

Tom Homan, Trump's "border czar" who has advocated for ending TPS, said Tuesday that the decision rests with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"If it expires, it's up to the secretary," Homan said when asked about TPS. "Temporary protected status means temporary. Let's face it, El Salvador is a much safer country than it's ever been now with a new president up there."

TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.

It was granted to El Salvador following two devastating 2001 earthquakes that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden extended TPS for El Salvador for 18 months to Sept. 9, 2026.

The vast majority of Salvadoran TPS holders have children born in the U.S. Many have lost their jobs and fear being detained, separated from their American family members, and deported to a country they barely know.

El Salvador, once one of the most violent places in the world, has become one of the safest countries in the Americas since Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele ordered mass arrests in 2022. In April 2025, the State Department upgraded El Salvador's travel advisory to its highest level, citing a drop in violent crimes and murders.

Bukele has been an ally of Trump's policy of mass deportations and was one of the first countries to receive deportees and held them at a mega prison in El Salvador also known as CECOT.

Human rights groups and advocates have denounced mass and arbitrary arrests, torture and disappearances in the Central American nation's prison system.

Trump received Bukele at the White House in April 2025 and invited him to participate in a military coalition to fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. Less than a year later, in July 2026, Trump and Bukele met again in Washington. The Salvadoran president has not publicly stated whether he requested an extension of TPS from the Trump administration.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Bukele asked Trump to extend TPS. It remained because there were lawsuits.

Salvadorans in the U.S. sent $9.9 billion in remittances to El Salvador last year, representing 24% of the country's gross domestic product, according to El Salvador's central bank.

Information for this article was contributed by Rebecca Santana of The Associated Press.

text:
The woman, a DACA recipient who has lived in Florida since she was a child, was arrested without a warrant at Logan Airport in July.

Earlier this summer, a Florida woman who traveled to Massachusetts to volunteer at a Tall Ships event was detained by ICE at Logan Airport. She was held at the agency’s Burlington facility for 10 days before a federal judge ordered her release. The government recently asked that that judge dismiss the woman’s lawsuit against ICE because she had been released.

The judge ruled in favor of the woman again this week, refusing the government’s request and granting her more time to file an amended complaint.

The woman, 32-year-old Maria Rosales, is a DACA recipient who has been living in the U.S. since her family fled persecution in Colombia in 1998. DACA, established in 2012, protects people who arrived in the country as undocumented immigrants at a young age from deportation. As the Trump administration continues to pursue mass deportations, Rosales’ case shows how the federal government is increasingly targeting DACA protections.

Rosales’ case is also notable for her description of conditions within the Burlington ICE facility, which has been the subject of numerous complaints by detainees, immigration lawyers, and public officials in recent years.

Rosales, who leads a nonprofit in the Orlando area that provides young people with performing arts opportunities, was arrested without a warrant by ICE agents at Logan on July 10. She attended a Noah Kahan show at Fenway Park days earlier, and was at Logan to fly back to Florida. Federal officials cited a final order of removal that was issued in 2017, but Rosales contends that she had no knowledge of that order until she was detained, according to court documents.

A 2014 notice began removal proceedings against her, but it “failed to state either a date or a time for a removal hearing,” according to a July decision written by Judge Myong Joun. Furthermore, a warrant for her removal “appears to have been completed at Burlington” after Rosales was detained there, Joun wrote.

“If I knew I had a court date I would have attended. When I was arrested at the airport I was not given a warrant for my arrest. I believe the warrant was fabricated at the detention facility,” Rosales wrote in a sworn affidavit dated July 20.

The Burlington facility, ICE’s regional administrative headquarters, is not a full-fledged detainment facility. Federal officials have acknowledged that the building is not equipped to keep detainees for long periods of time, yet ICE’s surging activity has sometimes led to major bottlenecks there. As detainees and immigrant advocates continue to voice concerns about the conditions inside, protests are a regular occurrence.

In her affidavit, Rosales described her stay in the Burlington facility.

“Housing conditions have been tough,” she wrote. “There’s been days we have not showered, we’ve been in the same clothes for weeks, and the food is inedible. Some of the girls here refuse to eat because the food is vile and they couldn’t stomach it.”

Rosales went on to describe how access to showers, medications, food, and water were inconsistent and sometimes lacking. As many as eight women were forced to share a room at once, she wrote.

A renewal application for Rosales’ DACA status was filed in 2023, and is still pending. She is arguing that this pending application should prevent her removal. Rosales “anticipates arguing that [federal officials] are illegally not reviewing and determining her DACA status and unduly delaying that determination” in violation of multiple laws, according to court documents.

On July 20, lawyers from U.S. Attorney Leah Foley’s office filed an emergency motion seeking to transfer Rosales that day to a jail in New Hampshire, saying that Massachusetts lacks an appropriate facility for female ICE detainees.

Joun, however ruled that the government “failed to demonstrate compliance with the statutory and regulatory procedures governing [Rosales’] detention” and ordered her release.

In court documents filed last week, Foley’s office argued that Rosales’ legal action should be dismissed.

“Petitioner now seeks to file an amended complaint and other submissions in the attempt to morph a clear habeas action into a separate civil action,” they wrote.

Joun instead gave Rosales a Nov. 3 deadline to file an amended complaint.

Spending scarce Forest Service time and money to help immigration agents harass families who are simply trying to enjoy the outdoors is a disgrace.”

CONCORD, N.H. — Legal groups that secured a June Supreme Court victory in Trump v. Barbara on behalf of babies who would have been denied citizenship under a failed Trump executive order filed new motions in the case today. The latest filings aim to protect people subjected to the president’s new executive order, which was signed in early August and again targets birthright citizenship.

The American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus, and Democracy Defenders Fund successfully argued the Barbara case.

On Aug. 11, they asked a New Hampshire federal court, where the Barbara lawsuit was first filed, to make it unquestionably clear that the citizenship of babies covered by that class-action lawsuit is protected despite the new executive order. In their new filings, they are asking the court to certify a new class given the latest executive order.

In its June ruling, the Supreme Court confirmed that the Constitution’s Citizenship Clause puts “the question of citizenship ‘once and forever [to] rest.’”

The following are comments on today’s filings:

“The Trump administration continues to threaten birthright citizenship, even after its definitive loss at the Supreme Court,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project and lead counsel. “We will never stop fighting to protect this fundamental constitutional principle.”

“The Constitution and the Supreme Court were exceedingly clear: Citizenship is a constitutional right given to all children born in America and any attempt to restrict that right is illegal,” said Amia Trigg, deputy director of litigation at the Legal Defense Fund. “Regardless of race, color, or ancestry, birthright citizenship protects children that are born here. And the president's latest attempt to rescind that protection is just another example of an egregious overreach by the executive branch.”

“Trump’s executive order on birthright citizenship is yet another attack on the rule of law,” said Aarti Kohli, executive director of the Asian Law Caucus. “The Trump administration is ignoring the needs of everyday Americans to target immigrant communities. We’re fighting in court to ensure all our rights are protected and stop this administration’s unlawful attempt to ignore the Constitution and Supreme Court.”

“Our latest motions demand accountability for Trump’s dangerous policies,” said Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund. “This administration cannot unlawfully strip the rights of babies and ignore the Constitution in order to achieve its political goals. We won’t let that stand, and we’ll continue our fight in court.”

SangYeob Kim, director of the ACLU-NH Immigrants’ Rights Project, said, “Birthright citizenship is the law of the land — as it has been for more than 150 years and as the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed once again just a few months ago. Cruel attacks on this core constitutional right must not be allowed to stand.”

“The president may keep signing unlawful executive orders, but the Supreme Court could not have been more clear when it ruled that neither the president nor Congress can end birthright citizenship,” said ACLU of Maine Executive Director Molly Curren Rowles. “We’ll continue defending the Constitution and the core principles reflected in the 14th Amendment: that with very few clear exceptions, every baby born on U.S. soil is a U.S. citizen.”

“Despite a clear ruling from the U.S. Supreme Court just weeks ago, the Trump administration is still trying to deprive babies born in the United States of their constitutional rights,” said Carol Rose, executive director at the ACLU of Massachusetts. “We cannot tolerate this brazen act of lawlessness. Boston Dynamics says ICE would have to follow the same terms and ethical rules as every other customer, including a ban on weaponizing the robots.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is trying to tap a local company for assistance.

According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE is planning to spend between $1 million and $2 million to to purchase Boston Dynamics’ Spot robots.

The formal procurement process lists an expected solicitation start date of Sept. 4. However, the government has not yet issued an RFP for this.

DHS said ICE wants to use the remotely operated robots to support public safety and law enforcement operations, including inspecting potentially dangerous areas, assessing hazards, and providing situational awareness without putting personnel at risk.

The robots, DHS said, could help improve officer safety and decision-making in incidents involving dangerous, confined, unstable, or otherwise difficult-to-access areas.

Boston Dynamics sells to many government agencies and public safety organizations. A company spokesperson said that the robots are used to keep people out of harm’s way and to help first responders in assessing dangerous situations. Examples include using Spot for hazardous gas detection, unexploded ordnance inspection, suspicious package investigation, search and rescue, subterranean or confined-space exploration, and structural assessments following fires, disasters, or other hazards.

The company did not say how ICE would use the robots.

Additionally, the company said that “any attempted weaponization of Boston Dynamics’ robots is strictly prohibited,” as outlined in its Terms and Conditions, ethical principles, and an open letter against weaponization.

“We pledge that we will not weaponize our advanced-mobility general-purpose robots or the software we develop that enables advanced robotics, and we will not support others to do so,” the open letter said. “When possible, we will carefully review our customers’ intended application to avoid potential weaponization.”

The open letter was led by Boston Dynamics and co-signed by five other leading robotics companies.

Gov. Maura Healey did not respond to a request for comment on ICE’s plans to purchase the Boston Dynamics robots. Healey has previously previously opposed ICE operating in Massachusetts, including signing legislation in August aimed at restricting the federal agency’s activities in the state.

At the same time, the Healey-Driscoll administration has backed Boston Dynamics and its expansion in Massachusetts, awarding the company $25 million to support its recently announced Waltham expansion.

“Boston Dynamics has played a central role in defining the global robotics industry from right here in our state, and it’s why we wanted them to choose Massachusetts as the site of their expansion,” Healey said in a statement at the time.

text:
ANNE ARUNDEL COUNTY, Md. — Tiago Alexandre Sousa-Martins, the man shot by ICE agents in Glen Burnie on Christmas Eve, has been released from immigration custody and reunited with his family.

A federal district court judge ordered his release after more than eight months of detention.

Sousa-Martins, 31, was shot multiple times — including in his back and thigh — and suffered a collapsed lung during a December 24, 2025, confrontation with ICE agents in a residential neighborhood in Glen Burnie, Maryland.

Anne Arundel County

Christmas Eve shooting involving ICE agents leaves two injured in Glen Burnie

Dominick Philippe-Auguste

Court records show ICE agents were conducting a targeted immigration enforcement operation when they approached a white van registered to Sousa-Martins. According to court records, agents attempted to box in his vehicle to question him about his immigration status. After a brief struggle, Sousa-Martins put the car in reverse, then into drive, damaging the agents' vehicles. Agents then fired at the van.

Sousa-Martins was charged with resisting arrest and destruction of government property. His federal criminal case concluded with a sentence of time served, but he remained in immigration detention until the court ordered his release.

Anne Arundel County

Man shot by ICE agents in Glen Burnie charged with resisting arrest

Rushaad Hayward

An ICE spokesperson previously told us that Sousa-Martins had resided in the United States illegally for 17 years, entering in December 2008 and overstaying his visa after it expired in February 2009.

We Are CASA and the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights filed a federal habeas petition on his behalf.

"This is the moment Tiago's family has been fighting and praying for: he is home," Alice Barrett, Managing Attorney at We Are CASA, said in a statement. "Since Christmas Eve, his children have been without their father and his family has lived with the uncertainty of whether they would be together again. Today, we celebrate with them. Tiago belongs at home, surrounded by the people who love him."

Sousa-Martins also released a statement following his release.

"I want to express my deepest gratitude to We Are CASA. I truly don't know where I'd be without them. They stepped in when I needed it most, not only supporting me through my own ordeal but also standing by my family every step of the way. So from the bottom of my heart, thank you," Sousa-Martins said. "Today, I can finally say I am free. It was a long and difficult battle, but I'm here to tell you that it is possible. Please, don't ever lose hope. Don't give up."

A second person who was present during the December confrontation, Solomon Antonio Serrano-Esquivel, suffered minor injuries and was also taken to a hospital at the time of the incident.

MEMPHIS, Tenn. — It’s been about a week and a half since a Berclair nightclub was raided by ICE agents who seized more than 120 people.

Wednesday, numerous organizations say they are now trying to help the children who are now left without parents and scrambling to figure out where to live.

In the dead of night, an enormous ICE operation targeted a Memphis nightclub. The Department of Homeland Security tells us 121 people were arrested. Now, families of those detained feel the fallout.

“Right now we have a lot of family members that are picking up the pieces,” said Gisela Guerrero. “That includes getting in touch with their loved on that was detained, some people are still struggling to make contact, get on the phone with them.”

Guerrero is one of those trying to help those affected. She says the organizations she works with, MICAH and Vecindarios 901, are also trying to establish legal support.

“Children that have been left behind, mortgage payments, rent payments, utility bills, all of that has been left behind and so anybody who is left is now scrambling to figure out what needs to be covered, how soon does it need to be covered,” she said.

They have to figure out where to get additional income to pay for these expenses.

“We have a lot of children where either one or both parents have been detained,” she said. “We know of one family who the household now has eight children within it because of the people that were detained that evening.”

The Department of Homeland Security tells us five people from Honduras and Mexico were arrested during the raid. They say the five have criminal histories and are now facing various charges.

“Outside of that there is no report on everybody else that was detained, we still haven’t heard,” Guerrero said.

She says the immigration system is broken.

“So for the many people who might be wondering for these people if they have children, if they have all these responsibilities here, why didn’t they apply for documentation status?: Guerrero said. “We just really want people to remember this is incredibly complicated, it’s incredibly expensive and so cumbersome.”

text:
Dozens of people gathered outside the immigration detention center on the Tacoma Tideflats on Wednesday to speak about how a recent surge in flights transferring detainees to ICE facilities in other parts of the country have hurt families and strained detainees’ access to attorneys.

Hundreds of people were removed from the Northwest ICE Processing Center last month over 17 flights, according to organizers for La Resistencia, an immigrant-rights group that has been monitoring the flights from King County International Airport.

Guadalupe Gonzalez, an organizer with the group, said Wednesday that the frequency of the flights was at an all-time high. He said as of Sept. 3, La Resistencia had observed 109 flights this year, and he expected the number to soon surpass the 122 flights they saw throughout last year.

“We saw the most flights in a month ever this past August at 17,” Gonzalez said. “We also saw 757 people be removed. That’s the highest so far this year. We had a few months last year that exceeded that, but that’s still very high. Even though we saw 757 people be removed, we only saw 89 people be brought in. So it’s clear that we’re seeing an escalation.”

The NWIPC is operated by a contractor for the federal government, the GEO Group. It is the only federal immigration detention center in the Pacific Northwest, and it has a capacity for 1,600 detainees.

Angelina Godoy is a University of Washington professor and the director of the university’s Center for Human Rights. During the news conference, she said the Center for Human Rights has been researching conditions in the NWIPC for 10 years and published more than 12 reports documenting different forms of “systematic cruelty.”

What’s new, Godoy said, is that immigration enforcement in the Seattle area and throughout Washington has reached “unprecedented heights.” She said the latest data released by the federal government showed more people were being arrested now compared to the peak of immigration enforcement under former President Barack Obama’s administration.

“More people are being brought into the system, and they are also experiencing new forms of cruelty, including the mass transfers that sever their ties to community, families and attorneys,” Godoy said.

A representative for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to emailed questions Wednesday about the recent rise in flights.

Three women shared stories during the morning news conference about their loved ones’ suddenly being transferred out of the NWIPC. All but one declined to provide their name to reporters.

One woman who spoke by phone during the news conference said through a Spanish interpreter that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested her son on July 22. She said ICE followed him from a Home Depot, where he was gathering supplies for a painting job. She said he was detained at the NWIPC, and he had a court date set for Sept. 10.

In the middle of the night, the woman said, she learned that her son was being transferred to an ICE facility in San Diego before his court date. She said the news broke her heart.

“There’s no one who can visit him,” she said through an interpreter. “He’s far away now.”

Another woman said through an interpreter that her spouse was detained at the NWIPC. By the time they found a lawyer within their budget, she said she learned that he was being transferred to an ICE facility in Mississippi.

“When those terrifying 48 hours hit, you know those 48 hours when my husband told me he was going to be transferred to Mississippi, the lawyer wasn’t able to help,” she said through the interpreter.

In a phone call Wednesday, Seattle immigration attorney Bart Klein told The News Tribune that Western Washington is a “really liberal jurisdiction” for judges. He said he believes the spike in transfer flights is an effort to avoid putting detainees in front of them.

Klein said people held in detention essentially get “no notice” that they will be transferred to a facility in another state. He said a telltale sign of an impending transfer is when a detainee’s access to commissary is cut off or the tablet they can use to contact people outside the facility no longer works.

“I train everybody, you call me right away,” Klein said. “The moment your tablet doesn’t work, you’re on the phone, man. You’re getting notice out. You know, somehow you tell your roommate, your cellmate, call, call.”

The lack of notice makes it difficult for attorneys to challenge the transfer in court before it occurs. And once the person is flown out, Klein said it can be one or two days before they get access to a phone again. If their attorney isn’t licensed to practice law in the new jurisdiction, they would need to get a new attorney.

“And then it’s impossible to find anyone because they go to these really rural jails and nobody goes there,” Klein said.

text:
The United Nations’ top human rights official has called on the United States to halt deportations to Haiti and investigate the deaths of at least 23 migrants in U.S. immigration custody since the beginning of 2026.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk raised concerns about U.S. immigration enforcement practices on Monday during the opening of a session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, calling for greater scrutiny of detention conditions and accountability for deaths in custody.

Türk urged U.S. authorities to conduct thorough investigations into each of the deaths and provide answers to the victims’ families.

He also raised concerns about migrants being returned to countries where they could face serious danger, specifically citing Haiti, which continues to grapple with widespread gang violence, displacement and a humanitarian crisis.

“I urge the United States to halt the return of people to places where they could suffer irreparable harm, including Haiti, and to ensure due process for all removals to third countries,” Türk told the council.

His comments come as the United States expands immigration enforcement measures, including arrangements to transfer some deportees to third countries with which they may have no previous connection.

Türk stressed that deportations must comply with international human rights protections and that migrants should not be returned to countries where they face the risk of irreparable harm.

The UN rights chief also expressed alarm over reported plans by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves.

Türk warned that introducing the devices could “increase the violence associated with their operations.”

His remarks add to international scrutiny of U.S. immigration policies, particularly the treatment of migrants in detention, the use of force during immigration enforcement operations and the transfer of deportees to third countries.

The call to suspend deportations to Haiti comes as the Caribbean nation remains engulfed in a prolonged security crisis that has forced large numbers of people from their homes and severely disrupted access to essential services.

The UN has repeatedly warned about the risks associated with returning people to Haiti amid the deteriorating security and humanitarian conditions.

Türk’s appeal also underscores the principle that governments should not return people to countries where they face serious threats to their lives, safety or fundamental rights.

text:
Over the past weeks, the number of Immigration and Customs Enforcement flights out of Seattle’s Boeing Field has increased. Their cargo is immigrants, many with long-standing ties to Washington state who are being flown by ICE to different facilities across the country.

Since late August nearly 500 people have been flown out of Boeing Field, according to county records. Detainees who spoke to KUOW said they’re often notified a night before a flight is supposed to happen. During the night, communications are shut down between detainees and the outside world, so they have no way of letting their lawyers or family know about plans to relocate them. The abrupt flight plans also interrupt the flow of immigration hearings scheduled in the courtrooms of the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

“Prior to the second Trump administration, we only had one flight a week. When Trump 2.0 started, we started seeing three flights a week. Now the norm has become around four flights a week,” said Guadalupe Gonzalez. Gonzalez works with La Resistencia, an immigrant rights group that maintains communication with detainees and tracks ICE flights from Boeing field. Those flights are also tracked by King County.

ICE has not responded to KUOW’s questions about the increase in flights. In late August for the first time five flights were documented in a single week, according to La Resistencia and King County records.

The increase in flights began soon after attorneys at the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project won a lawsuit that makes it easier for detainees to have a bond hearing while locked up at the Tacoma ICE center. Many of those who have been flown to other locations either had a recent initial court hearing, or were about to have one where they could have requested a bond hearing.

Families of detainees who have been removed from the Tacoma center held a press conference Wednesday raising the alarm about the flights. A woman who lives in Seattle told the crowd that the practice of these interrupting flights continues unabated. She said her son, who was seeking asylum, was supposed to have a court hearing this week.

“But then they didn’t allow him to arrive at that audience date in Tacoma,” the woman said in Spanish. “Instead, they moved him before that.”

Detainees told KUOW people are being flown to Virginia, Texas, and Mississippi. Arizona is also on that list, said Eli Villa-Malone, a Yakima attorney providing pro-bono consultation services to detainees. Many of the people calling for consultation are long-standing members of the community, Villa-Malone said.

She said during lockup, immigrants are pressured to self deport instead of finding a legal path to stay in the U.S. Being moved to a new state complicates that legal process.

“If I do see a viable case for somebody who's in El Paso, I can't take it. We can't do anything. We could maybe try and finagle ICE and request that they be moved back to Tacoma so that they could have access to their attorney. Ultimately ICE has discretion to decide where somebody's gonna be detained,” Villa-Malone said.

For the woman whose son was flown out before his hearing, and the other families at the press conference, the unexpected relocations have caused turmoil.

“One lives with a terrible anguish, a pain caused by ICE,” the woman said. “One feels that in those moments the world ended, the world shifts and everything comes down on you – that no solution is found.”

Villa-Malone echoed those sentiments.

“ It's further separating them from any lifeline that they have with their communities, and then it's making it 20 times harder for them to get an attorney because of course, once you're detained and you're moved, you're from Washington, you might know an attorney from Washington, but you certainly aren't gonna know one [in another state],” she said.

She said the increase in flights out of Washington tracks with the increased number of people being pulled into immigrant detention and the need to make space for more beds as more immigrants are being detained in Tacoma.

Around 2,200 people have been arrested and detained at the Northwest ICE Processing Center from January to July. They are immigrants across the spectrum of status and interactions with law enforcement. Some have green cards and decades-old infractions. Others are in the country without legal status. The majority have no criminal conviction and have long-standing familial and community ties to the region that go beyond immigration status.

“What those numbers mask is the pain, the deliberate cruelty, and a lot of what you hear vibrating in the voices of the family members who are sharing their stories,” said Angelina Godoy, director of research at the UW Center for Human Rights.

The Tacoma immigrant lockup has been the center of detainee complaints surrounding food quality, medical care, and a lack of administrative accountability — documented by Godoy and her researchers.

It’s also a centerpiece for deportation efforts in the Pacific Northwest.

title: Maryland Father Shot by ICE on Christmas Eve Reunited with his Family - We Are CASA
description:
VIRGINIA – After more than eight months of detention, a federal district court judge ordered Tiago Alexandre Sousa Martins’ release from ICE custody.
“Since Christmas Eve, his children have been without their father and his family has lived with the uncertainty of whether they would be together again.
So from the bottom of my heart, thank you,” said Tiago Sousa Martins.
Instead of spending Christmas with his family, Sousa-Martins was hospitalized and suffered months of incarceration and immigration detention.
The Amica Center for Immigrant Rights provides unwavering legal defense and strategic litigation for immigrant children and adults facing detention and deportation.
text:
VIRGINIA – After more than eight months of detention, a federal district court judge ordered Tiago Alexandre Sousa Martins’ release from ICE custody. Today, he has been released and is finally home with his family.

“This is the moment Tiago’s family has been fighting and praying for: he is home,” said Alice Barrett, Managing Attorney at We Are CASA. “Since Christmas Eve, his children have been without their father and his family has lived with the uncertainty of whether they would be together again. Today, we celebrate with them. Tiago belongs at home, surrounded by the people who love him.”

“Today, we celebrate Tiago’s release and reunion with his loved ones. But our work does not end here: we remain committed to holding ICE accountable and ensuring all immigrants are treated with dignity and humanity,” said Sam Hsieh, Deputy Program Director of the Immigration Impact Lab at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights.

After a months-long liberation campaign led by national powerhouse nonprofit We Are CASA, including the filing of a federal habeas petition by We Are CASA and the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, Sousa Martins, a 31-year-old Maryland father, has been released from immigration custody.

“I want to express my deepest gratitude to We Are CASA. I truly don’t know where I’d be without them. They stepped in when I needed it most, not only supporting me through my own ordeal but also standing by my family every step of the way. So from the bottom of my heart, thank you,” said Tiago Sousa Martins. “Today, I can finally say I am free. It was a long and difficult battle, but I’m here to tell you that it is possible. Please, don’t ever lose hope. Don’t give up.”

On Christmas Eve 2025, Sousa-Martins left his family to go to work, and ICE followed him to a residential neighborhood in Glen Burnie, Maryland. Agents surrounded his work van with vehicles and yelled at him, ordering him to get out. Rather than de-escalating given his understandable fear and panic, agents broke his window and opened fire, striking him multiple times, including in his back and thigh. He suffered serious injuries, including a collapsed lung.

The Trump regime’s account of the incident subsequently changed after Anne Arundel County Police contradicted key details in the government’s initial description of what happened.

Instead of spending Christmas with his family, Sousa-Martins was hospitalized and suffered months of incarceration and immigration detention.

He was repeatedly deprived of adequate medical care to recover from ICE’s gunshot wounds. Yet, even after his federal criminal case concluded with a sentence of time served, he remained separated from his family as the campaign launched for his liberation continued.

Today, his family, We Are CASA, his attorneys, and an organized people-powered movement has brought Tiago home.

###

Note: Moving forward, “We Are CASA, Inc.” will be operating under the name “We Are CASA.” Thank you for updating accordingly. With more than 192,000 lifetime members across 46 states, We Are CASA is a national powerhouse organization building power and improving the quality of life in working-class Black, Latino/a/e, Afro-descendant, Indigenous, and immigrant communities. We Are CASA creates change through a power-building model that blends human services, community organizing, and advocacy to serve the full spectrum of its members’ needs, dreams, and aspirations.

The Amica Center for Immigrant Rights provides unwavering legal defense and strategic litigation for immigrant children and adults facing detention and deportation. They fight for the rights, safety, and unity of immigrant communities, standing with those trapped in our nation’s fundamentally flawed immigration system.
