text:
For Immediate Release:

Date: September 8, 2026

Media Contact:

Rafael Bernal | Rafael.Bernal@mail.house.gov | 202-841-4844

D.C. Circuit Sides with CHC and 115 Members of Congress to Block IRS from Handing Taxpayer Data to ICE, Calls Trump Administration Objections ‘Weak Sauce

Court finds the administration's data-sharing scheme “indisputably contravenes” federal privacy law.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit unanimously upheld a lower court's order blocking the Internal Revenue Service from turning over confidential taxpayer information to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The ruling in Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS delivers a decisive victory for the Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC), which led an amicus brief signed by 115 Members of Congress urging the court to uphold the taxpayer privacy protections Congress enacted in the wake of Watergate.

The unanimous ruling in Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS is a rebuke of an administration that built a system to hand over people's private tax records to deportation agents, cut every corner along the way, and then admitted it under oath. The IRS released 47,289 taxpayer records to ICE. Yet for more than nine out of ten, the agency never checked whether ICE had supplied a real address, as the law requires, and ICE listed the same employee as the point of contact on all 1.28 million requests it filed.

The D.C. Circuit did not mince words.

The court found the IRS's new process “indisputably contravenes” federal privacy law and is a “far cry” from the careful, case-by-case review the agency used for decades. It brushed aside the administration's complaint that the injunction was burdensome as “weak sauce.” It also warned that the IRS is “now on notice twice over,” noting that the government and its personnel face steep civil and criminal consequences for willfully disclosing protected taxpayer information.

"Today the court affirmed what we have argued from the very beginning: no administration is above the law, and paying your taxes does not mean surrendering your right to privacy," said CHC Chair Rep. Adriano Espaillat. "This administration built a machine to strip millions of Americans of protections Congress put in place fifty years ago after Watergate. One hundred fifteen Members of Congress stood up and told this court what Congress actually intended when it wrote Section 6103. Today, the D.C. Circuit agreed. This is a win for working-class families, the Latino community, and for every taxpayer in this country."

The Congressional Hispanic Caucus has led Congress's legal engagement on IRS-ICE data sharing since the practice first came to light. This is the fourth amicus brief CHC has led on the issue:

April 30, 2025 — CHC led more than 100 House Democrats in an amicus brief in Centro de Trabajadores Unidos v. Bessent at the D.C. District Court.

July 9, 2025 — CHC led 93 House and Senate Democrats in an amicus brief in Centro before the D.C. Circuit.

September 2025 — CHC filed an amicus brief in Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS at the D.C. District Court. On November 21, 2025, Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly granted a preliminary injunction halting the data sharing.

March 2026 — CHC led 115 Members of Congress in an amicus brief before the D.C. Circuit defending that injunction on appeal, the largest congressional amicus brief CHC has led this Congress.

The case was brought by the Center for Taxpayer Rights, Main Street Alliance, the Communications Workers of America, and the National Federation of Federal Employees, represented by Democracy Forward. Today, the prohibition on IRS-ICE data sharing remains in place as the case proceeds.

Today's opinion can be found HERE.

El Circuito de DC falla a favor del CHC y 115 miembros del Congreso para bloquear al IRS de entregar datos de contribuyentes al ICE y califica las objeciones de la administración Trump de "argumento endeble"

El tribunal determina que el esquema de intercambio de datos de la administración "contraviene indiscutiblemente" la ley federal de privacidad.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Hoy, el Tribunal de Apelaciones del Circuito de DC confirmó por unanimidad la orden de un tribunal inferior que bloquea al Servicio de Impuestos Internos (IRS) de entregar información confidencial de los contribuyentes al Servicio de Control de Inmigración y Aduanas (ICE). El fallo en el caso Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS representa una victoria decisiva para el Caucus Hispano del Congreso (CHC), que lideró un escrito amicus firmado por 115 miembros del Congreso instando al tribunal a mantener las protecciones de privacidad de los contribuyentes que el Congreso promulgó tras el escándalo Watergate.

El fallo unánime en Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS es un reproche a una administración que construyó un sistema para entregar los registros fiscales privados de las personas a los agentes de deportación, ignoró todas las salvaguardias en el camino y luego lo admitió bajo juramento. El IRS entregó 47,289 registros de contribuyentes al ICE. Sin embargo, en más de nueve de cada diez casos, la agencia nunca verificó si el ICE había proporcionado una dirección real, como lo exige la ley, y el ICE listó al mismo empleado como punto de contacto en las 1.28 millones de solicitudes que presentó.

El Circuito de DC no se anduvo con rodeos.

El tribunal determinó que el nuevo proceso del IRS "contraviene indiscutiblemente" la ley federal de privacidad y está "muy lejos" de la revisión minuciosa caso por caso que la agencia utilizó durante décadas. Desestimó la queja de la administración de que la orden judicial era onerosa calificándola de "argumento endeble". También advirtió que el IRS "ahora ha sido notificado dos veces", señalando que el gobierno y su personal enfrentan graves consecuencias civiles y penales por divulgar deliberadamente información protegida de los contribuyentes.

"Hoy el tribunal confirmó lo que hemos argumentado desde el principio: ninguna administración está por encima de la ley, y pagar impuestos no significa renunciar al derecho a la privacidad", dijo el Presidente del CHC, el Rep. Adriano Espaillat. "Esta administración construyó una maquinaria para despojar a millones de estadounidenses de las protecciones que el Congreso estableció hace cincuenta años tras el Watergate. Ciento quince miembros del Congreso se levantaron y le dijeron a este tribunal lo que el Congreso realmente pretendía cuando redactó la Sección 6103. Hoy, el Circuito de DC estuvo de acuerdo. Esta es una victoria para las familias de clase trabajadora, la comunidad latina y cada contribuyente de este país."

El Caucus Hispano del Congreso ha liderado el compromiso legal del Congreso sobre el intercambio de datos entre el IRS y el ICE desde que la práctica salió a la luz por primera vez. Este es el cuarto escrito amicus que el CHC ha liderado sobre el tema:

30 de abril de 2025 — El CHC lideró a más de 100 demócratas de la Cámara en un escrito amicus en el caso Centro de Trabajadores Unidos v. Bessent ante el Tribunal de Distrito de DC.

9 de julio de 2025 — El CHC lideró a 93 demócratas de la Cámara y el Senado en un escrito amicus en el caso Centro ante el Circuito de DC.

Septiembre de 2025 — El CHC presentó un escrito amicus en el caso Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS ante el Tribunal de Distrito de DC. El 21 de noviembre de 2025, la jueza Colleen Kollar-Kotelly otorgó una orden cautelar preliminar que suspendió el intercambio de datos.

Marzo de 2026 — El CHC lideró a 115 miembros del Congreso en un escrito amicus ante el Circuito de DC en defensa de esa orden cautelar en apelación, el escrito amicus congresional más grande que el CHC ha liderado en este Congreso.

El caso fue presentado por el Center for Taxpayer Rights, Main Street Alliance, la Communications Workers of America y la National Federation of Federal Employees, representados por Democracy Forward. Hoy, la prohibición del intercambio de datos entre el IRS y el ICE permanece vigente mientras el caso continúa.

description:
That’s why AFSC’s New Jersey Immigrant Rights Program has been working to reach businesses before ICE does.
During the first seven months of the administration, ICE publicly reported 40 worksite enforcement actions resulting in more than 1,100 arrests.
Advocates and local news outlets documented dozens of additional raids targeting small businesses that employed large numbers of immigrant workers.
“Community members are afraid to leave their homes because of ICE,” says Community Organizer Glendy Tsitouras, who leads the project.
Such stops have led to the deaths of community members including Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
text:
Early in the morning on November 19, 2025, dozens of masked federal agents—many of them heavily armed—descended on a seafood market in Newark, New Jersey. As bewildered bystanders looked on, agents zip-tied at least 13 workers, loaded them into vans, and drove away. The chaotic scene sent shockwaves through the community, leaving family members and local business owners wondering if they’d be next.

This wasn't the first workplace raid in New Jersey under the current administration, and it wouldn't be the last. That’s why AFSC’s New Jersey Immigrant Rights Program has been working to reach businesses before ICE does.

As the Trump administration rapidly expanded immigration enforcement, workplace raids became an increasingly common tactic. During the first seven months of the administration, ICE publicly reported 40 worksite enforcement actions resulting in more than 1,100 arrests. The true number, however, is likely higher. Advocates and local news outlets documented dozens of additional raids targeting small businesses that employed large numbers of immigrant workers.

These raids are horribly destructive. They break up and impoverish families, deter people from seeking employment or accessing essential services, and destabilize local economies.

While AFSC's Immigrant Rights Program provides legal support to people affected by immigration enforcement and advocates for policies that strengthen immigrant protections, we also recognize that prevention is essential.

Since earlier this year, AFSC has been visiting businesses throughout Newark, Red Bank, and surrounding communities, from restaurants and nail salons to small manufacturers. We provide Know Your Rights trainings directly to owners, managers, and employees—usually on the spot.

“Community members are afraid to leave their homes because of ICE,” says Community Organizer Glendy Tsitouras, who leads the project. “The one place they do still go is to work, because they have to. It’s work, home, work, home. So, we figured we’d be able to reach more people by meeting them at work, as opposed to inviting them to meetings or workshops.”

During these trainings, Glendy starts with issues specific to the workplace: what rights workers have during encounters with ICE, the difference between judicial and administrative warrants (only the first one legally requires you to let ICE onto private property), and how employers should respond if federal agents arrive.

Once Glendy opens the floor for questions, however, the conversation often expands to a much broader range of immigration-related issues, from family immigration to detention. The goal is simple: to ensure that workers and employers have accurate information so they can make informed decisions—whether at work or anywhere else.

"There is so much confusion right now,” she says. “People are desperate to understand what’s really happening, but they’re bombarded with misinformation. I spend a lot of time clarifying incorrect or misleading stuff they’ve seen on social media. Understanding the current situation doesn’t make the current situation good, but not understanding it makes it that much worse. People are more likely to put themselves in harm’s way or fall victim to increasingly common scams targeting immigrants.”

Although ICE's mass deportation campaign continues to inflict enormous harm, there is growing evidence that community education is making some enforcement tactics less effective. In a recent CNN article, experts noted that ICE has increasingly relied on traffic stops as business raids and traditional home enforcement have become more difficult. Such stops have led to the deaths of community members including Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

Expanding networks of community organizers educating immigrants and employers about their constitutional rights have made it harder for agents to conduct arrests inside businesses and homes using administrative warrants, since more people now understand they’re not legally required to open their doors unless agents present a judicial warrant signed by a judge.

For Glendy, the trainings are only the beginning. The workers she meets are invited to join a growing network that serves as a rapid-response communication hub where community members can ask immigration-related questions, share information, and stay connected to trusted resources. Each new business strengthens a broader network of mutual support that helps immigrant communities stay informed long after a single training has ended.

"We've met with hundreds of people in Newark, but I think the impact has been much wider,” Glendy says. “Word gets around fast in immigrant communities. The people I speak to go home and speak to their family and friends, and it keeps going. If we can expand this initiative to other parts of the state, I think we could really transform the information landscape.”

text:
Elected officials were demanding answers Tuesday after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement confrontation with protesters in Frederick turned violent over the weekend.

And they weren’t the only ones.

“People were legitimately scared and pretty much terrorized by ICE for two full days before things escalated on Friday night. If you didn’t take anybody into custody, why did you even show up?” asked Tatiana Santos, a member of Indivisible Frederick Forward who witnessed some of what happened in the Tasker’s Chance neighborhood Friday night.

Protesters turned up Thursday after they learned that ICE agents were in the neighborhood, apparently staking out a house.

On Friday, after blocking the street, protesters could be seen locking arms and going to the house as a human barrier, according to video of the incident provided by Hagerstown Rapid Response.

At that point, the video shows ICE agents moving in, grabbing and pushing the protesters, with at least one agent hitting a person on the ground with a baton, the scene illuminated by the headlights and police lights of ICE vehicles on the scene.

Lacking federal funds, local groups press to continue legal aid for immigrant children

“It felt like they [ICE agents] were just terrorizing people. You don’t get brutal with people. It’s inhumane,” Soolah Kemp said Tuesday. She was a member of the Hagerstown group that showed up to support residents in the Frederick neighborhood.

Santos and Kemp called on the Maryland Attorney General’s Office to investigate what happened, but the office declined to comment Tuesday.

Representatives with ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond Tuesday to requests for comment.

Jennifer Gerlock, manager of public affairs with the city of Frederick, said in an email Tuesday the city isn’t aware of any arrests made by federal authorities during the incicent. Frederick Police, who were called to the scene at 9 p.m. Friday in response to “escalating tensions between protesters and federal agents,” did not make any arrests at the scene, Gerlock said.

“FPD was not notified in advance of the federal law enforcement operation and was not involved in its planning or execution,” Gerlock said. “Our officers’ role was to maintain public safety, protect life and property, and help prevent further escalation between those gathered and the federal agents conducting the operation.”

Gerlock continued: “Officers worked to ensure that individuals could lawfully exercise their constitutional rights while also helping to prevent actions that could lead to physical confrontations or arrests. FPD was not there to assist ICE in carrying out its federal enforcement operation.”

Gov. Wes Moore (D), asked Tuesday about the Frederick incident, said his office was monitoring the situation throughout the Labor Day weekend. But he expressed concerns about “this latest iteration of ICE,” which he said is larger than the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Agency and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

“While I know that there are still things that are being investigated right now, it’s a continuation of the challenge that we have with this latest iteration of ICE,” he said. “The … continued problem that I have with how these actions are being used and utilized — not with our communities, but just in and to our communities — is something that I continue to have very real challenge and very real issues with.”

Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-6th), whose district includes Frederick, said the confrontation is “deeply concerning.”

“I am especially disturbed by reports that ICE agents used force against Frederick residents,” McClain Delaney said in a statement. “These allegations demand immediate answers and a full, transparent investigation.”

Del. Kris Fair (D-Frederick), whose district includes the Tasker’s Chance neighborhood but wasn’t present when ICE was there Friday, hopes an investigation by state and federal officials will occur to determine if anyone’s civil rights were violated, especially after he watched video footage of the “erratic behavior” of ICE agents.

“We continue to watch the brutalization of our communities by overly aggressive law enforcement power structures,” Fair said. “I’m hoping that our society as a whole can look at this situation truly, deeply, and reflectively, and ask itself if this is the kind of society that we want to live in where law enforcement goes in without any regard for public safety and escalates a situation which was otherwise non-existent prior to Thursday.”

He said Congress has “the power of the purse string here. ICE answers to them. They need to utilize their unilateral power that they have to rein in these out-of-control federal agents.”

text:
A block on the IRS from sharing taxpayer data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement will continue after a federal appeals court upheld an order Tuesday prohibiting the tax agency from disclosing massive amounts of sensitive information to the Department of Homeland Security component.

In considering a district court’s ruling in Center for Taxpayer Rights v. IRS that put the stay in place, the three-judge panel in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit took issue with several elements of the IRS-ICE pact, which it referred to in its ruling as the “Data-Exchange Procedure.”

The court ruled that the agreement “indisputably contravenes the requirements” laid out in federal tax code, specifically the section that guarantees privacy for taxpayer returns and information. The IRS processed ICE’s request for the addresses of nearly 1.3 million taxpayers, returning more than 47,000 matches to the DHS unit.

The IRS-ICE policy under the Trump administration automates the review of millions of records without individual reviews or other ways to ensure compliance, the court added, a “far cry” from how data-sharing between agencies is supposed to work and a “dramatic change in agency policy.”

The appeals court had little time for the administration’s complaints that the preliminary injunction that halted the data-sharing was “highly unusual and harmful,” calling that argument “weak sauce” given that the district court allowed the IRS to file notifications “under seal” so that any potential criminal investigative activity would be shielded from disclosure.

“Importantly, the district court’s advance notice requirement reasonably balances the government’s interest in making lawful disclosures with the plaintiffs’ interest in preventing unlawful disclosures that, if made, would likely be difficult or impossible to remedy,” the judges wrote.

The appeals court also shot down the Trump administration’s argument that the district court order would hinder law enforcement efforts, writing in the opinion that “that’s a gripe with Congress, not the court.”

“As we have explained, the Data-Exchange Procedure is likely contrary to law,” the opinion said. “The government has no legitimate interest in conducting criminal investigations in violation of the statute.”

In closing, the court offered a warning to the Trump administration over the handling of the data-sharing agreement, pointing specifically to the IRS’s release of information last summer that revealed incomplete data requests from ICE that the tax agency fulfilled. Those requests violated the memorandum of understanding between the agencies and potentially federal privacy law.

“The IRS is now on notice twice over regarding the legal inadequacies of its summer 2025 disclosures,” the court wrote. “The government and its personnel face steep civil and criminal consequences for willful disclosure of information in violation of section 6103.”

Nina Olson, executive director of the Center for Taxpayer Rights, celebrated the ruling in a statement, calling the court’s order “a resounding victory for the protection of all taxpayers’ right to the confidentiality of their tax information in the hands of the IRS.”

“Congress has set strict parameters around the sharing of taxpayer information for a reason — that trust in the tax system depends on protection of taxpayer information,” she added. “By unlawfully sharing return information with ICE, the IRS violated that trust. The court’s order today is a step toward restoring it.”

Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, which represents the Center for Taxpayer Rights and the other plaintiffs — Main Street Alliance, Communications Workers of America, and the National Federation of Federal Employees — said in a statement that the organization was “pleased the court has again acted to stop this unlawful behavior.”

“The privacy laws enacted in the post-Watergate era exist to prevent abuses of power just like this,” Perryman said. “The administration has already admitted to being careless and irresponsible with our sensitive, personal information, and now yet another court has held the administration in check.”

text:
A White House website referencing undocumented immigrants as "aliens" who "walk among us" has drawn strong pushback from civil rights advocates. Critics argue the platform uses rhetoric that dehumanizes non-citizens and misrepresents regional immigration data.

The site, which details millions of immigration encounters nationwide, features a tracker showing local arrest figures, including 542 in Seattle, 487 in Tukwila, and 716 in Yakima. Though the online interface attributes these statistics directly to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

When FOX 13 Seattle reached out to federal officials regarding the data, they said the inquiries went back to the White House, stating the numbers reflect more than just ICE operations.

Human rights advocates warn that the website's framing ignores the real-world demographics of immigration enforcement and uses rhetoric designed to isolate non-citizens.

Rhetoric and dehumanizing framing

The federal platform frames non-citizen populations as a covert threat, using language that mimics sci-fi tropes. Civil rights groups caution that referring to immigrants in this manner actively feeds public hostility and xenophobia.

"Honestly, it's the same sort of dehumanizing rhetoric that we've seen from this administration over and over again, and it's disgusting and incredibly troubling," said David Montes, staff attorney at the ACLU of Washington. "Immigrants make up an integral part of our community and are important members of the fabric of our society, and they should not be dehumanized by this."

Montes noted that the administration's messaging relies heavily on division.

"They're trying to make it seem like these folks are just totally different than people who are citizens, and it's just not true at all," said Montes. "As I said, immigrants are an important part of our community who have the same values as all of us."

Dissecting criminality and data surges

While the administration's digital site associates localized arrest counts with criminal charges, legal experts and independent studies reveal a vastly different picture.

"We know that 60 or 70% of the people that they have arrested for immigration violations do not have any criminal history," Montes said. He points out that the administration often manufactures arrests by targeting individuals in administrative settings, such as immigration court hallways.

Recent findings support these concerns. According to data analyzed by the University of Washington Center for Human Rights, immigration enforcement in the Pacific Northwest experienced a sharp surge, recording nearly 2,250 arrests in the final three months of the year. The research indicates that the majority of those targeted during this enforcement spike had no prior criminal records.

Concerns over hotline and vigilantism

The website encourages members of the public to report "suspicious aliens" and features closing remarks assuring readers that apprehending non-citizens ensures they are in "good hands" before deportation.

Legal defenders argue these statements obscure documented mistreatment inside detention centers and promote dangerous racial profiling.

"They're trying to reach an arbitrary quota, and this is a piece of, frankly, propaganda that's meant to make that more palatable to people," Montes said. He warned that soliciting public tips encourages vigilantism, retaliation, and aggressive tactics that endanger both citizens and non-citizens alike.

title: Trump Asks Supreme Court to Restore Immigration Database Checks of State Voter Rolls
description:
The Justice Department says SAVE itself does not remove anyone from voter rolls and merely provides states with federal information.
The Social Security Act generally requires Social Security numbers and certain related records to remain confidential.
Sauer argues that the duty necessarily permits DHS to check other federal records, including Social Security data, when responding to those requests.
Granting the request would allow DHS to resume the expanded SAVE system without waiting for the D.C.
What remains blocked is the expanded version that combines Social Security information with bulk-search capabilities.
text:
The Trump administration has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to revive a federal system that allows states to conduct large-scale citizenship checks of their voter rolls using immigration and Social Security records, less than two months before the November midterm elections.

The Department of Homeland Security filed an emergency application Tuesday, September 8, seeking to suspend a lower-court ruling that dismantled an expanded version of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system, commonly known as SAVE.

The administration says the database gives states an important way to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voting-rights and privacy groups contend that the system relies on records that can be outdated or inaccurate and could cause eligible citizens, particularly naturalized Americans, to be wrongly flagged as noncitizens.

The case, Department of Homeland Security v. League of Women Voters, is before the Supreme Court as No. 26A308. The administration is asking the justices for emergency relief while its appeal continues in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the lower court’s ruling “indefensible” and told the Supreme Court it threatens election integrity by preventing the federal government from using Social Security data when states request citizenship verification.

A federal district judge and a divided federal appeals court have so far rejected the administration’s arguments.

U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan ruled June 22 that the government unlawfully transformed SAVE by combining federal databases containing information about millions of Americans. She found that the modified system violated the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act and ordered the changes set aside.

The D.C. Circuit refused by a 2-1 vote on September 4 to suspend her ruling while the government appeals. Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan and Judge Robert Wilkins concluded that the administration had not made the strong showing required to obtain a stay. Judge Gregory Katsas dissented.

The dispute centers on changes DHS began making to SAVE in 2025.

Federal, state, and local agencies had traditionally used SAVE to verify immigration or citizenship status for government benefits, licenses, and other programs. Its usefulness for voter-roll reviews was limited because searches generally required an immigration identifier, such as an alien registration number, that natural-born U.S. citizens do not have.

The administration expanded the system after President Donald Trump signed a March 2025 executive order directing federal agencies to provide states with greater access to federal information for checking citizenship and voter eligibility. The White House said the changes were intended to strengthen election integrity and prevent noncitizens from registering or voting.

DHS modified SAVE so users could search using Social Security numbers and submit large batches of names rather than checking individuals one at a time.

Under the expanded process, a user can upload information including a person’s name, date of birth, and full or partial Social Security number. SAVE checks Social Security Administration records and, when necessary, other federal systems to determine whether the government can confirm that the individual is a U.S. citizen.

If the system cannot confirm citizenship, it does not formally declare the person a noncitizen. Instead, the state or other government agency conducting the search may be prompted to obtain additional proof from that person.

That distinction is central to the administration’s Supreme Court argument.

The Justice Department says SAVE itself does not remove anyone from voter rolls and merely provides states with federal information. Any decision to challenge or cancel a voter registration is made by state officials, the government argues.

The plaintiffs say the distinction offers little protection when the federal data itself is inaccurate.

The lawsuit was brought by the League of Women Voters, several state League affiliates and the Electronic Privacy Information Center. They argue that Social Security records do not always reflect later changes in citizenship status.

A person who obtained a Social Security number while legally present as a noncitizen may later become a naturalized U.S. citizen without updating the citizenship designation in Social Security records. Using that information in a mass voter-roll review could therefore produce a false indication that federal records cannot confirm the voter’s citizenship.

That concern played an important role in the D.C. Circuit’s ruling.

The appeals court cited sworn declarations from U.S. citizens in Louisiana and Virginia who obtained Social Security numbers before naturalization and said Social Security records continued to identify them as noncitizens. Both states had agreed to use modified SAVE for voter-list maintenance.

The appellate majority also pointed to evidence that inaccurate citizenship information had already resulted in voters being required to prove citizenship to remain registered and, in some instances, facing cancellation of their registrations.

The legal dispute is not limited to election policy.

A major part of the case concerns federal privacy law and the circumstances under which Social Security information can be shared between government agencies.

The Social Security Act generally requires Social Security numbers and certain related records to remain confidential. Sooknanan found that the expanded SAVE system unlawfully allowed Social Security information to be used and disclosed through a new federal verification system without sufficient statutory authorization.

The administration argues that a separate federal immigration statute gives DHS the authority it needs.

Under 8 U.S.C. § 1373, DHS must respond when a federal, state or local government agency asks it to verify an individual’s citizenship or immigration status for a lawful purpose. Sauer argues that the duty necessarily permits DHS to check other federal records, including Social Security data, when responding to those requests.

The government also contends that the Social Security Act’s confidentiality provisions do not prohibit the data exchanges involved in SAVE.

The D.C. Circuit majority was not persuaded at the emergency stage.

It concluded that the government had failed to raise some of its Social Security Act arguments at the proper time before the district court. The majority also said that even considering those arguments, the administration had not demonstrated a strong likelihood of ultimately succeeding.

Katsas disagreed.

In dissent, he concluded that the government was likely to show that the expanded system complies with the Social Security Act and that the balance of harms favored allowing it to operate while the appeal proceeds.

The Supreme Court is not being asked to decide the entire case at this stage.

The administration is seeking a stay, an emergency order that would temporarily suspend Sooknanan’s judgment while the government continues its appeal. Granting the request would allow DHS to resume the expanded SAVE system without waiting for the D.C. Circuit to issue a final decision.

A denial would leave the lower court’s order in effect while the litigation continues.

The timing makes the request more significant.

The November 3 midterms are approaching, and several Republican-led states have already used citizenship data from the expanded SAVE system to compare against voter-registration records. Reuters reported that some states canceled registrations after individuals were flagged as noncitizens, while the plaintiffs say eligible citizens have also been wrongly identified.

The case arrives at the Supreme Court alongside another major election dispute involving the administration’s attempt to impose new federal requirements on mail-in ballots.

In that separate case, the Justice Department is asking the justices to allow a U.S. Postal Service rule requiring states to provide lists of mail-ballot recipients and use specially approved barcoded envelopes. A federal judge blocked those requirements shortly before states began sending ballots.

Together, the cases place two parts of the administration’s broader election agenda before the Supreme Court shortly before voting begins nationwide.

The SAVE dispute could have consequences beyond the 2026 election.

A Supreme Court ruling allowing the expanded system to operate could strengthen the federal government’s role in helping states conduct large-scale citizenship checks using information gathered for immigration and Social Security purposes. Leaving the lower-court decision intact would reinforce statutory limits on how federal agencies can combine and disclose personal information, even when the government says it is being used to enforce voting qualifications.

Federal law already prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The dispute before the Court concerns the method used to identify potentially ineligible voters and the safeguards required when federal records are used to do so.

For now, states can still use the older version of SAVE for individualized citizenship inquiries. The D.C. Circuit specifically noted that the lower court’s ruling does not eliminate the longstanding verification system. What remains blocked is the expanded version that combines Social Security information with bulk-search capabilities.

title: Attorney General Weiser leads state coalition defending limits on ICE warrantless arrests
description:
“Federal immigration agents are not above the law.
“This court order does not stop ICE from enforcing immigration law.
The court later found that ICE continued making arrests in violation of the injunction.
The coalition argues that the injunction does not interfere with lawful federal immigration enforcement.
Instead, it requires immigration officers to operate within the limits Congress established and protects the public from the broader harms caused when federal agents act outside their lawful authority.
text:
Sept. 8, 2026 (DENVER) – Attorney General Phil Weiser today co-led a coalition of attorneys general in urging a federal appeals court to uphold a lower court order requiring U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to comply with statutory safeguards when making warrantless arrests.

In an amicus brief filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit in Ramirez Ovando v. Mullin, the coalition argues that the preliminary injunction against ICE serves the public interest by requiring federal immigration officers to comply with existing legal guardrails. Federal law allows immigration officers to make an arrest without a warrant only when there is probable cause to believe a person is unlawfully present and is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

“Federal immigration agents are not above the law. Congress put clear limits on when ICE can arrest someone without a warrant, and the Trump administration cannot simply ignore those safeguards in pursuit of its mass deportation agenda,” Attorney General Weiser said. “This court order does not stop ICE from enforcing immigration law. It simply requires ICE to follow the law when doing so.”

A federal district court in Colorado issued the preliminary injunction after finding that ICE officers had made unlawful warrantless arrests without determining whether individuals were likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained. The court later found that ICE continued making arrests in violation of the injunction. Federal officials appealed the injunction to the Tenth Circuit.

The brief emphasizes the importance of the flight-risk requirement, which prevents federal agents from making warrantless arrests without an individualized determination that a person is likely to flee. The states argue that disregarding this safeguard creates widespread consequences, including reduced school attendance, disruptions to businesses and local economies, avoidance of medical care, and diminished trust in law enforcement that can make victims and witnesses less likely to report crimes.

The coalition argues that the injunction does not interfere with lawful federal immigration enforcement. Instead, it requires immigration officers to operate within the limits Congress established and protects the public from the broader harms caused when federal agents act outside their lawful authority.

Colorado and California co-led the brief and were joined by Arizona, Connecticut, District of Columbia, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

Read the amicus brief (PDF).

text:
The Department of Homeland Security is running a police unit that uses Americans' financial records to predict whether they could commit crimes and is turning over their names to local police.

404 Media reports that the DHS's Predictive Intelligence Targeting Teams, or PITT, are feeding intelligence to local law enforcement, who are then pulling people over who are not suspected of any specific crimes. In one case, a PITT unit analyzed the financial activity of Kyle Olson, who was driving across Montana. Local police pulled him over, claiming that his license plate was obstructed. He was later charged with a DUI, according to the publication.

The documents from that case are what led to 404 Media's discovery. Olson was provided a DHS document explaining the rationale behind his traffic stop, written by Border Patrol Agent Matthew Phelps, who is assigned to the "Spokane Sector Border Patrol Targeting & Intelligence Division (TID)—Predictive Intelligence Targeting Team (PITT)."

Phelps wrote that his job entails reviewing "law enforcement–sensitive databases," including financial activity, to build intelligence before the government hands it over to local police. Phelps handed over "information contained within law enforcement-sensitive systems suggesting financial activity patterns commonly associated with illicit narcotics activity," the document states. He handed it over to Montana Highway Patrol, who pulled over Olson.

"It was relayed to me by U.S. Border Patrol targeting analyst Matthew Phelps that he had identified a vehicle that had indicators of possible narcotics trafficking," wrote Sergeant James Beck of the Montana Highway Patrol. Olson had marijuana edibles, marijuana cuttings, and butane hash oil in his car from his job at a licensed cannabis farm in California, which he was transporting to his home in Wisconsin.

At least one PITT unit is based near Spokane, Washington, and patrols the U.S.-Canada border, while another is based near Laredo, Texas, near the border with Mexico. U.S. Customs and Border Patrol, which is also part of DHS, already uses automatic license plate readers, and those are integrated into the agency's predictive policing tactics.

The concept is ostensibly to find people who may have already committed crimes, but 404 Media didn't find any instances of this occurring. Instead, the government seems to be using predictive policing to create pretexts to pull over and detain people. Border Patrol refused to answer the publication's questions about what financial activity it's monitoring, and if it had a warrant to pull over Olson.

A CPB spokesperson told 404 Media in an email that "U.S. Border Patrol uses intelligence-informed analysis and planning to support national security operations, allocate resources, and help identify potential threats and bad actors to public safety. These efforts are conducted consistent with applicable law, policy, privacy protections, and oversight requirements.

"For operational security reasons, we do not discuss specific analytical methods, data sources, targeting criteria, investigative techniques, system capabilities, or deployment details. Public disclosure of such information could compromise law enforcement operations and investigations as well as creating safety risks for agents and the public," the statement said.

text:
One person was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents near San Diego City College Tuesday, while another person was pursued by agents onto the campus, according to the San Diego Community College District.

At around 9:30 a.m. Tuesday, ICE agents in unmarked vehicles stopped a vehicle near the intersection of 16th and C streets, according to district officials. The driver was taken into custody, while the passenger fled onto the campus.

SDCCD officials said the passenger is a San Diego City College student, while the arrested driver is believed to be a City College student.

District officials said the pursuing ICE agents "quickly stopped as they recognized they were entering a college campus. The agents went back to their vehicles and left. ICE is no longer in the area and did not engage with anyone else on campus."

What led to the vehicle stop and arrest is unknown. ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

SDCCD said it is "providing support" to the passenger, but "due to the sensitive nature of this matter, no additional details will be shared about the impacted individuals."

SDCCD said in a statement, "This intrusion by law enforcement is both disruptive, unwelcome, and in conflict with the SDCCD's core values. City College and the SDCCD are reaching out with counseling and legal services to support students and employees who were affected by this activity. The safety and wellbeing of students and employees will always be the district's highest priority, and we remain committed to maintaining access to all members of our community."

The campus' police department had no interaction with the ICE agents, nor did they provide any assistance to ICE, per a district policy prohibiting its participation in immigration enforcement activities, according to SDCCD, which said the ICE agents left the campus "before any district representative could engage with them."

The incident also did not lead to any campus closure and classes were continuing as scheduled.

text:
The Trump administration is expanding its immigration enforcement efforts through a new Justice Department interpretation that could require reporting across an entire state government, not just agencies that administer certain federal benefit programs.

The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued a legal opinion Sept. 1 reversing a nearly 30-year-old interpretation of a 1996 federal welfare law. DOJ announced the change publicly the following day.

The law requires states participating in Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF, and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, to provide the Department of Homeland Security with information about people the state knows are unlawfully present in the United States.

Since 1998, DOJ had interpreted that requirement as applying only to the state agencies administering TANF or SSI.

The new opinion says the word “state” should instead be read to include the entire state government and all of its component agencies.

DOJ says the change does not create a new legal obligation, but rather restores what the department now considers Congress’ original intent.

“When a state chooses to participate in TANF, it accepts the obligation to report illegal aliens in the United States,” Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser said in a DOJ statement.

The department says states that fail to comply could eventually face consequences, including the loss of program funding. The opinion applies prospectively, meaning states will not face penalties for relying on the previous interpretation in the past.

The change comes amid an escalating political and legal battle between New York and the Trump administration over immigration enforcement.

Earlier this year, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a package of immigration laws that included the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which prohibits state and local law enforcement agencies from entering into 287(g) agreements with federal immigration authorities. Those agreements allow designated state and local officers to perform certain federal immigration enforcement functions.

Hochul has argued that local police, jails and other taxpayer funded resources should remain focused on local public safety rather than federal civil immigration enforcement.

ICE previously confirmed to Spectrum News 1 that it planned to expand its federal detention facility in Batavia by 100 beds after New York ended that local cooperation.

Republican state Sen. George Borrello represents the district that includes the Batavia facility and has been a vocal critic of the state’s immigration policies.

Asked whether the new DOJ interpretation puts New York on a collision course with Washington, Borrello said the conflict is already underway.

“Well, there’s no doubt that’s a collision course. It’s already a collision course,” Borrello said.

Borrello said he sees the issue as one of federal authority and argued that Washington is enforcing rules tied to federal law and federal funding.

“The federal government is enforcing federal law,” Borrello said. “They’re enforcing the Constitution, particularly when it comes to federal rules regarding citizenship and what it means to actually be considered a refugee or an asylum seeker.”

He also pointed to a broader Republican argument that New York is spending too much on benefits and services for noncitizens.

“The Democrat one party rule in New York state has been more focused on providing generous benefits to people who are not even citizens of New York, let alone citizens of the United States, versus the people of New York State that actually fund these things,” Borrello said.

The DOJ opinion, however, is specifically focused on the reporting obligations tied to state participation in TANF and SSI.

The central legal question is not whether unauthorized immigrants qualify for those two programs, but whether New York’s participation in them can be used to trigger a reporting requirement across the entire state government.

New York Attorney General Letitia James has already challenged a separate Trump administration policy involving TANF and immigration related information.

In August, James sued over a federal policy that sought broader access to TANF recipient data, including personal information that could be shared with federal immigration authorities.

In response to the latest DOJ interpretation, a spokesperson for James told Spectrum News 1 the office is reviewing the guidance.

“We are reviewing the guidance and will take action as needed to protect New Yorkers’ rights and services,” the spokesperson said.

Spectrum News 1 also requested comment from Hochul’s office, SUNY and the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance on how the new interpretation could affect New York agencies.

The DOJ opinion does not direct every state employee to independently investigate someone’s immigration status.

Rather, the law deals with individuals the state already knows are unlawfully present.

The new interpretation could still raise broader questions about which state agencies have reporting obligations and what information could establish that knowledge.

DOJ can change the executive branch’s interpretation of a federal statute, but it cannot change the language Congress enacted.

If New York rejects the new interpretation and the federal government later attempts to withhold funding, the dispute could become another federal court battle between Albany and Washington.

text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Speaker Emerita Pelosi joined Representative Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24), along with Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Top Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Adam Schiff (D-CA), and 13 of their colleagues in filing an amicus brief in California v. Wright, pending in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, to challenge the Trump Administration’s use of the Defense Production Act (DPA) to facilitate the restart of the Sable Offshore oil pipeline system along the California Central Coast.

The brief argues that the Administration has failed to identify a legitimate national defense need for Sable’s crude oil and that the DPA order does not satisfy the statutory requirements for invoking this extraordinary authority. Sable produces crude oil—not finished fuels used by the military—and the order does not establish a connection between Sable’s production and an unmet military fuel requirement.

“The Trump Administration’s abuse of the Defense Production Act to revive the Sable pipeline is an unlawful corporate giveaway masquerading as a national security measure,” said Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi. “California communities know the devastating consequences of offshore oil spills. Congress created the Defense Production Act to protect our national security—not to reward political allies, endanger our coastline and override vital environmental safeguards.”

An excerpt from the brief is below.

“This case is not about national defense. It is about a heavily leveraged, crude oil company asking the President to transform the Defense Production Act (DPA) from a statute designed to ‘assure the availability of domestic energy supplies for national defense needs,’ 50 U.S.C. § 4502(a)(5), into a corporate rescue operation for political allies; a rescue that advances the Administration’s political preference for fossil-fuel development at the expense of all other concerns. The Department of Energy’s (‘DOE’) March 13, 2026 order (the ‘Wright Order’) comes nowhere close to identifying a need for Sable crude oil or pipelines in the Order’s generalized invocation of California’s military presence and increased reliance on foreign crude. DOE never explains why those general circumstances create a national-defense need for Sable’s crude, much less how restarting its beleaguered pipelines would meet one.

“Merely invoking “national defense” or an “emergency” does not insulate executive action from the statutory prerequisites that Congress imposed in the DPA on the exercise of delegated authority. Enforcing these requirements, i.e., that the Secretary establish the statutory predicates for invoking the DPA, does not amount to second-guessing genuine executive judgments about national defense. Instead, enforcement honors the conditions precedent Congress imposed to prevent abuse of the DPA. DOE’s failure to satisfy these statutory prerequisites invalidates the Wright Order.”

Separate Fight Over Citizenship Verification The IRS ruling follows another high-profile legal battle involving the administration's efforts to leverage federal databases, this time in the election arena.
Circuit denied the administration's request to stay a lower court ruling that blocked implementation of an expanded version of DHS' Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE.
When the administration sought emergency relief, the appeals court refused.
text:
The Trump administration suffered another legal setback Tuesday when a federal appeals court blocked an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) program used to share taxpayer information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), marking the second major court ruling in recent days involving administration efforts to use federal data systems in immigration and election-related enforcement.

In a unanimous ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld a lower-court order preventing the IRS from continuing a data-sharing arrangement with ICE that had already resulted in more than 47,000 taxpayer records being disclosed to immigration authorities. The court found that challengers were likely to succeed in arguing that the program violated federal tax confidentiality laws.

In a statement to Newsweek, the Center for Taxpayer Rights (CTR), which brought the case, said the court upheld the "fundamental right to the confidentiality of taxpayer return information."

Read More on Politics

"It made clear that Treasury and the IRS can’t do end runs around carefully crafted statutory exceptions to confidentiality just because it wants to or thinks it knows better," a spokesperson said. "All US taxpayers should be relieved by the court’s order today."

The decision comes days after the same appeals court declined to pause a separate ruling against the administration's expanded SAVE citizenship-verification system, which is at the center of a broader legal battle over voter-roll maintenance and citizenship checks ahead of this year's midterm elections.

The practical impact of the two court cases may be felt most acutely in states that hoped to use expanded federal databases to verify voter citizenship before November's elections.

“DHS strongly disagrees with this ruling," a DHS spokesperson told Newsweek Tuesday. "We will continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal, and this ruling in no way prevents us from doing so.”

Newsweek also reached out to the White House, the IRS, and the League of Women Voters for comment Tuesday afternoon.

Court Says IRS-ICE Policy Likely Violated Federal Law

The IRS case stems from a 2025 agreement between the tax agency and ICE under which immigration officials sought address information on people they said were under criminal investigation for failing to comply with final deportation orders.

According to court filings, ICE requested information on roughly 1.28 million people. The IRS subsequently developed what it called a "Data-Exchange Procedure" for processing those requests.

The appeals court found that the process likely conflicted with Section 6103 of the Internal Revenue Code, a post-Watergate taxpayer privacy law that tightly restricts when tax information can be shared with other federal agencies.

Among other findings, the court said that the IRS disclosed taxpayer information even when ICE requests lacked information required by statute. Judges noted that the system accepted requests where address fields contained entries such as "Unknown Address," "Failed to Provide" or "NA NA," despite federal law requiring agencies to provide the taxpayer's name and address before obtaining return information.

The court also found that more than 90 percent of the records disclosed to ICE were generated through a TIN-matching process that did not verify whether a valid address had been supplied.

"The Data-Exchange Procedure indisputably contravenes the requirements of section 6103," Judge Cornelia Pillard wrote for the panel.

The judges further noted that government attorneys acknowledged during oral arguments that some disclosures occurred "not in compliance with the statute."

Why the Case Matters

The ruling is significant because it limits one of the administration's efforts to use existing government databases to aid immigration enforcement. The panel emphasized that taxpayer privacy protections were strengthened after Watergate amid concerns about executive branch misuse of sensitive information.

The court also rejected government arguments that the IRS procedure was merely an internal operational process and therefore shielded from judicial review, holding instead that it constituted reviewable "final agency action" under the Administrative Procedure Act.

For immigration advocates and taxpayer-rights groups, the decision represents a major victory. The court found that organizations challenging the policy had presented evidence that immigrant taxpayers became less willing to engage with tax assistance programs because of fears their information could be shared with immigration authorities.

"As far as going forward, we will need to see if the government appeals the ruling," the CTR said. "We will also need to see what, if any, changes to procedures they may make in light of this ruling. And of course, there are about 43,000 taxpayers whose return information has been found to be unlawfully shared with ICE by two courts [the district court and the court of appeals]—these taxpayers must be notified so that they may seek damages against the government for this unlawful disclosure."

Separate Fight Over Citizenship Verification

The IRS ruling follows another high-profile legal battle involving the administration's efforts to leverage federal databases, this time in the election arena.

Last week, the D.C. Circuit denied the administration's request to stay a lower court ruling that blocked implementation of an expanded version of DHS' Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE.

Historically, SAVE was used primarily to verify immigration status for eligibility determinations involving certain government programs. Under changes implemented in 2025 following a Trump executive order, the system was expanded to allow searches using Social Security numbers, access to additional Social Security Administration records and bulk queries covering large numbers of people.

The administration argued that the changes would help states verify citizenship and maintain accurate voter rolls. According to court records, the modified system allowed state and local agencies to submit bulk requests and verify citizenship using Social Security records in ways that were not previously available.

A coalition that included the League of Women Voters challenged the system, arguing that it violated federal privacy and Social Security laws. In June, a district judge sided with the challengers, concluding that DHS lacked statutory authority for portions of the expanded system and that it violated multiple federal statutes.

When the administration sought emergency relief, the appeals court refused. The panel said the government had failed to make the "strong showing" needed to justify a stay and noted that many of its central legal arguments were raised only after the district court had already ruled.

The court also pointed to evidence that some U.S. citizens were incorrectly flagged because Social Security records had not been updated after naturalization, potentially requiring them to provide additional proof of citizenship or risk removal from voter rolls.

Potential Supreme Court Battle

Both cases could ultimately reach the Supreme Court.

The IRS decision only concerns a preliminary injunction, not the final merits of the lawsuit. However, the D.C. Circuit repeatedly stated that challengers are likely to succeed in showing the IRS program violated federal law.

The SAVE litigation is also ongoing, with the government on Tuesday asking the Supreme Court to take up the case. The appeals court's recent order addressed only whether the administration was entitled to emergency relief while the appeal proceeds. The underlying questions about the legality of the modified system remain before the court.

Taken together, the cases underscore a growing legal battle over how far the federal government can go in using taxpayer, immigration and Social Security data to advance immigration enforcement and election-integrity initiatives, issues likely to remain politically charged as the 2026 midterm campaign enters its final weeks.

text:
143

(OSV News) — Touring the U.S.–Mexico border between Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, and El Paso, Texas, Archbishop Stefan Hesse of Hamburg said the towering fortifications and razor wire dividing the two border communities evoked a painful memory in his own country’s history: the Berlin Wall.

“In a way, the inhumanity and massiveness of these border fortifications reminded me of the Berlin Wall, which divided the German capital for nearly 30 years and caused great suffering for the people living there,” Archbishop Hesse told OSV News in an Aug. 31 interview.

“I found the border situation to be disturbing,” added the archbishop, who serves as chairman of the German bishops’ conference’s migration commission. “Two cities that had essentially grown together into one — and whose populations remain connected in many ways — are now hermetically separated by a border wall and razor wire.”

Archbishop Hesse embarked on an Aug. 20-27 “solidarity trip” to assess the humanitarian reality along key migration routes, the German bishops’ conference said in a statement published Aug. 20.

Special envoy for refugee issues

Also serving as the conference’s special envoy for refugee issues, the archbishop has embarked on similar trips in past years, including Ukraine, Kenya and Egypt. During his visit, Archbishop Hesse met migrants, volunteers, aid agency representatives, civil and church leaders, including Bishop Mark J. Seitz of El Paso, immediate past chairman of the U.S. bishops’ Committee on Migration.

Bishop Seitz and Dylan Corbett, executive director of the Hope Border Institute, a migrant advocacy agency based in El Paso, hosted the archbishop’s delegation.

Recalling his visit to Mexico, Archbishop Hesse told OSV News that, due to restrictive U.S. policies, the country that was once “a country of origin and transit” has now become “a destination country for migrants” and is also facing additional challenges from deportations “out of the U.S.”

The German prelate said he was struck by two distinct encounters, one “with an elderly gentleman from Cuba whom I met at the church-run Albergue Belén (“Bethlehem Shelter”) in Tapachula.”

“He lived and worked in the U.S. for 46 years, was well integrated, and has now been deported to southern Mexico — to a region he doesn’t know and where he has little prospect of a dignified life in his old age. His fate is like that of a tree that has been uprooted,” he said.

The second was with a young man from Ciudad Juárez who, at a young age, was involved in organized crime and had also worked as a “smuggler” who guided people along the treacherous border.

Faith, family help man escape ‘clutches’ of organized crime

“The young man told me with remarkable openness how, with the help of his faith, he finally managed to escape the clutches of organized crime. Now he is involved in a project that helps young migrants find their way in Mexico,” the archbishop said.

Amid the suffering of those along the border, Archbishop Hesse told OSV News that he had heard and witnessed that “without the Church’s services, the situation would be much worse.”

“Approximately 80% of the shelters are run by the Church. There, refugees and migrants not only receive a roof over their heads but are also treated with dignity as human beings,” he said.

One such example, he noted, was the CAFEMIN shelter run by the Sisters of St. Joseph in Mexico City, who “truly brings Pope Francis’s four verbs to life: welcoming, protecting, promoting and integrating migrants.”

However, the archbishop also noticed that there is a “wide gulf” between Christian shelters that are “centered on the dignity of every single person” and detention centers “where migrants are primarily viewed as a threat.”

Sense of humanity is ‘being lost’

“Certainly, it is the state’s responsibility to regulate migration. But during my trip to Mexico and the U.S., I also witnessed what happens when migration is treated exclusively as a security issue: A fundamental sense of humanity ends up being lost,” he told OSV News.

In Ciudad Juárez, Archbishop Hesse was joined by Bishop Seitz in a visit to a migrant youth center. The delegation also visited faith-based migrant shelters and shared meals with migrants, many of them stranded in the city as a result of U.S. border restrictions.

The group also met with representatives from Jesuit Refugee Service-Mexico and Derechos Humanos Integrales en Acción, two organizations working with migrants on the ground and supported by the Hope Border Institute’s Border Refugee Assistance Fund.

In El Paso, Archbishop Hesse visited Mount Cristo Rey, a sacred pilgrimage site at the border in Sunland Park, New Mexico. The site is in the Diocese of Las Cruces but sits right at the edge of the El Paso Diocese.

Briefing on Mount Cristo Rey legal battle

The Hope Border Institute briefed the German delegation on the legal battle now facing the mountain. The Trump administration wants to seize 14 acres that include the pilgrimage site to build a section of the border wall. Several Church entities have filed a court challenge to the Trump administration’s claim it can use eminent domain to seize private property for public use.

Archbishop Hesse also met with leaders and guests at Annunciation House, an El Paso migrant shelter, and with staff from Estrella del Paso, El Paso’s local Catholic legal service provider for immigrants and refugees. The delegation additionally observed immigration court proceedings.

“We were honored to welcome Archbishop Hesse to El Paso and Ciudad Juárez to share the work of welcome in our borderlands community,” Corbett said in a Sept. 8 statement sent to OSV News. “The example of people of many faith traditions here at the border to accompany those in need demonstrates what is possible at borders and local communities around the world.”

Gratitude for El Paso Diocese welcome

In his interview with OSV News, Archbishop Hesse expressed his gratitude to the bishop for welcoming him to the Diocese of El Paso and noted the diocese’s support for migrant initiatives in Mexico.

However, he said, what stood out was “the spiritual dimension,” where people on either side of the border “see themselves as one large Catholic community on both banks of the Rio Grande.”

“When Bishop Seitz and I celebrated a beautiful Mass in Ciudad Juárez with Mexicans, Americans and migrants, the bishop summed it up perfectly: In the Church, there are no borders. That is how Catholicism is brought to life,” he told OSV News.

Drawing a parallel between the migration crisis in the U.S. and growing tensions in Europe, especially in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and in countries along the Mediterranean sea routes, Archbishop Hesse expressed concern that, in most circumstances, “the rule of law and the respect for human rights are declining.”

Nations seen as too focused on ‘deterrence, externalization’

“As soon as wealthy countries focus primarily on deterrence and externalization, they fail to live up to their humanitarian responsibilities and risk losing sight of human dignity,” the archbishop said.

Ensuring safe pathways for people seeking protection, while dedicating “sufficient resources for development cooperation,” he said, would help reduce risks for those fleeing their homeland and address “the root causes of forced migration.”

“Surely people in the industrialized nations of North America and Europe have their own set of worries,” Archbishop Hesse told OSV News. “However, it is important to keep reminding ourselves of the situation in other regions of the world.”

“If we, as Americans and Europeans, reflect on such examples of charity and allow ourselves to be moved by them, we can succeed in overcoming our tendency to indifference and self-centeredness,” he said.

Junno Arocho Esteves is an international correspondent for OSV News. Follow him on X @jae_journalist.

text:
Two House Democrats introduced legislation to prohibit federal immigration agents from using electric "shock gloves" during immigration enforcement operations, highlighting potential dangers.

The move follows a plan by Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) to acquire the devices for immigration agents.

Reps. Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania and Delia Ramirez of Illinois announced the legislation, known as the No Shock Act, on September 3. The bill would bar the use of "shock gloves" by federal law enforcement officers enforcing immigration laws and would also apply to state and local officers operating under federal immigration enforcement partnerships.

Read More on News

A "shock glove" is defined as a glove capable of delivering an electric shock when applied directly to a person's body, including the CTG-5 G.L.O.V.E., or Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, manufactured by Kentucky-based Compliant Technologies LLC.

The legislation follows DHS plans to spend approximately $16.7 million on 6,000 gloves for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) personnel. The gloves are designed to deliver an electrical stimulus through direct skin contact and are marketed by the manufacturer as a compliance and de-escalation tool for law enforcement and corrections officers.

Under the proposed legislation, the Homeland Security Secretary would be required to prohibit the use of shock gloves by federal officers enforcing immigration laws. The bill would extend the prohibition to law enforcement agencies participating in the federal government's 287(g) program, which allows certain state and local officers to perform immigration enforcement functions.

A spokesperson for DHS told Newsweek, "Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers."

Rep. Ramirez said in a press release: "Under no circumstances can DHS be trusted with electric shock gloves and the power to inflict ‘sudden’ death.' After opening a Congressional inquiry to demand that DHS immediately halt the acquisition and deployment of electric shock gloves, I’m joining Rep. Dean to prohibit these cruel devices from being used during immigration enforcement."

The Compliant Technologies website states: "CD3 Technology is not risk free and should be treated seriously like any other weapon. Follow all laws, agency policies, and Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) when deploying the G.L.O.V.E. CD3," and warns "may result in injury or death if not followed or observed."

Ramirez also called for dismantling DHS, saying lawmakers should "take every weapon, every dollar, every authority away" from the agency.

"For nearly two years, we have witnessed grotesquely un-American behavior from ICE agents—the tragic killing of innocent Americans, the wrongful arrests of lawful residents and peaceful protesters, and the inhumane conditions at ICE facilities across the country," Rep. Dean said. "Now, DHS seeks to further arm ICE agents with electric shock gloves, enabling them to inflict even more pain with zero accountability."

The legislation has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee. As of Tuesday, the bill had not attracted bipartisan support among its listed cosponsors.

How Would They Be Used?

The proposal comes weeks after DHS' planned purchase of the gloves drew public attention. While ICE has not publicly released deployment guidelines, experts have said the devices could be used during arrests, detention facility operations and other close-contact encounters.

Compliant Technologies describes the G.L.O.V.E. as a "conductive distraction and de-escalation device" that functions as a standard glove until activated. The company says the technology is designed to gain compliance from resistant individuals and does not leave lasting marks. Manufacturer guidance also states the gloves should not be used as punishment or solely in response to verbal noncompliance.

A spokesperson for DHS said, "ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.

"Our officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training."

DHS said the devices would be issued to personnel in Homeland Security Investigations and Enforcement and Removal Operations, ICE's two principal operational divisions.

Critics Raise Concerns

A letter from Ramirez and 49 other reps to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin dated August 31 raises safety concerns about the gloves which deliver a 380-volt shock, and includes claims they violate the Convention Against Torture.

Opposition to the gloves has also emerged in the Senate. On August 27, Senator Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada and 15 other senators called on the Trump administration to abandon plans to equip ICE officers with electric shock gloves. In a letter to ICE, the lawmakers urge the agency to cancel the proposed purchase and requested detailed information about the devices' intended use, training requirements, safety protocols, oversight mechanisms, and accountability measures if the acquisition proceeds. The senators also raise concerns about the necessity of the devices and ICE's planned use of a no-bid procurement process for the contract.

Civil rights groups such as the ACLU have raised concerns about the planned deployment of the devices, while supporters of less-lethal law enforcement technologies argue such tools can provide officers with alternatives to higher levels of force.

Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and ICE official, told Newsweek, "There's a real tactical downside that officers have mentioned to me, that while wearing the glove, you can't readily use your firearm or another less-lethal option, which can put the officer in a worse position."

"Where I could see a limited justification is in a controlled, custodial setting, where the environment is contained, and the officer isn't juggling multiple threats. But for arrests being made out in the community, vehicle stops, at-large arrests, neighborhood operations, I would have serious concerns."

Concerns about the use of shock gloves have also surfaced outside immigration enforcement. Earlier this year, Omaha Public Schools banned the devices for school security personnel after officials confirmed they had been used on two students.

The No Shock Act faces an uncertain path in Congress, where Republicans control both the House and Senate. To become law, the measure would need approval from both chambers and the signature of President Donald Trump.

The bill is one of several Democratic-led efforts to impose additional oversight and accountability measures on DHS and ICE as the Trump administration continues to carry out its flagship mass deportation policy. The issue could also become part of the debate ahead of this year's midterm elections, when Democrats will seek to regain control of Congress.

text:
In March 2025, over 230 Venezuelan migrants were flown on private airplanes to El Salvador’s Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo (CECOT) mega prison. There, the men were subjected to cruel, inhumane, and degrading treatment. They were physically and psychologically tortured, forced to survive in punitive conditions, and held incommunicado for over four months.

CSI Aviation and Global Crossing Airlines, the private companies that flew the men to CECOT, had rushed to arrange transportation services, even as proceedings before a court seeking to halt the flights unfolded, alongside widespread public reporting and scrutiny. The company undertook this transfer with the Trump administration, pursuant to a well-publicized agreement between the Salvadoran and U.S. governments that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly lauded as “the most unprecedented, extraordinary, extraordinary migratory agreement anywhere in the world.”

In CECOT, the men endured systematic abuse, sexual assault, extreme heat, overcrowded cells, and ritualized violence and humiliation. All the while, the Administration publicized and celebrated their degradation as a means to advance its mass deportation policy, incite self-deportation, and threaten would-be migrants.

In July 2026, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and partners filed a class action lawsuit against CSI Aviation and Global Crossing Airlines, seeking accountability for their role in the torture of the Venezuelan men deported to CECOT.

What is the legal argument in this case?

This case asserts claims under ​​42 U.S.C. § 1985 and 1986 that CSI Airlines and Global Crossing Airlines conspired with the United States government to deprive the men they flew to CECOT of their civil rights. It also asserts that the airlines violated Plaintiffs’ safe conducts under the Alien Tort Statute and raises claims of false imprisonment, negligence, and negligent and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

What is the status of this case?

The case is pending.
