text:
BOSTON — Governor Maura Healey today released new guidance and resources to implement the PROTECT Act, providing state government actors, health care providers, law enforcement agencies, and employers with clear direction as additional protections for residents under the law take effect.

The new guidance addresses protections for nonpublic areas of state property and in health care facilities, limits state and local law enforcement participation in civil immigration enforcement, and a new state law requirement for employers to notify workers in writing if ICE is going to inspect employee records.

“We passed the PROTECT Act to keep people safe from the dangerous tactics we are seeing from ICE here in Massachusetts and across the country,” said Governor Maura Healey. “This guidance makes clear what officials across state government, health care providers, law enforcement agencies, and employers need to know and do if they come across ICE. The PROTECT Act is about keeping our communities safe, protecting people’s rights and preserving the trust that allows people to seek care, report crimes and access the services they rely on.”

“The PROTECT Act gives communities across Massachusetts important protections, and this guidance helps turn those protections into practice,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “Our employers, health care providers, law enforcement officers and state employees are on the front lines serving people every day. We want to make sure they have the clarity and support they need to do their jobs, keep people safe and continue providing the services that families and communities depend on.”

Governor Healey signed the PROTECT Act on August 5, establishing some of the strongest protections in the nation against abuses by federal immigration authorities. The law limits civil arrests in courthouses, schools, child care programs, nursing homes and nonpublic areas of health care facilities; restricts the use of state property for civil law enforcement; strictly limits state and local participation in civil immigration enforcement; strengthens protections for workers and families; and creates a state civil rights remedy for constitutional violations.

The guidance released today includes:

State Property

Governor Healey and the Executive Office for Administration and Finance (A&F) issued statewide guidelines limiting civil law enforcement activity in nonpublic areas of state property.

Under the guidelines, civil law enforcement activities, including civil arrests, are prohibited in designated nonpublic areas of state buildings and other property, unless they are required by state or federal law or to administer a state or federally supported program, authorized by a valid judicial warrant or judicial order, or necessary to address a specific and immediate health or safety threat.

The Act applies broadly to any property owned, leased, occupied, controlled by or used for business by the Commonwealth, except courthouses. The guidelines instruct state agencies and other Commonwealth offices to review their property portfolio and designate areas as “nonpublic,” with the goal of preserving access to essential public service and the ability to conduct business with the state, without fear or intimidation.

“We, as an administration, take the health and safety of residents of Massachusetts seriously,” said Administration and Finance Secretary Matthew J. Gorzkowicz. “No one should be afraid to access state buildings or the government services to which they are entitled. These guidelines will ensure people feel safe and protected by their state government.”

Health Care Facilities

The Executive Office of Health and Human Services (EOHHS), Department of Public Health (DPH), Department of Mental Health (DMH), Department of Developmental Services (DDS) and MassHealth developed guidance and a model policy to help health care providers implement new protections for nonpublic areas of their service sites. The law requires covered providers to establish policies for interactions with law enforcement engaged in civil law enforcement, including federal immigration enforcement, within 30 days of today.

“No one should have to weigh their health and safety against the fear of immigration enforcement,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Kiame Mahaniah, MD, MBA. “The PROTECT Act will help residents maintain access to services they need, and ensure that places where people go for care will remain a trusted resource.”

The requirements apply to a broad range of providers, including hospitals, community health centers, clinics, mobile clinics, nursing and rest homes, emergency medical services, adult day health centers, substance use disorder treatment programs, certain physician and advanced practice nursing practices, providers serving people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, and certain MassHealth day habilitation providers.

Under the Act, certain covered providers must designate a point of contact for interactions with civil law enforcement, identify nonpublic areas where people receive care or discuss protected health information, or that are otherwise not open to the public, and establish procedures so staff, volunteers, and administrators know how to respond to requests from civil law enforcement. Civil arrests are not allowed in those designated nonpublic areas without a judicial warrant, except as otherwise required by law or to administer a state or federally supported program. Covered providers required to adopt a policy under the Act must do so by October 4. Today’s release of guidance and a model policy by the Healey-Driscoll Administrations is designed to assist in those efforts.

Law Enforcement and Civil Immigration Enforcement

The Executive Office of Public Safety and Security (EOPSS), Municipal Police Training Committee (MPTC) and Massachusetts Chiefs of Police Association (MCOPA) developed new roll call training materials to help police officers, dispatchers, records staff and other law enforcement personnel understand the PROTECT Act’s requirements and how they apply to day-to-day public safety work.

Beginning today, the law limits when state and local law enforcement may inquire about, record, share or act on a person’s immigration or citizenship status. It also restricts the use of state and local personnel, facilities, equipment and other public resources to conduct or participate in federal civil immigration enforcement and prohibits holding someone past the time they are otherwise eligible for release based solely on an immigration detainer.

The guidance makes equally clear what the PROTECT Act does not change. Massachusetts law enforcement can continue investigating and enforcing criminal laws, making lawful arrests with a judicial warrant, conducting booking procedures, keeping the peace, responding to emergencies and working with federal, state and local partners on criminal investigations.

If a crime or breach of the peace occurs during a federal civil immigration operation, officers may respond to address the public safety issue while remaining separate from the civil immigration enforcement activity itself.

Notice to Employees of I-9 Inspections

The Executive Office of Labor and Workforce Development (LWD), Office for Refugees and Immigrants (ORI) and Attorney General’s Office issued guidance to help Massachusetts employers comply with a new state law requirement to notify employees of upcoming inspections of I-9 employment eligibility records by ICE.

Under the PROTECT Act, Massachusetts employers must provide employees with written notice within 48 hours of receiving a Notice of Inspection from ICE for I-9 forms or other employment records, except where otherwise required by federal law.

The Administration is also providing employers with a sample notice that can be used or modified to comply with the law. Notice must be provided individually to employees and should be provided in the employee’s primary language; posting a notice at the workplace alone does not satisfy the requirement.

“This guidance gives employers clear steps to follow while ensuring workers receive timely and accurate information,” said Secretary of Labor and Workforce Development Lauren Jones. “By making sure employers and employees are informed, we are strengthening workplace protections and helping employers across the state understand and meet their responsibilities under the PROTECT Act.”

Today’s guidance builds on guidance released by Governor Healey last month to help K-12 schools and child care programs implement the PROTECT Act. Those resources provided model policies and procedures for responding to civil law enforcement, reviewing requests for access, protecting confidential information and communicating with students and families.

Earlier this year, Governor Healey also signed Executive Order 650 to protect access to essential state services and issued statewide guidance to schools, child care providers, colleges and universities, health care facilities and places of worship on interacting with federal immigration enforcement.

The Healey-Driscoll Administration will continue working with state agencies, employers, health care providers, law enforcement and communities across Massachusetts to fully implement the PROTECT Act and ensure its protections are carried out effectively statewide.

text:
A protest in a Frederick neighborhood turned violent Friday night as Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers clashed with demonstrators, leaving some injured and prompting calls for an investigation.

Protesters gathered near Stoneybrook Court after ICE vehicles were spotted in the area on Thursday. By Friday, more than 100 community members had joined the demonstration, chanting and linking arms in opposition to the federal immigration enforcement activity.

“We were attacked. Our community was physically attacked by federal law enforcement officers,” Frederick City Council President Cesar Diaz said. “In the past, we’ve seen them come in, they do something, they kidnap someone and then they leave. This time, they stuck around.”

Witnesses said ICE officers appeared to be targeting a specific house and began driving SUVs onto sidewalks, ordering protesters to move.

“He started to really come at me and so I moved off. There was another woman there with me, and then, there was another protester sort of in front, like caddy-corner to me. He actually plowed into that person and started pushing them with his car,” said Soolah Kemp, a protester.

Kemp also described how a group of protesters later linked arms in front of the home.

“They were just standing there. It wasn’t like they were fighting. They weren’t. They just linked arms,” Kemp said.

Video from the scene captured the moment officers physically engaged with protesters.

“(They were) beating people with batons, kicking them, punching them, throwing people on the ground, just to attempt to get into the front door of this home,” said Tatiana Santos, who is with Indivisible Frederick Forward.

Protesters suffered cuts and bruises, with some requiring hospitalization. Frederick police eventually arrived to deescalate the situation. Witnesses said ICE officers broke into the home and later spoke with the family inside.

“We were asked to be quiet so that they could have a conversation with ICE and then ICE left,” Santos said.

Witnesses said it did not appear that ICE made any arrests during the incident.

Diaz expressed concern about the implications of the encounter.

“This is the first time that’s happened in Frederick. I think that level of action is the first time that’s happened anywhere in Maryland, and now, people are concerned. Is this the new normal? Is this an escalation?” Diaz said.

Diaz also noted that he had not seen a warrant for ICE’s activity. Community members are now calling on the Maryland attorney general to investigate the incident.

Baltimore City Councilwoman Odette Ramos, D-District 14, criticized the officers’ actions, writing: “Shame on ICE for their violent, unconstitutional behavior.”

Requests for comment from the governor’s office, Frederick police, and ICE have not yet been answered.

text:
STOCKHOLM, Sweden (AP) — A far-right Belgian party was likely not entitled to use IKEA’s trademarks to promote an anti-immigration campaign and may have caused “significant detriment” to the furniture giant’s reputation, the European Union’s highest court ruled on Tuesday.

In 2022, the Belgian far-right and Flemish separatist party Vlaams Belang unveiled what it called the “IKEA Plan – Immigration Really Can Be Different” at a press conference, using IKEA-style logos, signs and imagery to present proposals aimed at tightening immigration rules in Belgium.

IKEA brought an infringement action before a Belgian court, arguing its trademarks were used illegally. In response, the Vrijheidsfonds association, which was in charge of the campaign on the party’s behalf, argued that its use of the company’s trademarks without permission was protected by freedom of expression.

The Belgian court referred the case to the European Court of Justice (ECJ), which found that “the use of those IKEA trade marks may cause significant detriment to the repute of those trade marks and to the interests of their proprietor.”

The court said invoking freedom of expression in such cases requires the trademarks to be used in good faith or in the public interest, conditions that did not appear to be met. It added that it did not appear that using IKEA’s reputation to disseminate a political message took precedence over IKEA’s rights and interests.

While the Belgian court will make the final decision, it is expected to take the ECJ’s guidance into account when issuing its ruling.

“Inter IKEA fully believes in – and deeply respects – freedom of expression,” the company said in a statement welcoming the ruling. “At the same time, it cannot accept the use of the IKEA trademarks in ways that damage their reputation or distinctive character, particularly when such use serves no other purpose than to free-ride on the reputation of the IKEA brand.”

text:
Mr President,

In Syria, we welcome the steps taken by the government on its political transition, including convening a new parliament, addressing Assad-era legacies, and engaging the international community. But the situation remains delicate. We urge the government to proceed in an inclusive and representative way, protecting the rights of all Syrians.

In South Sudan, the human rights situation remains fragile, while developments cast doubt on prospects for peaceful, inclusive and credible elections. We remain concerned by violence against civilians, restrictions on political space and continued impunity, including conflict-related sexual violence. All parties must demonstrate restraint, engage in dialogue and ensure accountability.

China has yet to implement the recommendations of the Office of the High Commissioner’s Xinjiang Assessment. Evidence of violations in Xinjiang and Tibet persists, freedom of religion or belief is being further restricted, and the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress risks undermining the rights of individuals belonging to minorities. We welcome the High Commissioner’s continued engagement on these issues.

Finally, five years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the human cost continues to grow. As Russia continues its assault on Ukraine’s sovereignty, the international community must not look away. We remain steadfast in our support for Ukraine and in efforts to hold Russia to account.

Thank you.

text:
An analysis by a Kentucky policy center shows the number of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in the commonwealth continues to grow as the number of local agencies helping ICE has exploded over the past year.

The Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, using data from the Deportation Data Project, showed the number of ICE arrests in Kentucky is at close to 5,000 since President Donald Trump took office in 2025.

An increasing number of those ICE-related arrests are a result of the growing number of Kentucky law enforcement agencies with agreements with ICE to enforce immigration policy, the data showed.

In January 2025 the number of ICE arrests in Kentucky was 114. By July 2026, the number of monthly ICE arrests grew to 443. About 15.8% of those arrests were credited to local law enforcement agreements, the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy analysis showed. In November 2025, only one ICE arrest was credited to local law enforcement.

The Trump administration has pushed an aggressive agenda to deport people who have entered the country illegally.

As part of that crackdown, the administration has pushed local agencies to sign agreements with ICE to augment those enforcement efforts, commonly referred to as 287 (g) agreements.

Data from ICE show a five-fold increase in the number of Kentucky jails, police and county sheriffs who have signed those agreements from July 2025 to August 2026.

In July 2025, a Lexington Herald-Leader review of those agreements showed 11 agencies with formal agreements with ICE. In August 2026, that number had jumped to 55 agencies.

There are financial incentives for local law enforcement to participate. As part of a July 2025 federal budget and spending bill, local law enforcement can now receive up to $7,500 per ICE trained employee, $100,000 to buy vehicles and other equipment and money to cover some overtime and retirement benefits, according to ICE’s website.

The above benefits are for police agencies that sign task force model agreements. The task force model allows officers trained by ICE to enforce immigration law during routine police activity, like traffic stops. This model was once discontinued over concerns about racial profiling, but it was revived by the Trump administration in January 2025.

The other agreements include the jail enforcement model, which allows jail officials to interrogate those who are arrested and detained about their immigration status. The warrant service officer model allows a designated jail employee to serve ICE warrants on people in custody.

The vast majority of Kentucky law enforcement agencies, 52, with agreements with ICE have task force model agreements. Counties can have multiple agreements. For example, Grayson County agencies have signed agreements for all three models.

Lexington has no ICE agreements, the data shows. Agencies in Central Kentucky with ICE agreements include the Scott County Sheriff’s Office and the Winchester Police Department.

text:
In 2025, 89 million people lived or worked near a U.S. facility with high-risk chemicals. In terrorists' hands, these chemicals could inflict mass damage, including impacts equal to a nuclear explosion.

This Q&A discusses chemical facility security, including staff vetting. A Department of Homeland Security program had facilities vet their staff for links to terrorism. But the program ended in 2023 and facilities can't access the watchlist on their own.

Without federal options to vet staff for this purpose, these facilities are vulnerable to insider terrorist attacks.

We recommended DHS implement options to vet staff for terrorist ties.

Chemical Facility Operations

Chemical facility with pipes and two workers in blue jumpsuits and yellow hard hats.

What GAO Found

The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is the sector risk management agency (SRMA) for the U.S. chemical sector, responsible for implementing programs to assist facility owners and operators in identifying and mitigating security risks. In 2007, DHS established a regulatory program to mitigate security risks for high-risk chemical facilities. As part of this program, CISA required facilities to vet their personnel and certain unescorted visitors for terrorist ties against the U.S. government’s terrorist watchlist. Vetting against the U.S. terrorist watchlist is an inherently governmental function that the private sector cannot perform on its own; therefore, CISA set up a process with options facilities could use for such vetting. Authorization for the regulatory program lapsed in July 2023. The program, including personnel vetting, was discontinued. High-risk chemical facilities are now responsible for identifying and mitigating their own security risks.

According to CISA officials and selected private sector stakeholders GAO interviewed, losing access to the terrorist vetting process is the most significant challenge high-risk facility owners and operators have faced since the discontinuation of CISA’s regulatory program and it has left a gap in chemical facility security that poses substantial risks. The statutory authority that establishes SRMA responsibilities specifies that SRMAs are to implement security programs to assist stakeholders in identifying and mitigating risks to their assets and systems. As of May 2026, CISA said it was exploring whether the agency’s SRMA authority could be used to set up a vetting process. Without federal options for the terrorist vetting of personnel, facility owners and operators lack a critical tool to protect their facilities from an insider terrorist attack and from potential disruptions to critical national supply chains.

From fiscal years 2024 to 2025, the number of CISA active personnel dedicated to chemical sector activities declined from 214 (96 percent of authorized positions) to 52 (25 percent of authorized positions). The active personnel did not include full-time personnel scheduled to separate from CISA by the end of calendar year 2025 through deferred resignations programs. CISA said the reductions have necessitated reducing or eliminating services, such as most on-site facility assessments, but also said the agency continues to offer other services, such as security training and cybersecurity guidance. Selected private sector stakeholders told GAO that CISA’s personnel reductions and the loss of experienced staff have reduced their contact with CISA regarding facility security vulnerabilities.

Chemical Facility Warehouse and Operations

Why GAO Did This Study

According to DHS, as of 2025, more than 89 million people lived or worked within 2 miles of a U.S. facility using high-risk chemicals. DHS estimates that should high-risk chemicals be weaponized, it could cause significant harm to surrounding populations, from fatalities within the facility to the equivalent impact of a nuclear explosion.

GAO was asked to examine DHS’s efforts to mitigate security risks to the U.S. chemical sector. This report addresses, among other issues, CISA and sector stakeholder assessments of sector security following the discontinuation of a facility regulatory program, effects of the lack of a federal terrorist vetting process for chemical facility personnel, and effects of fiscal year 2025 reductions in CISA personnel on sector support services.

GAO reviewed relevant statutes, CISA guidelines and procedures, and CISA data on full-time authorized positions and active agency personnel for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. GAO interviewed CISA officials; conducted site visits to five chemical facilities; and interviewed private sector stakeholders, including representatives from the private sector coordinating council, three industry associations, and six chemical companies.

title: The Alachua County Commission signed an anti-ICE resolution. What's next?
description:
After four months of debate and concerns about risks to state funding, the Alachua County Commission passed a resolution Aug. 11 opposing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in the county.
The resolution also highlights concerns about the expansion of immigration enforcement in Alachua County.
The GINI proposal Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative’s five-point petition was first presented to the Alachua County Commission April 28 during public comment.
Alachua County Attorney Sylvia E. Torres said the state hasn’t pushed back against Orange County’s resolution, but the Florida Attorney General’s office could issue a warning to it or Alachua County for passing a resolution conflicting with state law like the 287(g) agreement.
The Alachua County Sheriff’s Office signed the agreement, while the Gainesville Police Department hasn’t.
text:
After four months of debate and concerns about risks to state funding, the Alachua County Commission passed a resolution Aug. 11 opposing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in the county.

Drafted by the Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative, the three-page resolution expresses a commitment to ensuring all residents, regardless of immigration status, feel safe interacting with law enforcement and seeking social services. It warns against discriminatory actions by law enforcement, but does not mention ICE specifically.

The resolution also highlights concerns about the expansion of immigration enforcement in Alachua County. It urges federal immigration officers to clearly identify themselves and inform residents about the purposes of law enforcement activities.

The board voted 4-0 to sign the resolution, with Commissioner Mary Alford absent. In an Aug. 12 Facebook post, Alford wrote that she was absent from the meeting and agreed with the resolution, but believed it could bring “unwanted attention” to Alachua County.

In June, Jacob Torner, the vice president for programs at the TaskForce for Ending Homelessness, wrote to city and county officials that passing an anti-ICE resolution could cause the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to view Gainesville and Alachua County "less favorably" when awarding federal funds for local services.

The GINI proposal

Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative’s five-point petition was first presented to the Alachua County Commission April 28 during public comment. The resolution didn’t make it to the agenda until June 23, when the commission unanimously voted to delay the decision so it could discuss it with the county attorney.

The petition was also brought to the attention of city commissioners during the public comment portion of a June 18 meeting.

During a July 16 meeting, the Gainesville City Commission voted to postpone the decision on the resolution despite over a dozen public commenters encouraging the commissioners to support it. It’s unclear when the city commission will revisit the decision.

The county’s meeting

County commissioners and staff discussed the resolution for over two hours Aug. 11, weighing potential risks to state funding, such as grants given to the city and county by the state.

Ahead of the vote, commissioners considered actions by other counties, like Orange County, which passed a similar resolution opposing current ICE operations in March to oppose a rumored ICE detention facility in east Orlando.

Alachua County Attorney Sylvia E. Torres said the state hasn’t pushed back against Orange County’s resolution, but the Florida Attorney General’s office could issue a warning to it or Alachua County for passing a resolution conflicting with state law like the 287(g) agreement.

The 287(g) agreement allows state and local law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration operations. The Alachua County Sheriff’s Office signed the agreement, while the Gainesville Police Department hasn’t.

“There’s a history of the attorney general sending out letters that say, ‘What you’ve done is not within your authority’ or that it is ‘malfeasance or misfeasance in office,’ ordering you to basically repeal the action or threatening removal from office,’” Torres said in the meeting.

However, the GPD issued a general order Aug. 27 requiring officers to report anyone they suspect is in the country illegally. The move was made to comply with state requirements, which is mandated by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

During public comment at the county’s Aug. 11 meeting, more than 10 residents and activists took to the podium to encourage commissioners to support the resolution.

Before the vote, Commission Chair Ken Cornell said he didn’t plan to support the resolution. However, after hearing public comment and support from fellow commissioners, Cornell voted in its favor. He said the non-binding resolution, which has no legal weight, would help build public trust.

Is the resolution purely symbolic?

Although the county passed a resolution publicly opposing current ICE operations, the decision doesn’t guarantee or require an end to local law enforcement cooperation with ICE.

Andrea Jacoski, a University of Miami law professor and associate director of the university’s immigration clinic, said the resolution seems to be a symbolic gesture acknowledging community concerns. It can’t supersede state and federal ICE operations in the county, she added.

“I don't actually know that passing a resolution will pull away from their obligation to actually continue to share information or effectuate ICE detainers,” Jacoski said.

ICE detainers, or immigration holds, are written notices sent by ICE to local or state law enforcement asking them to hold a person so ICE can take them into custody.

While the county’s resolution may not prevent ICE operations entirely, Jacoski said, it can build public trust and demonstrate solidarity with its immigrant communities.

“It's important, and it's good that people are recognizing that it is very harmful for our immigrant neighbors and the large immigrant population across Florida,” she said.

Community reactions

After months of discourse, Alachua County Commissioner Marihelen Wheeler said the resolution upholds the county’s responsibility to care for its residents by encouraging ICE officers to treat them fairly.

“It has very nice words put together to ask that folks here don’t wear masks and that they treat people well and that they don't profile anybody,” Wheeler said. “But again, it’s not binding, and so, more than anything, it’s an acknowledgment that there are communities being jeopardized by the tactics coming out of Washington and now out of Tallahassee.”

Wheeler added she’s done far more for immigrants than support a non-binding resolution.

In an attempt to promote binding change, Wheeler said she’s addressed community concerns like GINI’s with U.S. Rep. Kat Cammack and her team, who represent Alachua County and the surrounding area in the U.S. House of Representatives.

“[Cammack] knows that this is a topic that I'm most concerned about,” she said. “So we sat down together … and we were trying to come up with some ideas that we might be able to address the concerns of the community in a more face-to-face and direct way.”

Her relationship with Cammack began when Wheeler ran against former U.S. Rep. Ted Yoho in 2014. Cammack was his campaign manager at the time.

Wheeler looks back at her 2014 campaign for House and her platform on immigration as evidence of her decadelong support for immigrants.

She suspects the Gainesville City Commission has been waiting for the county commission’s decision to make its own about the resolution, she added.

While waiting on the city commission’s vote, she said, she’s been gathering a group of volunteers to talk with Cammack.

“What I’m trying to do is set up a meeting with those folks who were willing to go to have this discussion about what is happening,” she said, “and what we can expect in the future and how we might be helpful in trying to get some kind of immigration reform policy going.”

Having achieved the county’s approval, GINI representative Ethan Maia de Needell said the organization is now focusing its efforts on the city.

He said future work with the county will aim to make the county’s social services more accessible to the immigrant community. GINI hopes to help facilitate those efforts and hold the county accountable, he added.

“The demands in the resolution are not extreme,” he said. “They are simply a gesture of what the city prioritizes, which we hope are the constitutional rights of its residents.”

Contact Aaron Zagal Yaji at azagal@alligator.org. Follow him on X @azagalyaji.

title: ICE dragged him from his doorstep in January. His elderly partner fears he'll die in detention
description:
Now, after nearly eight months in ICE detention, Vela Gonzalez can barely stand, his loved ones say.
By the time she made it to the door, Vela Gonzalez was being dragged down the street.
His lawyer and partner say Vela Gonzalez looks like a shell of what he once was.
As the months dragged on, Lee Arguello had to leave her longtime home and move in with a niece in Lynwood.
It’s not much of a home without Vela Gonzalez, and she needs money to continue supporting him, she said.
text:
Rafael Vela Gonzalez was a few steps away from the front door of his Silver Lake home when two Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents grabbed him in early January.

The 66-year-old, originally from El Salvador, had been in the U.S. since he was a teenager. His boyish grin was a fixture in his tight-knit neighborhood for more than three decades.

Neighbors always waved at Vela Gonzalez as he walked his German shepherd, Chico. He retired as a handyman a few years ago but passed the time caring for his aging partner, Vivian Lee Arguello, and doing odd jobs around the neighborhood to make ends meet.

He built the baby crib that welcomed a couple’s first child. He painted bedrooms, took charge of the block’s recycling efforts and fixed countless plumbing problems.

Now, after nearly eight months in ICE detention, Vela Gonzalez can barely stand, his loved ones say.

A mysterious rash has spread across his legs, and blood oozes from the sores. He doesn’t know what caused it, but his feet are so swollen he struggles to walk. He complained of stomach pain for weeks, until he collapsed in his cell in June, said his lawyer, Barbara Darnell, and spent nearly a week in the hospital.

“The biggest fear for a lot of the family is that he was just either going to disappear or he was going to get sick in there and die,” said Ashley Cabrera, 23, a loved one whom Vela Gonzalez calls his niece. “He keeps complaining about these health concerns and the facility doesn’t care.”

The Adelanto ICE Processing Center has, for years, been accused of substandard living conditions. Detainees have reported worm-like creatures in their drinking water, launched hunger strikes, and signed onto class-action lawsuits in recent months, decrying poor food, sanitation and medical care.

A federal judge in mid-July sided with detainees, who argued their constitutional and disability rights were being violated, and ordered the government overhaul conditions at the center.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said all immigrants receive comprehensive medical care when they enter ICE custody, including medical, dental and mental health services as available.

Similar complaints have been filed against detention centers nationwide. Thirty-three people died in ICE custody in 2025, according to agency data, triple the deaths from the year prior. Four detainees have died in Adelanto since September.

Lee Arguello fears Vela Gonzalez will suffer the same fate.

The 81-year-old and Vela Gonzalez have been together for more than 30 years, since she first hired him to do some carpentry in her home. She relied on him for nearly everything, from maintaining the house to tracking her medicine and cooking meals.

The pair never married because Lee Arguello wasn’t able to divorce her former husband, who took off decades ago, she said.

Lee Arguello, a U.S. citizen born in Los Angeles, now struggles to live without Vela Gonzalez. The housework piled up, the yard is overgrown, her expenses have risen and she can’t keep up with her health now that he is gone.

“He tells me … that he’s looking forward to coming home, and I hate to disappoint him and tell him that he might not come home. So I don’t say anything,” Lee Arguello said. “It’s heartbreaking.”

That day in January, Lee Arguello was on her couch in the living room, just steps away from the front door, when she heard Vela Gonzalez’s piercing scream.

“Vivian!” he said, his voice barely audible above the barks of his dog, Chico.

Lee Arguello’s mobility issues make it difficult to walk without assistance. By the time she made it to the door, Vela Gonzalez was being dragged down the street. The guilt eats at her, she said.

“I couldn’t do anything to help him,” Lee Arguello said. “It’s so, so difficult not knowing what’s going to happen.”

Video of the January incident went viral, and landed on Cabrera’s Instagram feed before Lee Arguello was able to call her.

Cabrera watched in horror as the man she’d called an uncle for nearly two decades was detained.

Vela Gonzalez was dragged down the concrete steps and pushed to the ground by two agents, before a third agent emerged to handcuff him, according to video footage reviewed by The Times. Another video angle shows agents holding him by the collar as they walk him down the street.

Vela Gonzalez has few blood relatives in the U.S., but formed a chosen family over his time in the country.

Cabrera and her family met him nearly two decades ago through church and he quickly became friends with Cabrera’s mom.

Since then, Vela Gonzalez has rarely missed a family event, she said. At some point along the way, she started calling him uncle.

“We’re just trying to help Rafael as much as we can, trying to get him to a safe place,” Cabrera said.

Close relatives of Cabrera and Vela Gonzalez initially assumed ICE would clear up the issue. Vela Gonzalez always believed he had legal status, said Darnell, his attorney.

He arrived in the U.S. at age 19, just over two years after he was forced to join the Salvadoran army at the outbreak of the nation’s brutal civil war. He received death threats, and his nephews were murdered, his lawyer said.

Vela Gonzalez arrived in time to qualify for the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, which provided nearly three million undocumented immigrants a path to citizenship. He applied for amnesty then, and received a temporary green card, his lawyer said.

Homeland Security claimed the office sent a notice advising him to submit an application for a permanent green card, as the temporary card expired in 1997, Darnell said. Vela Gonzalez never received the notice and didn’t know he had to apply for permanent status, she said.

Vela Gonzalez carried the temporary green card in his wallet for nearly five decades. When he lost his wallet in 2023, he submitted an application to get the card replaced, which his attorney suspects put him on ICE’s radar. The application was denied in April 2025.

He was detained during a targeted operation, the Homeland Security spokesperson said, and will remain in custody pending removal proceedings.

Word of Vela Gonzalez‘s detention quickly spread and soon after, the video had landed in a group chat for residents of the area.

Neighbors were outraged, said Vincent Brook, a retired college professor who’s lived in the neighborhood for 48 years. The community was already outspoken against ICE, but hadn’t felt the impacts first-hand until Vela Gonzalez was taken.

“This happening in our own community, it added fuel to the fire, you know?” Brook said. “Anybody I spoke with was enraged about it.”

Around 30 community members gathered for a vigil organized by Brook 10 days after Vela Gonzalez was taken. His loved ones set up a GoFundMe, which raised nearly $50,000 in a matter of days.

“He’s lived a lifetime of being there for his neighbors,” Cabrera said.

Vela Gonzalez and Lee Arguello spoke daily after he was detained. When two days passed without a call from him in June, she knew something was wrong.

Vela Gonzalez complained for weeks of stomach pain and his legs were only getting more swollen.

“With me, he tries to appear normal, but I could tell he wasn’t the same,” Lee Arguello said.

She called the detention center and was told Vela Gonzalez was taken to the hospital.

The center refused to give her and Darnell any information on his health status or whereabouts, citing HIPAA laws, Darnell said. Loved ones eventually heard from Vela Gonzalez’s roommate, who said he collapsed in his cell right after a court hearing.

“They were literally hiding him from us,” Cabrera said. “He’s telling them every day that he wants medical attention and they’re not giving it ... and then he randomly disappears with no communication.”

Vela Gonzalez was hospitalized for acute bronchitis and sepsis from June 17 to June 22, a Homeland Security spokesperson said. He’s receiving ongoing treatment for psoriasis.

“When circumstances require notification to a detainee’s attorney, ICE follows applicable notification policies and procedures,” the spokesperson said.

His lawyer and partner say Vela Gonzalez looks like a shell of what he once was. He’s lost weight and his hair falls out in clumps. He had long maintained a clean-shaven appearance, but started growing out his beard in detention.

It’s now thick and reaches inches below his chin. He refuses to shave until he’s released, Cabrera said.

It shouldn’t be much longer now, he tells her.

But the trappings of his and Lee Arguello’s life are falling apart.

Overgrown foliage has invaded the front yard of the Silver Lake home that Vela Gonzalez used to maintain. The trash has piled up and the trinkets he has collected for their garden are gone — a bleak reminder of his absence, said Halley Albert, 30, a neighbor.

Vela Gonzalez’s request for bond was denied in July and the court deemed him a flight risk. Darnell appealed the decision in August, citing his decades in the country.

Chico, his German shepherd, was sent to a foster family in March and permanently rehomed last month. The dog was restless without his owner, and would look for men who resembled Vela Gonzalez on every walk, Cabrera said. The family couldn’t manage the dog’s care.

Chico had hardly left Vela Gonzalez’s side since the couple took him in about four years ago. He was devastated to hear he lost his dog.

As the months dragged on, Lee Arguello had to leave her longtime home and move in with a niece in Lynwood.

She’s decided to put her house up for sale. It’s not much of a home without Vela Gonzalez, and she needs money to continue supporting him, she said.

She’s since tracked down her ex-husband and the divorce is in process. One day soon, she said, she will finally get to marry Vela Gonzalez.

His charisma makes him friends everywhere he goes, she said, so she wasn’t surprised to hear he’d started to form bonds with fellow detainees. When they get out, he says, they plan to start a contracting business together.

“We’re going to get married, even if he’s detained,” Lee Arguello said. “My hope is he will not be deported, and he’ll come back and we’ll have a good life together.”

title: From NJ to Louisiana and back: One Elizabeth woman's path through ICE detention
description:
(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor) The immigration agents stormed the Savino Del Bene warehouse from every angle: emergency doors, loading docks, the main entrance.
Rosero described her journey from the warehouse floor to her detainment at the Elizabeth Detention Center to the LaSalle ICE processing center in Louisiana to her uncertain future back in Elizabeth.
Immigrants’ fear and silence makes it difficult for local advocates to track the people ICE agents take.
“I just knew I didn’t want to leave my daughter alone.” Rosero first was held at the Elizabeth Detention Center, two-and-a-half miles from her apartment.
One night after barely eating the detention center food, she said — looking disgusted while recalling it — she sat on her hard mattress observing her uniform.
text:
Protesters with Ice Out rally outside the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)

The immigration agents stormed the Savino Del Bene warehouse from every angle: emergency doors, loading docks, the main entrance.

By the time they reached Lourdes Rosero, the warehouse’s cafeteria had been converted into a processing station, with agents holding laptops, checking names against lists. Dogs and drones circled outside. Black cars parked along the front lot as far as Rosero could see.

It was the brisk morning of Oct. 29, 2025, when Rosero got detained at a warehouse in the Avenel section of Woodbridge where she had worked daily for months.

“It was like watching a movie,” she said in an interview in Spanish at her second-floor apartment in Elizabeth. “Like they were going after narcos. Not me. It was like they were looking for something very criminal.”

Countless raids have happened in New Jersey since President Donald Trump launched a mass deportation and detention effort at the start of his second term. The raid that swept up Rosero and roughly 50 other workers was one of the largest here since the crackdown began.

The New Jersey Monitor met with Rosero and her daughter, Diana, immigrants from Ecuador who have lived in New Jersey since 2021, over the course of several months. Rosero described her journey from the warehouse floor to her detainment at the Elizabeth Detention Center to the LaSalle ICE processing center in Louisiana to her uncertain future back in Elizabeth.

As a woman living in the U.S. without citizenship, she fears what’s next for her and for others who came to America seeking a better life under a new era of immigration enforcement.

Rosero is one of roughly 11 million immigrants living in the U.S. without legal status. An estimated 500,000 live in New Jersey, with most coming from Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and Ecuador, according to the Migration Policy Institute.

She and her daughter flew here in 2021 and overstayed their visa after seeing what they said was the “chance to have better days in our lives,” and the possibility to escape the domestic abuse she suffered for years from her former partner in Ecuador.

Rosero believed she took a legal path. She filed for asylum, obtained an employment authorization document allowing her to legally work, and paid some taxes. She had no prior criminal charges or conviction.

When agents approached her the morning of the warehouse raid, she handed over her work permit believing it would prove she could legally be there. They handcuffed her, and she still hasn’t gotten that work permit back.

“I thought to myself, ‘I’m different because I have a work permit to be here, maybe the others don’t. I’m good, just stay calm. I have protection,’” she said. “Then I saw they didn’t care. They weren’t treating me any different. I said, ‘Why are you detaining me if I have a work permit? Look, I’m working here legally.’”

The agent told her she had two options. She could sign a form for voluntary self deportation and receive $1,000 to restart her life in Ecuador, though she wasn’t sure where she’d end up because the Trump administration has not been deporting people to their native countries. Her other choice: She could be detained and fight her case through the judicial system.

It was a choice thousands of immigrants like her across New Jersey have faced in recent years — fight to stay, or take the money and go.

She texted Diana, who continued to work so they could pay rent that month.

“Fight, Ma,” her text said.

With two migrant detention centers in New Jersey regularly cycling through thousands of people arrested in mass raids or individual targeted stops by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, immigration court hearings are a revolving door of people trying to find out what’s happening to them.

Newark is home to one of the state’s two immigration courts. People largely appear virtually from jail — though not necessarily in New Jersey — and speak through an interpreter. Many appear in orange or tan jail uniforms, sitting in a metal chair for a hearing lasting mere minutes. Sometimes it takes longer to bring in the next detainee than to hold the hearing itself.

On a December day, one judge saw a steady procession of cases, more than 20 people in one hour. Some were seen hours after being detained. Others had their cases rescheduled after months of detention.

Among the detainees: A mother who sat with her son in her lap. A woman, 27 weeks pregnant, who left the hospital for the hearing. A Passaic County man who begged the judge to give him a work permit, to no avail. And a Toms River man who the judge decided to deport to Ecuador instead of the man’s home country of Colombia.

Other than a prosecutor representing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, lawyers aren’t typically present. The judge presents a few options: fight the case, accept voluntary departure to countries like Honduras and Ecuador, or explore options for relief with an attorney.

The absence of lawyers is not incidental, said Amy Torres, executive director of the New Jersey Alliance for Immigrant Justice. Unlike U.S. citizens who get arrested, immigrants detained by ICE do not have the right to a lawyer provided by the government, leaving many scrambling hours after an arrest.

“It is on them to find the representation,” Torres said. “And when we know people are getting transferred within a day at times, sometimes put on the path to deportation within a day, you can imagine how difficult it is to find a pro bono attorney within that period of time. It’s just nearly impossible — but that’s exactly how it’s set up to be.”

Nationally, voluntary departures increased by 28-fold in 2025 compared to the prior year, according to the Deportation Data Project, a group that uses public records to track immigration enforcement, detention, and deportations. While ICE is supposed to publish numbers, the agency’s tracker is not updated regularly.

Before Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, ICE was carrying out roughly 300 arrests nationally per day. That number spiked to more than 1,500 per day by July 2026, the Deportation Data Project found. In New Jersey, the numbers were even higher: immigration agents arrested 2,080 people in July, the highest monthly total in four years and a nearly 150% increase from May to July.

New Jersey now ranks eighth in the nation for immigration arrests.

Some people ICE arrests have criminal convictions, but largely for petty offenses. An analysis by the Prison Policy Initiative found that 34% of people ICE arrested in New Jersey between May and October 2025 had pending criminal charges, with the most common charge being a traffic offense. The data did not break out what share of New Jersey detainees had no criminal record at all.

One of the defining features of Trump’s second term — distinct even from his first — is the widening of who ICE targets, Torres said.

“It actually doesn’t matter if you were undocumented or not,” she said. “We’re seeing even people with valid work visas, student visas — we’re even seeing green card holders — being detained and arrested by ICE. Things that used to be a safeguard, like a green card, that’s no longer the case.”

ICE officials did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Department of Homeland Security officials have repeatedly defended their sweeping enforcement against visa holders, green card holders, and even people with pending applications, saying any status short of citizenship does not protect people from arrest. Trump has framed the crackdown as a fulfillment of a 2024 campaign promise, claiming ICE targets the “worst of the worst.”

The White House’s website characterizes enforcement as “protecting U.S. sovereignty and safeguarding American communities.”

“By prioritizing enforcement and accountability, the administration is restoring integrity to the immigration system and ensuring the law is applied consistently. These efforts protect American workers, reduce strain on local communities, and reinforce the nation’s right to control its borders and determine who enters the United States,” the website reads.

ICE has grown its footprint in New Jersey since Trump’s second term began. Former Gov. Phil Murphy, a Democrat, signed a 2021 bill banning public and private entities from entering into contracts to house immigrant detainees, but a federal judge struck down the private entities provision as unconstitutional. That allowed private prison firm CoreCivic to retain its contract to detain immigrants at the 300-bed Elizabeth Detention Center and cleared the way for Geo Group to open Delaney Hall, a 1,100-bed immigrant jail in Newark, in May 2025.

Federal officials plan to convert a vacant Roxbury warehouse into a mass processing center that could handle nearly 1,500 people. Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Attorney General Jen Davenport, both Democrats, and the township’s GOP leadership sued in March to block the project, arguing officials bypassed required environmental and procedural reviews before purchasing the $129 million site. The Trump administration in June said it was abandoning the Roxbury plan, then reversed course in July.

U.S. Rep. Rob Menendez, a Democrat whose district includes Delaney Hall, has visited the facility dozens of times since it opened. He regularly meets with detainees inside and checks on medical services and food options in the jail, which he says are both substandard. He maintains the detention center never should have opened.

He noted that 2026 marks just the second year of Geo Group’s 15-year contract with the federal government to house detainees at Delaney Hall.

“It makes me sad. Sad that this is the reality,” he said, speaking outside the jail while alarms blared, as they often do randomly when protesters and press gather. “I fear that not enough people are waking up or opening their eyes to what’s happening here, and that if more people don’t engage and see what’s happening, then they’re going to be silent while these things are happening in all of our communities.”

Menendez remains cautiously optimistic, though, and says he believes the injustices happening inside the immigration detention centers will end someday.

“I hope it’s tomorrow. I hope it’s the day after. I wish it was January of last year, but I know it will end, and we just have to do our best to keep people safe and limit the damage until it is done, finally,” he said.

That damage already is growing. Rosero’s arrest is part of a string of large-scale ICE operations that have hit New Jersey over the past year, uprooting families and workers from their Garden State homes.

The raid that led to Rosero’s arrest saw 46 people detained by federal agents. In July 2025, agents arrested another 20 or so people at Alba Wine and Spirits in Edison. The following month, they took 29 people from an Edison warehouse. This past June, they detained 18 people at El Oaxaqueño, a family-owned restaurant and market in Lakewood, including six of its workers.

Last November, agents raided a seafood market in Newark, the second at that location since Trump took office. Heavily armed agents in masks and bulletproof vests surrounded the business and shut down nearby streets. Alarmed neighbors shouted at them.

That time, 13 workers were taken to Delaney Hall. But agents swiftly move people from facility to facility, meaning detainees don’t always remain in New Jersey for long.

Sometimes, people are taken in one-off instances: a pastor stopped by agents in unmarked cars in March, a contractor pulled over near the Long Branch Home Depot and taken to Delaney Hall, an 18-year-old detained after visiting her friend at the Elizabeth Detention Center. Immigration groups like Eyes on ICE regularly post on social media when they spot agents detaining residents in places like North Plainfield, Freehold, and Dover.

At a know-your-rights meeting held by local immigration group Make the Road, a landscaper named Victor said a homeowner threatened to call ICE on him after arguing with his boss over the cost. He feared returning to work, knowing co-workers had seen those threats carried out. Other attendees shared stories of the dictatorships they escaped in Latin America and parallels they see under the Trump administration. Even those who have become U.S. citizens said they were scared, asking about racial profiling.

Immigrants’ fear and silence makes it difficult for local advocates to track the people ICE agents take. Torres described enforcement over the past 20 months not as a coordinated strategy but as deliberate disorder: mass raids at warehouses one week, arrests at immigration hearings the next, then targeted stakeouts, then nothing at all.

“The most consistent thing that we’ve seen is chaos,” Torres said. “Whenever we think we’re learning about a new emerging trend, things shift.”

Rosero considered voluntarily leaving. On one hand, it would allow her to return to her home country, where many of her relatives remain, with $1,000 in her pocket. But she had spent years seeking asylum and had obtained a work permit.

“I was between the sword and the wall,” she said. “I just knew I didn’t want to leave my daughter alone.”

Rosero first was held at the Elizabeth Detention Center, two-and-a-half miles from her apartment. She spent eight days there, along with other women from the warehouse. Then an agent woke her at 3 a.m. ordering her to collect her things, and Rosero and other detainees were chained at the waist and handcuffed. They were loaded into a van, and when one woman who spoke English overheard agents talking about airports and airplanes, panic spread through the group.

They were flown to a detention facility in LaSalle, about two miles northwest of Jena, Louisiana. She believes she arrived at 1 a.m., but she was losing track of time and days. Rosero had no lawyer confirmed to help her, and her daughter — in between work shifts at a daycare center — was piecing together contacts, drawing on a network of immigration organizations in New Jersey to find lawyers and navigating the mountain of paperwork she suddenly faced.

In Louisiana, Rosero was handed an orange uniform. Detainees donned other colors if they were seen as “problems,” Rosero said, or if they were to be deported. She was depressed upon arriving at the dingy facility, and although she made friends, she struggled to see the path forward, she said.

One night after barely eating the detention center food, she said — looking disgusted while recalling it — she sat on her hard mattress observing her uniform. She unfolded the pants in the dim light of the cell block and spotted writing along the leg: “I trust in my God, because for Him, nothing is impossible.”

She cried as she recounted how she felt seeing that. It gave her the strength and courage she had sought throughout her journey.

“I had complained so much about the uniform. That it was torn, used, dirty. And then I saw that, and I said, ‘Forgive me, Father. You’ve given me a message,’” she said.

On Nov. 13, she had a hearing via Zoom inside the jail, where a judge set bail at $15,000. She doesn’t recall what was said, mostly because it unfolded entirely in English and she felt so emotional. But when the translator finally addressed her, she understood the payment requirement. Diana had been working with local organizations to help cover the bail, paid it by Nov. 18, and Rosero was released.

“I felt peace. It felt like freedom,” she said.

A volunteer from a Louisiana-based immigration group picked her up, fed her dinner, housed her overnight, and helped her board a plane the next morning to Newark, where Diana met her.

It’s been nearly a year since her arrest. Rosero remains unable to work without her permit. She measures her recovery in blocks walked outside her apartment. For the first few weeks, she didn’t step outside at all, staying inside her two-bedroom home. Then she started pacing the backyard. Then the front.

Recently, she started walking to the bodega on the corner, and to Christ the King Church near Elizabeth. She’s still apprehensive when she has to walk to Broad Street, and remains cautious of black cars passing by her.

“That tranquility, the feeling of being able to go anywhere, knowing you’re not doing anything wrong, of feeling truly free, it’s totally gone,” she said. “I don’t know when it will come back. I didn’t do anything wrong when I was arrested, so I fear it can happen again at any moment. I’m working my way to bravery.”

In February, she appeared virtually before an immigration judge for the first hearing in her asylum case. She barely spoke — the hearing was in English and she didn’t understand most of it. The judge set an August deadline to present her evidence, including notarized documents and proof of when she entered the country. The cost of her legal battle has grown to an amount she can barely say out loud, more than $25,000. Most of it is funded through community organizations and her daughter’s hourly salary. They keep a tight budget for food and rent, although their landlord is understanding of Rosero’s situation.

She’s studying for an insurance license now, looking for new ways to support herself and her daughter. She’s also in therapy to work through the nightmares and trauma of what she suffered. She keeps in touch with women she met at the jail through a WhatsApp group chat, “Las Gallinas,” or The Chickens.

She attends prayer groups, and constantly thanks God for helping her stay in America and keeping her from returning to Ecuador, where she says things have gotten worse as drugs run rampant and criminals take over towns.

Some days, Rosero says she’s fine, finding her way to the next day. But other days, she sees through her window a black car driving by slowly.

Her next court date is later this month. She’s hoping she will have her work permit again by then, despite her confusion about how to get it reissued and her fear of visiting government offices.

Still, she remains positive.

“God brought me here for a reason,” she said. “I still have many things to do.”

title: Introducing the Immigration Updates Dashboard - Free Movement
description:
For several months now I’ve been working on automating and centralising our various update channels into a single easy-to-use tool: the Immigration Updates Dashboard.
What is the Immigration Updates Dashboard?
The Immigration Updates Dashboard is a simple way to stay up to date with developments in immigration law.
More on that another time; it allows searches of the material in the database in order to answer immigration law questions.
AI was used to write the code to construct the Immigration Updates Dashboard.
text:
Keeping up to date in immigration law is hard. The Home Office rewrites guidance constantly, the official change notes are often vague to the point of useless and trying to monitor the Home Office, the courts, the tribunals, Parliament and various agencies all at once can, not to put too fine a point on it, drive you round the bend.

At Free Movement, we know that better than most. The problem is why we exist, really. For years we’ve been using an unholy combination of RSS feeds, email alerts, social media and simple manual checks on websites to keep track of things. We filter through all that, update our readers when we think something significant has happened and we include our own comment and analysis.

For several months now I’ve been working on automating and centralising our various update channels into a single easy-to-use tool: the Immigration Updates Dashboard. We use it internally already and we are now pleased to invite you to use it too.

Importantly, email subscriptions are now available for Free Movement members for all alerts or for different category of alerts: you can choose.

Here’s a video walk-through I recorded, or you can read about it the old fashioned way below.

What is the Immigration Updates Dashboard?

The Immigration Updates Dashboard is a simple way to stay up to date with developments in immigration law. It is one of two doorways into an auto-updating database we have created of immigration law content from various government sources. It checks every hour, day or week depending on the category of content and if it finds something new, it downloads it and adds it to the database.

The Dashboard displays what has been added to this database, shows what has changed since the last version of a document and offers email alerts when something new is added.

The stand out feature is the tracked changes view for Home Office policies. Want to know what has changed since the last version? It’s easy:

The Dashboard also provides an at-a-glance AI summary based on the tracked changes, which we’ve found far more useful than the Home Office’s own often woeful version.

The other doorway into the database is the Immigration Law Search tool. More on that another time; it allows searches of the material in the database in order to answer immigration law questions.

The categories of content in the database are Home Office policies, parliamentary reports and questions, inspections and audits, research and data, case law and sponsors. Each category can be filtered. Home Office policies can be filtered by topic: asylum, work and stay, family and settlement and so on. Parliamentary material can be filtered by library briefings, parliamentary questions, select committee reports and so on. Case law can be filtered by court or tribunal. And so on.

How does it work?

The Dashboard is automatic. We’re a very small team at Free Movement and we’ve always relied on automation right from the early days of the blog, when it was a one-man-band. RIP Yahoo! Pipes 2007-2015. It helps us keep the cost of membership as low as possible. This is our latest experiment.

The checks for new updates at various sources run on a clock, the downloads are coded to be automatic, the tracked changes are coded to be automatic and so on.

When it detects, downloads and adds something new, you can see it for yourself on the Dashboard itself or you can opt to receive an email alert.

Email alerts are only available to members, who can choose between notifications of all updates on all topics either daily at 4pm or weekly at Friday 4pm or can subscribe to once-per-day updates on individual topics if they prefer:

Asylum & human rights — protection claims, asylum support, appeals

Citizenship & nationality — British citizenship, nationality, passports

CPINs — Country Policy and Information Notes

Enforcement, detention & removals — detention, deportation, civil penalties, border control

EU & EU Settlement Scheme – EU/EEA citizens’ rights, EUSS, Brexit

Family & settlement — family visas, settlement, permanent stay

Immigration case law

Parliament, inspections & research

Work & study — sponsor licences, Skilled Worker, students

Other immigration guidance — fees, biometrics, general grounds

The emails are just alerts with a short summary and a link back to the dashboard.

If you are on Bluesky, the ImmigrationBot account shares links to all new dashboard arrivals and we’ve also automated a weekly post to our company LinkedIn account with a short summary of the most recent updates.

Does the dashboard use AI?

AI was used to write the code to construct the Immigration Updates Dashboard. This is often referred to as “vibe coding” because one does not need to know code to actually do it. I haven’t written any proper code since I was a teenager and paying a coder to do all of this would have been commercially non-viable.

When something goes wrong — all software always goes wrong eventually, or encounters an unpredicted situation and, like me, has a meltdown — we use AI to diagnose the problem and fix it. We’re not coders but we’re finding that AI can be used to create things that would never previously have been commercially viable.

In operation, the Dashboard uses AI to summarise new documents. New or changed Home Office policies get an AI summary of the changes that have been mechanically identified. Cases with no official headnote get a short AI summary. Some of the parliamentary materials get a very, very short AI summary of just a few words.

AI is also used to conduct a filtering exercise. Seven of the fifteen sources feeding the parliament, inspections and research tabs have an AI model deciding relevance: written parliamentary questions, select committee reports, Bills, National Audit Office reports, detention inspections, oral statements and written ministerial statements. Parliament and the inspectorates publish far more than just the immigration material in which we are interested and there is no other filter for it. The other eight sources use keyword or structural rules, or are curated immigration-specific collections.

Can non-members use it?

Yes, but to a limited extent. A non-member can see the front page of the Dashboard and can navigate between the different sources to see what is new. They can search that day’s sponsor register and also follow links to the original sources, for example on gov.uk or on the National Archives. To that extent, non-members can benefit from the centralised hub we have set up, the filtering for immigration content we conduct and also can see the start of the AI summaries.

Only members can see the full AI summaries, the tracked changes, the full version histories and the searchable historic sponsor register.

Whether you are a member or not, take a look and see if you find it useful. We do.

title: ICE wrongfully arrested him. Will his lawsuit change how courts hold agents accountable?
description:
Instead, people suing federal agents must rely on a narrow remedy created by the courts — one the Supreme Court has sharply restricted in recent years.
“There has to be a way to hold federal officers accountable when they are plainly violating the U.S. Constitution,” said Carol Garvan, legal director for the ACLU of Maine.
In 1971, the Supreme Court opened a small legal window to sue federal law enforcement in the case of Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents.
The same goes for people assaulted by federal officers versus a local police department.
Carvajal-Muñoz’s federal lawsuit also makes a claim against officers for violating his constitutional rights under the Maine Civil Rights Act.
text:
In January, as the Trump administration launched an immigration crackdown in Maine, Juan Sebastián Carvajal-Muñoz was intercepted on his way to work. The civil engineer from Colombia told officers he had a visa through his employer, but the immigration agents who arrested him did not seem to care. According to the federal lawsuit he later filed against them, they smashed his window, dragged him out of his car while pointing a Taser at him, cuffed him, forced him into the back of an unmarked SUV and drove him across state lines.

Officers released him from an ICE facility in Massachusetts around 9 p.m. that evening, when they realized they had no reason to hold him. He was left stranded in a different state with sore wrists, a broken car window, and the unshakeable fear that it could happen again.

Officers are rarely charged with a crime for abusing a civilian, so a lawsuit is often the best recourse if someone believes their rights were violated. Congress has explicitly given people the ability to bring such lawsuits against state and local officials, but there is no equivalent for addressing constitutional violations by federal officials. Instead, people suing federal agents must rely on a narrow remedy created by the courts — one the Supreme Court has sharply restricted in recent years.

Nevertheless, Carvajal-Muñoz filed suit in federal court this spring with the help of the ACLU of Maine, part of a broader search by immigrant rights attorneys for ways to hold officers responsible. Preserving the ability to sue is crucial, they say, as federal authorities increase their arrests of immigrants and citizens.

“There has to be a way to hold federal officers accountable when they are plainly violating the U.S. Constitution,” said Carol Garvan, legal director for the ACLU of Maine. She noted that Carvajal-Muñoz was arrested even with a Real ID on hand, which proved his legal status. “That is something that lingers for him (and) people all over Maine and all over the country. You start to think, what could protect you if there is this kind of violation?”

In an email, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security wrote that any officers who violate policy are “held accountable,” and that “DHS law enforcement methods abide by the U.S. Constitution including the Fourth Amendment.” The spokesperson did not respond to questions about civil suits.

In 1971, the Supreme Court opened a small legal window to sue federal law enforcement in the case of Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents. The Court ruled that Webster Bivens could sue federal drug enforcement officers after they forced themselves into his home in New York, threatened to arrest his wife and kids, searched his house, and arrested him, all without a warrant.

Over the next decade, the Court ruled that Bivens could apply in two other contexts — sexual discrimination in federal employment, and deliberate indifference to medical needs in a federal prison — but since then, it has repeatedly blocked many lawsuits staking claims based on the Bivens case. In recent years, lower federal courts have also been reluctant to rule in a plaintiff’s favor in such cases.

In one 2024 court decision, a federal judge noted that circumstances where a court could extend Bivens were “as rare as the ivory-billed woodpecker.” In the case, federal prisoner LaQuan Johnson was attempting to sue corrections officers for failing to protect him from multiple attacks and denying him medical care afterward. “Just like its natural history analogue,” the judge wrote, “both the decision and the bird are staring extinction in the face.”

In 2022, Andrew Fields tried to sue the federal Bureau of Prisons and its employees over prolonged abuse he said he suffered inside a federal prison in Virginia. Officers locked him in painful restraints, beat him with fiberglass shields and slammed his head into a concrete wall, his complaint said. In a rare win for federal prisoners, the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled his case should proceed. But the Supreme Court reversed that decision last summer, sending the case back to the Fourth Circuit, which affirmed the dismissal of the case.

The Court’s application of Bivens has created some arbitrary differences in who can sue and who cannot, said attorney Gregory Cui with the MacArthur Justice Center, who worked on Fields’ case. “If they punch you in the face you have no remedy, but if they don’t give you your medicine you do have a remedy,” he said of people in federal prisons, based on the situations where courts have said Bivens applies. Similarly, people in federal prisons have few avenues to sue their jailers, he said, while those in state prisons “20 miles down the road” have far more remedies available – though these cases are also difficult to win.

The same goes for people assaulted by federal officers versus a local police department. In 2020, for example, the Supreme Court ruled that a family could not sue a federal Border Patrol agent after he shot and killed their 15-year-old son.

The Supreme Court further narrowed Bivens in 2022, when a bed-and-breakfast owner attempted to sue a Border Patrol agent for allegedly forcing his way onto the property and throwing the owner on the ground, in pursuit of a guest. The court’s ruling against the owner made it incredibly difficult to find “new contexts” in which Bivens would apply, and gave Border Patrol near immunity from such lawsuits.

That aperture may shrink even further this fall. The Supreme Court has agreed to take up another Bivens case, this time filed by a federal prisoner who says he was denied treatment for a broken tailbone that was a result of a prison fight. The Court will decide whether his claims are similar enough to one of the original Bivens cases to proceed.

The case is the latest opportunity by an increasingly conservative Supreme Court to whittle away Bivens so that it is largely a “dead letter,” Cui said. “The fact that (the court) is doing this now in the midst of one of the most dangerous expansions in the use of federal law enforcement is alarming. We could argue about this kind of legal issue in normal times, but these are not normal times.”

Civilians can file cases under a law called the Federal Tort Claims Act, but the law carries limitations. The liability is with the United States government rather than an individual officer, cases are heard by a judge instead of a jury, and a plaintiff can’t sue for punitive damages. Under the second Trump administration, the ACLU has filed 54 such claims related to immigration enforcement across 17 states and Washington, D.C. Currently, a group of Jan. 6 rioters are also using this route to try to win money from the federal government over their arrests and incarceration.

Given the limited avenues for relief and intensified immigration enforcement, attorneys across the country are increasingly looking for ways to use state law to go after federal officers instead. Carvajal-Muñoz’s federal lawsuit also makes a claim against officers for violating his constitutional rights under the Maine Civil Rights Act. While more states are passing and trying to use similar state laws to hold federal officials accountable, attorneys say they are largely untested.

Garvan hopes that if Carvajal-Muñoz’s case succeeds, it will be a blueprint for lawsuits in Maine and across the country. “If we are not able to bring a claim under Bivens and we are not able to bring a claim under our state’s Civil Rights Act, then people are left without a remedy at all,” Garvan said. “We’re really hopeful that this could be a tool.”

Similar laws exist in states like Illinois, New Jersey, New York, California and Massachusetts, and many legislatures are considering comparable bills. Minnesota legislators introduced a similar bill after the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, but it failed to pass. The Trump administration is currently fighting Illinois’ state law in court, a statute that only applies to those conducting immigration enforcement. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, and Rep. Hank Johnson, a Georgia Democrat, have also proposed a federal Bivens Act to codify nationally the right to sue a federal employee in court.

The agents who arrested Carvajal-Muñoz have until the end of September to respond to his suit. An attorney for the defendants declined to comment.

Carvajal-Muñoz, meanwhile, has tried to return to normal life after his detention, but the threat of rearrest or worse remains. In July, during an enforcement surge, ICE shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero – another immigrant who arrived in Maine from Colombia, had work authorization, and was accosted in his car in the early morning.

“For someone who has already been taken off the streets by ICE agents, seeing something like that makes it all the more scary,” Garvan said.
