text:
Texas Republican leaders are pushing ahead with efforts to crack down on alleged "birth tourism," even as a federal district court has blocked an effort by President Donald Trump to do the same nationwide. A federal judge temporarily blocked Trump's August executive order banning the practice last week.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

The ruling last Wednesday marked the latest defeat for Trump's efforts to curtail or restrict the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which grants U.S. citizenship to virtually anyone born in the United States, regardless of the legal status of the parents.

Trump signed an executive order on the first day of his second term denying automatic U.S. citizenship to anyone whose parents were in the United States illegally. On June 30, the final day of its 2025-26 term, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the definition of birthright citizenship as defined in the Fourteenth Amendment, ruling 6-3 that Trump's order was unconstitutional.

Trump responded by issuing a new pair of executive orders in August. One of these ordered the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to take steps to revoke the visas of any noncitizens coming to the U.S. for the purposes of giving birth and gaining U.S. citizenship for their children, as well as to permanently bar such noncitizens from entering the U.S.

"What the Supreme Court said is if you’re born on U.S. soil, you’re presumptively a citizen unless there’s some sort of a fiction, some reason why you’re not actually here," said Josh Blackman, a professor of constitutional law at South Texas College of Law Houston. "I think what Trump [was] arguing in this order is that if there’s allegations of fraud, that is you didn’t come here under the right circumstances, it’s as if you were really never here ... I don’t see that that clearly follows from the Supreme Court’s opinion."

Judge Deborah Boardman of the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland agreed. Boardman wrote in her decision, issued last Wednesday, that the Supreme Court's June ruling meant that Trump's August executive order "is almost certainly unconstitutional."

"The administration talked so much about birth tourism in their larger attempt to change to birthright citizenship that there are probably some voters who are thinking, ‘Well, why aren’t we seeing more action on this front?,'" said Julia Gelatt, associate director of the U.S. program at the Migration Policy Institute. "I think we may be seeing the administration trying to satisfy the people who they had sort of activated on the issue."

Gelatt said that the prospect of birthright citizenship being abused, particularly by private companies bringing in alleged birth tourists to make a profit, is something about which U.S. citizens have a right to be concerned. But she also said it's important not to exaggerate the extent of the problem.

"It’s a pretty small phenomenon," Gelatt said. "Less than 1% of U.S. births annually can be attributed to birth tourism. There are already policies in place that lead to higher scrutiny of travelers who may be coming while pregnant."

Houston immigration attorney Gordon Quan agreed. He said that even without new action from the Trump administration, U.S. consuls around the world already have wide latitude to prevent people from entering the U.S. for purposes of giving birth.

"It's not easy for anybody to get a visa," Quan said. "Millions of people every year are denied visas arbitrarily. The consul has total authority to give a visa or not. They don’t like the clothes you're wearing. They don’t like an answer you give. It’s a selective process."

How Texas Republican leaders are responding

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton didn't wait for the Supreme Court to issue its ruling on Trump's original birthright citizenship order before making his first move to crack down on alleged birth tourism. In late April, during his primary runoff to capture the Republican nomination for the U.S. Senate from incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, Paxton filed a lawsuit against the Houston-area De'Ai Postpartum Care Center — alleging the facility operated as a maternity hotel.

Paxton charged the center and its proprietors had violated a number of Texas laws in order to encourage Chinese nationals to come to the United States for the purposes of earning citizenship for their children. Those charges included conspiracy, unlawful concealment and harboring in violation of federal law, as well as violations of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

"America is for Americans, not foreigners trying to cheat the system to claim citizenship," Paxton said in a press release in April. "The Center's scheme not only facilitated an invasion of Texas, but it also involved shielding and facilitating violations of immigration law. Birthright citizenship is a scam that threatens national security, and I will do everything in my power to stop unlawful ‘birth tourism' schemes like this one."

De'Ai's attorney, Eric Nichols, declined to be interviewed for this story. But according to court documents, the defendants deny all allegations in the suit.

Immigration attorney Gordon Quan said he doesn't think much of the state's case.

"There’s this idea of anchor babies, the people coming in just to have a child, so the parents can get their green cards," Quan said. "Just because you have a child born in the United States doesn’t mean that you’re allowed to stay. That child cannot sponsor you until they're 21, and if you accrue unlawful presence, you have a 10-year bar to go back out of the country before you can come in."

Paxton is seeking an injunction to shut down the De'Ai Postpartum Care Center, which he said facilitates up to 20 births per day at locations in Houston, Sugar Land, Richmond, and Rosenberg. The next hearing in the case is scheduled to take place in Fort Bend County later this month.

The next moves came almost immediately after the Supreme Court issued its decision on birthright citizenship. State Rep. Brian Harrison, R-Midlothian, issued a call on social media for Gov. Greg Abbott to call a special session of the Texas Legislature to make birth tourism a state felony.

Abbott demurred, but a few days later, he directed the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HSSC) to open an investigation into the Mission Regional Medical Center in the Rio Grande Valley for allegedly promoting birth tourism packages aimed at Mexican nationals.

"Birth tourism is an illegal practice that exploits the extraordinary hospitality that the United States and Texas offer to millions of foreign travelers each year,” Abbott said in a press release in July. “Thousands of foreign travelers come to the United States under false pretenses to give birth and secure citizenship for their children. HHSC must investigate the hospital, a facility it regulates, for any violations of state law and contractual obligations.”

Paxton soon ordered his own investigation into Misson Regional Medical Center, as well as another health care provider in south Texas, Knapp Medical Center. Knapp did not respond to a request for comment, but Mission Regional did.

"We recognize that a very limited marketing campaign may have caused unintended misunderstanding and was immediately discontinued," a spokesperson for Mission Regional said in a statement. "The very limited campaign consisted of only two billboards located near the hospital and a website that generated very little patient volume, produced no financial benefit to the hospital, and was only intended as a service for the community, which is one of the most medically underserved regions of Texas, where approximately 30% of residents are uninsured and access to maternity care continues to decline."

Three weeks after the Supreme Court's decision, Abbott issued his own executive order.

"What I decided to do was to make sure that any agency in the state of Texas involved in whatsoever in providing licensing to any healthcare provider, they must be investigated to determine whether or not they are involved in in birth tourism, and if so take action against them, including what I call the death penalty for a business and that is to pull their license so they would not be able to operate," Abbott told Fox News.

Abbott said Texas would be working hand-in-hand with the Trump administration to crack down on the practice of birth tourism, reporting all the findings of its investigations to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The laws on the books

Lying about one's reason for coming to the U.S. to obtain a visa is already a federal offense. If a noncitizen is found to have come to the U.S. specifically to give birth and concealed that fact during her visa application process, that alone would be grounds for deportation and a ten-year ban on returning to the U.S.

The primary concern of both Texas and the federal government, according to former U.S. Border Patrol agent Ammon Blair, is not individual visa applicants but rather activity by transnational networks involved in human smuggling operations. Blair, who now works as a senior fellow at the conservative Texas Public Policy Foundation, said the most significant such networks are the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and Mexican cartels. He said such operations are extremely lucrative.

"For Chinese nationals we would see sometimes anywhere from $60,000 to $80,000 per person, and for those that are in the Western Hemisphere, maybe $8,000 to $10,000 per person," Blair said. "And so, if you were able to bust an entire network, you’re talking hundreds of thousands of dollars ... [even] millions, depending on how many people you bring into the United States."

Blair pointed to a range of existing federal statutes that could be used to prosecute such transnational operations, including making false statements on a visa application, wire fraud, health care fraud, money laundering and identity theft. But he said such networks are typically well organized and skilled at covering their tracks.

"Do the guys in the ground ... have the ability to actually conduct the investigations to go forward with this and create a case and show an established network to bring forth tourism into the United States, specifically for the idea of getting citizenship?" Blair said. "It’s going to take [not only] the Department of State, DHS, but all those that are actually local law enforcement — county sheriffs, your state law enforcement ... Texas DPS with their division of CID [Criminal Investigations Division] ... or the Texas Rangers."

Even then, Blair said, such networks frequently advertise their services using encrypted apps that are hard to identify and harder to crack. That means making charges stick often requires a lucky break for investigators.

"This is going to be very difficult unless we have those within this chain come forward," Blair said, "and either they are informants, or they come forward through human intelligence and communications, or say that the process went haywire and they felt like they were being trafficked."

text:
The Virginia State University Board of Visitors will meet on Friday, roughly a week after the legal team representing six professors fired late last year filed discrimination complaints against the university with the Virginia Attorney General’s Office of Civil Rights.

Faculty leaders have recommended the instructors, dubbed The Fired Six, be reinstated and cited policy violations in the “reorganization” process that led to their terminations.

Virginia State University faces questions after firing six agriculture research experts

VSU’s firing of the Agricultural Research Station faculty members drew heavy criticism and prompted questions about how the institution could remove tenured faculty members from their offices.

In May, a VSU Faculty Senate subcommittee found that the terminations, carried out by deans and human resource managers, violated the university’s termination authority policy, making them unauthorized and illegitimate.

The policy states that only officials at the vice presidential level or higher have the legal authority to dismiss staff and notify them of their release.

The committee has since determined that the university should restore the professors’ jobs and pay them lost wages.

VSU did not respond to questions about the findings or if it would act on the subcommittee’s recommendation.

Vitalis Temu, one of the fired professors, said VSU’s Board of Visitors, which is responsible for formally discussing and approving any major academic restructuring of university departments, had yet to respond to or take up the findings or recommendations made by his former colleagues, nearly four months after they were published.

“This is a shame for the university,” said Temu.

The controversial VSU dismissals followed federal government changes to agricultural research funding, policy priorities, and USDA operations..

In 2000, VSU was also the subject of another investigation involving the treatment of faculty members by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP).

Following that investigation, AAUP concluded the university violated academic due process and principles of tenure in dismissing two professors when it improperly changed and applied post-tenure review procedures, and placed the burden on the professors to prove they should be retained.

The school also failed to provide the faculty participation and procedural protections required for dismissal of tenured faculty, the AAUP probe found.

Background on the firings

The six faculty members were cut from VSU starting Dec. 16, after being called into individual meetings to discuss the research station’s transformational efforts.

Instead, at the meeting they learned their research programs were being sunset and their jobs were ending immediately.

The former professors said they declined to sign severance agreements at the meeting, largely because they didn’t have sufficient opportunity to review the documents. They said university personnel warned them they would lose any severance if they refused.

When they refused to sign, they were escorted off campus, required to surrender all items belonging to the university like equipment, identification and keys, and issued trespass warnings.

In February, following a rally for the fired faculty members, a university spokeswoman said VSU made “programmatic adjustments” in the College of Agriculture to align research and operations with the university’s strategic goals.

She said personnel matters are confidential and that the institution does not comment on individual employment actions.

More details of the Faculty Senate subcommittee’s findings

In addition to determining that the deans and HR staff who notified the professors of their terminations weren’t qualified to do so, the school’s Faculty Senate developed several recommendations for recourse and future action.

The group’s subcommittee recommended that the institution issue a formal apology, provide financial compensation if the institution cannot return overdue pay, and engage in a conversation with the faculty members to discuss the situation.

Joshua Erlich, the attorney representing the fired faculty members, said his clients are proud to have been vindicated by the faculty committee.

“VSU used this false reorganization as a pretext to terminate respected members of the VSU academic community, marching them out without time to pack up their offices, say farewell to their colleagues, or transition their research,” Elrich said.

“VSU’s conduct was illegal, destructive, and disrespectful. The Fired Six greatly appreciate this first step towards vindication and look forward to being made whole by VSU, whether through settlement or in court.”

text:
Wherever one stands on the issue of wide-scale detention and deportation of immigrants, it’s useful to see who profits and who, besides immigrants, gets hurt. For example, Knox County jails housed 3,500 ICE detainees in 2025. Through “force multiplier” programs like 287(g), limited local law enforcement resources in East Tennessee are diverted to processing, housing and transporting those detained by ICE operations.

Nationally, ICE appropriations in 2025 were $10 billion, a 400% increase since 2003 - money that could have gone to schools, public health and social services, infrastructure or paying down the national debt.

In 2025, $45 billion in tax money went to detention centers alone, with a paltry $800 million to court systems. Clearly, it’s more lucrative to detain people than to identify the mere 3-5% with felony convictions and release those with legitimate claims to residency.

Two corporations, the GEO Group and CoreCivic, run the vast majority of private prisons, which massively profit from the detention system. GEO, with $2 billion in ICE contracts, has seen a 700% surge in profits over 2024. Former GEO executive David Venturella is now acting head of ICE. CoreCivic’s ICE-sourced revenue has doubled. Both companies consistently max out contributions to ICE-favorable campaigns. Brokers for Donald Trump made 29 trades to private prison corporations in his second term.

One wonders if “protecting our borders” is the real issue when so few profit so hugely and national policy is so forceably skewed by financial interest.

Pamela Schoenewaldt, Knoxville, 37919

text:
A few years ago, it would have been unthinkable for a Labour frontbencher to use a statement about the kind of unrest seen in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend to talk about the ‘valid concerns’ that people have about immigration. That the Policing Minister Sarah Jones did that today shows how far the debate has moved: Labour knows that it cannot lump everyone who is angry about the scale of illegal immigration into the same ‘racist’ bucket. She made clear in the first few minutes of her statement to MPs this afternoon that ‘there can be no excuse for threatening behaviour or serious disruption’, and that ‘this government condemns the intimidating and thuggish behaviour shown by some of the protesters this weekend’. But she then moved to say:

None of that is in any way to minimise the very valid concerns of law-abiding people when they see vile criminal gangs exploiting our nation’s generosity, and people making illegal and unnecessary journeys to reach this country.

She added: ‘The frustration we see in our communities today is a product of chaos and crisis in the years that preceded the general election of 2024’. Only when describing one of the groups that organised one of the protests did she use the word ‘racist’, saying that ‘one was clearly organised by a group called the South East Patriots, which I think is part of Patriot Platform, which is a kind of far-right, racist platform’. She then told Portsmouth MP Amanda Martin that she was ‘absolutely right that there were people who were concerned about what they are seeing, but they are very different from the kind of racist, far-right thugs that we also saw over the weekend.’

Jones knows that both her party and the Conservatives are fighting not one another on this, but Reform. The Tories are trying to shrug off the legacy of the Boris-wave, which arguably has left a much deeper scar on the party than the Liz Truss mini-Budget that Labour likes to talk about so much. Labour has only recently managed to find a way of talking about immigration at all, and that is largely because it knows it has to, rather than because it wants to. Neither party, though, has managed to stop the boats or smash the gangs, or live up to any slogan that its leaders have produced over the past decade. And that’s why Jones had to say in response to Reform’s Suella Braverman that ‘of course people are scared and angry about the fact that, as they see it, the borders are not secure’.

She tried once again to point to Braverman’s own time in office as a Conservative as the source of that failed security. She was later accused by SNP MP Pete Wishart of ‘pandering’ to a ‘right wing agenda’, which she denied. But she and her party are having to respond to a much wider reaction in the public that means she cannot talk about these protests in isolation: she has to acknowledge that while there are far-right groups among the protestors, there are many, many more voters who are still highly agitated about the inability to secure the UK border.

name: Policy
title: What comes next for the 1 million people who have lost or will soon lose Temporary Protected Status
description:
At the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, 1.3 million individuals from 17 countries were living and working in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS.
As the administration turns its attention to the few remaining nations, most TPS holders have lost or will soon lose their protection from deportation and their authorization to work.
Many people who lose TPS are not eligible for any other immigration status.
Others may hope to switch to a different status, but most TPS holders cannot obtain a student or employment visa.
Some TPS holders from El Salvador and Sudan have lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years.
text:
At the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, 1.3 million individuals from 17 countries were living and working in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS.

TPS is a humanitarian form of protection from deportation for people who cannot return to their home countries because of an armed conflict, environmental disaster or other extraordinary circumstances.

In 2025, the Trump administration began terminating or not renewing TPS for those countries, making its way through 13 of them. As the administration turns its attention to the few remaining nations, most TPS holders have lost or will soon lose their protection from deportation and their authorization to work. Many will be separated from their families and the communities they have lived in for decades. Some will be forced to return to countries like Afghanistan, Haiti and Syria, all of which are on the U.S. State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list due to war, terrorism or other extreme violence.

As a law scholar who studies immigration detention, I can say that most people with TPS never had a path to anything more permanent, which means, as they face deportation, they have little recourse.

Challenges in court

In the fall of 2025, the Trump White House announced that it would not renew Syrian or Haitian TPS; Syria’s would expire in 60 days, Haiti’s in February 2026. Lower courts blocked both terminations, triggering appeals that took the cases to the Supreme Court.

In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled that federal courts cannot review most challenges to a TPS termination because, in the original 1990 law creating TPS, Congress barred judicial review of the decision to give a country TPS – or extend or end it.

James Percival, the general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, celebrated the decision, saying “Temporary Protected Status was always supposed to be temporary and can be canceled at the appropriate time.”

But the ruling means no court can consider whether a cancellation is, in fact, “appropriate,” or whether it follows the law.

Unanswered questions

When Congress passed TPS as part of the Immigration Act of 1990, it was responding to a specific failure: the ad hoc and inconsistent use of something called Extended Voluntary Departure, which permitted a noncitizen to remain in the U.S. regardless of their immigration status.

That discretionary relief allowed some displaced Salvadorans to remain in the U.S. during their country’s civil war in the 1980s, but its application was arbitrary and often discriminatory. Because the U.S. backed the Salvadoran government, Salvadorans were denied both Extended Voluntary Departure and asylum more than 90% of the time – not for lack of merit but because of the government they were fleeing.

Congress recognized a humanitarian need for more uniform protection for people who, like Salvadorans, faced a return to violence or extreme danger but were not covered by narrow asylum laws that require proof of targeted persecution.

A new protected status would “standardize the procedure for granting temporary stays of deportation,” Representative Sander Levin explained at the time.

“Refugees, spawned by the sad and tragic forces of warfare, should not be subject to the vagaries of our domestic politics as well,” Levin added. When the 1990 Immigration Act passed, El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS.

Congress avoided placing time limits on these new TPS designations, leaving that to the discretion of the presidential administration, which would evaluate a country’s humanitarian needs at least every 18 months. Whether TPS holders should ever gain something more permanent was left for future congressional action.

No next step

Not every person from a TPS-designated country is eligible for it. Anything that disqualifies someone from asylum – national security concerns, persecuting others or criminal history – also disqualifies them from TPS.

Congress did not want to incentivize unlawful immigration. For that reason, it wrote the law in such a way that TPS itself could not lead to permanent residence. Lawful permanent residents are eligible to become citizens after five years. TPS recipients, though living in the U.S. lawfully, are not classified as lawful permanent residents.

Congress has since passed laws creating a pathway to permanent residence for certain nationalities, including some with TPS – the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act, for example. It did not do so for most.

TPS designations for some countries have ended after a few years, like Rwanda and Guinea; others have been renewed for decades, like El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. Over the years, TPS became a kind of limbo status, dependent on each presidential administration’s regular evaluation of a country’s humanitarian conditions – and on Congress to turn TPS into a pathway to lawful permanent residence. For most, the latter never happened.

What happens when TPS ends?

Many people who lose TPS are not eligible for any other immigration status.

Lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a “green card,” is mainly available in three ways: through a close family relationship, like being married to a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident; through a job that requires special skills, like being a professional soccer player; or through asylum status.

Even if a person can apply for permanent residence, their immigration history, such as entering the U.S. without a visa or remaining in the U.S. without lawful status for a certain time, may be a permanent barrier.

TPS holders are given at least 60 days’ notice before termination takes effect, at which point they lose authorization to work and become undocumented, meaning they can be arrested by immigration officers at any time. There is little they can do in those 60 days that would allow them to lawfully remain in the U.S.

A TPS holder who has been continuously present in the U.S. for more than two years has a right to an immigration hearing before removal, where they may be able to apply for asylum or other relief. Others may hope to switch to a different status, but most TPS holders cannot obtain a student or employment visa. Some would have to apply from outside the U.S., some face years of quota backlogs, and some are from countries under a travel ban.

Past immigration violations or insufficient financial resources would also disqualify them. Most significantly, TPS holders are unlikely to convince an immigration officer that they intend to return home after their visa’s purpose is complete, as most visas require – especially someone from a country in distress due to violence or environmental disaster, the reason they have TPS in the first place.

Some 300,000 people from El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Lebanon are set to lose status this year. Ukraine and Lebanon are in active war, so terminating TPS means deporting those people to war zones, which is what TPS was meant to prevent. Some TPS holders from El Salvador and Sudan have lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years.

Perhaps the 1990 Congress did not anticipate that individuals with TPS would make the U.S. their home for so long. Whatever it envisioned, it did not limit TPS to a fixed time. In my analysis, Percival’s assertion that TPS was always meant to be temporary is not, by itself, an “appropriate” reason to end protection.

As Justice Elena Kagan stated in her dissent to the recent Supreme Court ruling, even if TPS does not promise “never-ending humanitarian protection,” the end of it for certain individuals – like the plaintiffs in Mullin v. Doe – could deliver them to “devastating, and indeed life-threatening, injury.”

Jean Lantz Reisz, Clinical Associate Professor of Law, Co-Director, USC Immigration Clinic, University of Southern California

text:
BENNER TOWNSHIP — Penn State’s airport has seen a dramatic surge in flights chartered by ICE to move people between detention centers in the United States.

While ICE has said such transfers are necessary for operational reasons such as bed space, immigration experts claim the practice is intended to cut detainees off from loved ones, wear them down, and make it harder to pursue legal challenges.

The State College Regional Airport is a roughly 40-minute drive from the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, the largest immigration detention facility in the Northeast. Since the beginning of the Trump administration, the facility’s average daily population has increased. Detainees and their advocates allege poor-quality food, inadequate healthcare, and inhumane conditions.

As part of its work to fulfill President Donald Trump’s campaign promise to “carry out the largest domestic deportation operation in American history,” ICE has dramatically expanded its Air network by growing its fleet of planes, strengthening partnerships with charter airlines, and widening its network of airports.

In 2025, the State College Regional Airport serviced just two ICE flights. Through July of this year, that number rose dramatically to 107, according to data from advocacy group Human Rights First.

Stay informed

Sign up for Talk of the Town, an update of the news that matters to your community — from the PA Wilds to Happy Valley.

Email address

Penn State owns both the State College Regional Airport and the Penn State Aviation Center. The former serves commercial flights, and the terminal is owned and operated by the Centre County Airport Authority. The latter is a fixed-base operator run by the university that serves private flights with fueling, hangar storage, and aircraft maintenance.

“There are no contracts between the airport and DHS/ICE. We do not have specific details about charter flights as we are limited by what the commercial charter company operating flights communicates to the airport,” said Wyatt DuBois, senior director of university public relations. “However, it appears there has been an increase in charter flights associated with DHS/ICE.”

ICE flights are handled like any chartered or corporate aircraft arriving at the airport, he told Spotlight PA in an email. Charter companies or brokers typically provide aircraft information and an estimated arrival time but not the name of the individual or entity arranging, or on board, the flight.

Like all airports that receive federal funding, the State College airport is required to comply with Federal Aviation Administration guidelines on accepting flights, DuBois told Spotlight PA in an email.

Aviation experts agreed with Penn State, telling Spotlight PA the airport can legally refuse flights only over indiscriminate safety concerns.

“If they have federal funding, they don’t have much of a leg to stand on legally to stop the flights from coming in,” said Frank Turney, a law professor at the University of Maryland and a solo aviation law practitioner for over 30 years.

When airports accept grants from the FAA, they are required by federal law to ensure “the airport will be available for public use on reasonable conditions and without unjust discrimination.” The only exception is if they’re unable to safely accept an aircraft.

Should an airport refuse ICE flights, the FAA can pursue several types of punishment, Turney said, ranging from fines to the freezing of federal funds in the pipeline. King County, Washington, was ordered by a federal court to accept deportation flights after it attempted to block them.

The FAA didn’t respond to several requests to comment for this story. ICE didn’t respond to multiple requests and then directed Spotlight PA to the Department of Homeland Security, which didn’t respond to questions by the newsroom’s deadline.

Meanwhile, Penn State has taken steps in recent months to get out of the airport business.

On Feb. 26, the university’s Board of Trustees unanimously voted to advance the transfer of the airport’s operating assets to the county authority. “Our fundamental mission as an institution of higher education is to provide a world-class education to our students,” Sara Thorndike, Penn State’s chief financial officer, said in a statement at the time. “Operation of the airport, while vital to the continued success of the university, does not directly support that core educational mission.”

Considering the current speed of negotiations, that transfer could take one to two years, a Centre County Airport Authority official said at a recent meeting.

At that same Aug. 27 meeting, about a dozen concerned residents gathered to oppose the flights.

One resident told the board during public comment that he was shocked to learn the airport had become a hub for ICE flights: “I would hope that you stop this, and I, just in good conscience, can’t be a resident here and let this happen.”

Authority Chair Chris Groshel told attendees that the airport authority is responsible only for the main terminal building and the parking lot.

“We don’t even know what’s going on,” Groshel said of ICE flights at the airport. “It’s not our area of control.”

‘ICE Air’ continues to grow

The number of people detained and deported under Trump has soared compared to his predecessor, with many arrests targeting people who do not have criminal convictions. DHS claims to have deported 675,000 people during Trump’s first year back in office.

ICE’s purse has also grown dramatically under the Trump administration. As of the end of June 2026, ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection had $152 billion in available funding. Some of that money is being used to expand ICE’s network of detention centers, though efforts to convert warehouses in Pennsylvania were later abandoned.

A pivotal part of the agency’s deportation infrastructure is ICE Air, which the agency says “facilitates the transfer and removal of aliens via commercial airlines and chartered flights.”

In July, ICE conducted 2,159 enforcement flights, including a record 329 removal flights to 37 countries, up 14% from the previous month and 59% from July 2025.

However, the vast majority of flights are domestic transfers or so-called “shuffle flights,” which move people to and between detention centers and deportation staging facilities across the United States. These shuffle flights reached a monthly record of 1,363 in July, a 75% year-over-year change, according to data from Human Rights First.

State College Regional Airport has been receiving ICE flights since at least 2025, Human Rights First’s data dashboard shows, but the number has dramatically risen. During the first seven months of this year, 107 ICE flights have flown into and out of State College — the 18th most flights of the 147 airports used for ICE enforcement, according to the nonprofit.

Routine ICE flights arrive at and depart from the airport three to four times a week. Most of those flights go to Alexandria, Louisiana, a main deportation staging facility.

Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee, and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the increase in domestic shuffle flights can be attributed to parallels in ICE arrests.

“Flights have just continued to increase month by month, and with the amount of funding — with the blank check that this administration has worked with Congress to give ICE the authority to carry out flights and other operations — I think we’re going to only see them increase,” Arvey said.

ICE has said these shuffle flights create bed space at crowded facilities and transport people with removal orders to deportation hubs, but immigration experts say the transfers are just another tool to isolate people who are detained and discourage them from fighting for release.

People detained by ICE can file petitions for habeas corpus, which require the government to justify why someone is being held. In most cases, those petitions must be filed in the federal district where the detainee is physically confined. Every transfer changes where that petition must be filed.

For those who can afford lawyers, no-notice shuffle flights give them little opportunity to contact their attorney. This, along with barriers to phone access while detained, makes it next to impossible for people to fight their cases, said Nancy Hiemstra, a professor at Stony Brook University who researches U.S. immigration enforcement policies.

“It is totally by design to deport people quickly,” Hiemstra said. “It means that a lot of mistakes will be made, but that is intentional. The Trump administration just wants to get people out.”

Fetaine Seddighzadeh, a special projects consultant at Human Rights First, echoed that argument. Being transported back and forth from facilities, and separated from legal representatives and support networks, discourages people who are detained, Seddighzadeh said.

People are given little to no notice when they’re selected to board a flight, Hiemstra said, calling this typical of the detention experience. For morning flights, they’re usually woken in the middle of the night, moved to a holding room with others, and kept in shackles. They are often crowded for hours in places with nowhere to lie down, sit, or use the bathroom.

“Often, the run-up to getting on to a flight is pretty awful,” Hiemstra said.

It’s common for people on flights to experience a range of abuses, such as not being given food or water for long periods of time, not being allowed to go to the bathroom, or being shackled at length, she added.

Depending on the destination of the flight, people can be in shackles for several hours, including while at the detention facility before boarding a bus to the airport, during the shuttle ride from the detention center to the airport, and the shuttle to their destination.

Spotlight PA previously spoke to a Berks County man detained by ICE for 45 days, who was flown from State College to Louisiana, then back again, with no information on where he was being taken. He was twice woken in the middle of the night and driven to the airport, fearing he would be deported to Mexico.

“They put a chain around us and tied it to our handcuffed hands, and they also handcuffed our feet throughout the whole transport process. Sometimes, when you stop and think about it, it feels inhumane,” Erasmo Zavala, who later won his release through the courts, said. “They treat you as if you really were some kind of criminal. But what kind of criminal dedicates himself to his family and mostly goes from work to home?”

Spotlight PA’s A.J. Rao contributed reporting.

Can human rights survive the current onslaught?
Or do the rule of law and human rights provide vital bulwarks to humanise, or even potentially reimagine migration governance?

Chair: Samantha Knights KC, Matrix Speakers: Ahmed Aydeed, Deighton Pierce Glynn Professor Siobhán Mullally, Established Professor of Human Rights Law; Director, Irish Centre for Human Rights, University of Galway; former United Nations Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons.
text:
Matrix, the Bonavero Institute of Human Rights and the Refugee Studies Centre (University of Oxford), and the Sutherland School of Law (University College Dublin) are co-hosting a series of webinars to explore the contested relationship between the rule of law, human rights and migration governance.

Commencing on 7 October 2026, the series will bring together experts from legal practice, advocacy, and academia to share expert insights into contemporary contestations across a range of fields – clarifying how and why political actors distort and undermine human rights commitments, and exploring whether current systems differentiating refugees, victims of trafficking and other migrants are fit for purpose. Are universalist commitments part of the problem or the solution in the face of anti-migrant politics and xenophobic policy reflexes? Can human rights survive the current onslaught? Or do the rule of law and human rights provide vital bulwarks to humanise, or even potentially reimagine migration governance?

Episode 1: After Chișinău and the EU Pact on Asylum and Migration: human rights, the ECHR and migration

Date: Wednesday 7 October 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

In the context of growing political pressure to restrict the already very limited rights of refugees and migrants, this webinar will examine the Council of Europe’s May 2016 Chișinău Declaration and the EU Pact on Asylum and Migration of June 2016. Our speakers will consider these recent legal developments and whether existing legal safeguards embedded in international and domestic law remain capable of protecting the rights of refugees and migrants in a challenging political climate.

Chair:

Professor Philip Leach, Middlesex University & Matrix

Speakers:

Professor Başak Çalı, Bonavero Institute of Human Rights

Professor Alice Donald, Middlesex University

Professor Andrew Forde, Dublin City University, Chairperson, Irish Refugee Council, Member, Irish Human Rights & Equality Commission

Episode 2:The Refugee Convention at 75 – Fatally limited or vitally focused?

Date: Wednesday 28 October 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

The 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees was drafted 75 years ago. It has evolved through formal additions (the 1967 Protocol), expansion (regional instruments in Africa and Latin America), and human rights driven evolutive interpretation. This webinar explores whether it is fit for purpose – does it meet the challenge to protect those fleeing war and conflict and climate crises? What additional sources of international protection are available or needed? What are the implications of current containment practices and the erosion of international protection?

Chair:

Eleanor Mitchell, Matrix

Speakers:

Professor Cathryn Costello, UCD & Matrix

Professor Catherine Briddick, Refugee Studies Centre, University of Oxford

Randhir Gayan Wanigasekara, UNHCR London

Episode 3: Is the international/domestic framework for trafficking effective?

Date: Wednesday 4 November 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

International, regional and domestic laws on trafficking aim to prevent trafficking, protect victims and ensure prosecution of perpetrators. This webinar explores whether the current regime meets its stated purposes, and whether anti-trafficking measures work when confronted with increasingly oppressive migration controls.

Chair:

Samantha Knights KC, Matrix

Speakers:

Ahmed Aydeed, Deighton Pierce Glynn

Professor Siobhán Mullally, Established Professor of Human Rights Law; Director, Irish Centre for Human Rights, University of Galway; former United Nations Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons.

Dr Maayan Niezna, University of Liverpool

Episode 4: Migration for work and education – myths and realities

Date: Wednesday 18 November 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

Migration for work and study are the most significant forms of migration in terms of numbers, including to the UK and Ireland. This webinar will explore the myths and realities surrounding the law and policy in these fields, examining the trade-offs in immigration policy, including the implications of temporariness for the right to work and human rights of migrants. Are temporariness and selectivity desirable or necessary features in this field, or a mask for precarity and discrimination? What would a human-rights based immigration policy look like?

Chair:

Professor Cathryn Costello, UCD & Matrix

Speakers:

Professor Diamond Ashiagbor, University of Birmingham & Matrix

Madeleine Sumption, Director, Migration Observatory, University of Oxford

Professor Martin Ruhs, Migration Policy Centre, European University Institute

Episode 5: The Rule of Law in Reimagining Immigration Law & Enforcement

Date: Wednesday 2 December 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

The ideal of the rule of law is poorly institutionalised in immigration law and enforcement. In this final seminar, we invite speakers to reflect on how the rule of law could be used to reimagine immigration law and enforcement, by taking state violations more seriously, tempering the coercive power of the state, enabling migrants to legalise their status, or even questioning the conception of sovereignty underpinning contemporary borders.

Chair:

Professor Cathryn Costello, UCD & Matrix

title: Supreme Court to consider unresolved proportionality question in EU deportation appeals
description:
Does national law preclude EU law protections having a role?
The Upper Tribunal (write-up here) initially held that while substantive EU rights are not imported into national law for post-Brexit conduct, some procedural protections still are.
Losing, or not exercising, the right of appeal under the regulations risks undermining the person’s position if the human rights appeal is successful.
EU proportionality The Court of Appeal had to grapple with what the correct reading of Articles 20 and 21 of the Withdrawal Agreement was.
The appellants argued that this meant following national legislation, but subject to an EU proportionality assessment.
text:
The Supreme Court has granted the appellants permission to appeal the Court of Appeal’s decision in Vargova and Molnar v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] EWCA Civ 31. The case will determine how to apply the Withdrawal Agreement to people with status under the EU Settlement Scheme who face deportation following criminal offences committed after 31 December 2020. Does national law preclude EU law protections having a role?

The Upper Tribunal (write-up here) initially held that while substantive EU rights are not imported into national law for post-Brexit conduct, some procedural protections still are. This included the right to be notified of a decision, to an effective remedy, and to a fair hearing, but not the EU principle of proportionality.

The Court of Appeal (write-up here) agreed that proportionality does not apply, but it did not go on to resolve the broader question of whether national law now applies exclusively.

The right of appeal

The decisions under appeal in these cases were ‘stage 1’ notices, not refusals of human rights claims. These attract a right of appeal under regulation 6 of the Immigration (Citizens’ Rights Appeals) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020, which allows a person with leave under the EU Settlement Scheme to appeal a decision to deport them.

On 25 June 2025, before the Court of Appeal hearing, the Home Secretary added regulation 6(1A), which defined a deportation decision as one made only after the person has been invited to make representations against deportation. So, not the first notice sent out. In practice, the Home Office now tends to attach the right of appeal to the refusal of the human rights claim itself (the ‘stage 2’ decision).

Anyone advising an EU national with status under the EU Settlement Scheme who has received a stage 2 decision should check they have been given, and have exercised, a right of appeal under regulation 6, whether granted at stage 1 or stage 2. The Court of Appeal held that a stage 1 decision does restrict a person’s residence rights under the Withdrawal Agreement, and so the appeal under regulation 6 should not be ignored.

If the Home Secretary has failed to consider important information already available to her (such as a trafficking decision or the correct position on the EU application) in issuing the decision it is possible to mount an effective challenge. It is vital to confirm, from the original indictment if possible, the dates of all offences relied on by the Home Secretary. This is an area prone to error. Sentences are not always passed chronologically so a later sentence could be for pre-31 December 2020 conduct. If the Home Secretary relies on such conduct, a person’s case must be considered under the public policy grounds set out in Chapter VI of the Citizens’ Rights Directive.

If a stage 2 decision, headed as a refusal of a human rights claim, also contains a right of appeal under regulation 6, this should be exercised, even if late, to ensure that the person has a remedy under the Withdrawal Agreement. At the very least this will confirm that the person is covered by the Withdrawal Agreement, however the protections come to be interpreted in practice. Losing, or not exercising, the right of appeal under the regulations risks undermining the person’s position if the human rights appeal is successful.

EU proportionality

The Court of Appeal had to grapple with what the correct reading of Articles 20 and 21 of the Withdrawal Agreement was. Article 20(2) allows residence to be restricted for post-Brexit conduct ‘in accordance with national legislation’, while Article 21 imports certain safeguards from the Citizens’ Rights Directive for decisions falling within the scope of the Withdrawal Agreement. The appellants argued that this meant following national legislation, but subject to an EU proportionality assessment.

The Court of Appeal disagreed. Mixing the two regimes risked inconsistent interpretations across member states. It also rejected the idea that proportionality counts as a ‘procedural safeguard’ capable of being imported under Article 21, as Article 21 does not confer an independent right to a proportionality assessment. The Supreme Court will have to look at how the safeguards in Article 21 should be applied.

Staying cases already in the tribunals

After the Court of Appeal’s judgment, the Upper Tribunal was reluctant to stay cases pending the outcome of the application to appeal to the Supreme Court. Now that permission has been granted, the tribunal appears more willing to stay cases where an appellant’s pre-Brexit residence, and the scope of any surviving EU law protections, form a substantial part of their case.

What difference might a positive outcome for the appellants make?

Some may be tempted to wonder what might change if the Supreme Court finds that decisions to deport EU nationals for post-Brexit conduct must comply with the EU principle of proportionality after all. The answer depends on whether the parties to the Withdrawal Agreement envisaged removing all consideration of a person’s historical integration in the UK under free movement law, and whether such integration is capable of reducing or outweighing the public interest in deportation.

The Supreme Court will now look at these arguments afresh in January 2027.

This article was co-authored by Julian Stern and William Shelley. Julian Stern represents Ms Vargova and Mr Molnar. William Shelley is a solicitor at Turpin Miller LLP. He is a member of the public law team and has been closely involved in the cases of Vargova and Molnar.
